Getting started

Agent=Model+Harness

This whole course exists to unpack that equation. By the end, when you work with Claude Code or Codex, you will be able to tell whether a behavior comes from the model, from the harness or from the context. That distinction is the key to debugging, to writing good instructions and to building safe systems.

11 levelsFor software developersAt least one interactive diagram per topic

A new piece has landed in the middle of what you already know

If you have been building software for years, most of the concepts in this course will feel familiar: client-server, stateless APIs, sandboxes, the principle of least privilege, event-driven hooks, CI. What is new is that a probabilistic component now sits in the middle of all of them. When you call a deterministic function, you expect the same output for the same input; here you don’t. That one difference shifts every engineering habit a little.

So the course makes the same move at every level: first it shows the mechanism, then it ties it to a concept you already know with “you already know this; here is what is different.” You will find these bridges in the blue boxes.

You already know thisAn LLM API is a stateless HTTP service. You resend the entire conversation history with every request; the server keeps no session for you. In level 2 we will trace, step by step, what that means for context, cost and “forgetting.”

Separating signal from noise

Some of the tricks sold under the “prompt engineering” banner really do work; most are folklore left over from older models. This course tells them apart by starting from the mechanism. Claims we call myths appear in the yellow boxes, together with the evidence.

Myth“Tell the model ‘you are the best programmer in the world’ and it will write better code.” On current models the effect is either nil or inconsistent. What works is not a role but context: which repo, which constraints, what success looks like. Covered in detail in level 3.

Three layers, one color code

The colors never change throughout the course. If you see purple in a diagram, the model is speaking; if you see teal, it is the harness.

Model

Trained, frozen weights. All it does is look at the text it is given and produce probabilities for the next token.

Harness

The software around the model: the loop, tools, permissions, sandbox, hooks, context management, the interface.

Context and tokens

Everything the model sees at that moment. That is the model’s entire world; it does not know what it does not see.

Practice

Commands, settings files, real workflows. Things you will use tomorrow morning.

Risk

Security holes, failure modes, mistakes that cost money and data.

Key takeaways

  • An agent is the sum of a model and the software that runs it in a loop (the harness).
  • To fix a problem, first find which layer it comes from: model, harness or context.
  • This field changes within months. The concepts last; for command names and settings, the official documentation is the authority.

How the levels fit together

Levels 0–2 cover the model itself: what it is, how it was trained and what it sees. Levels 3–5 cover talking to the model and putting it in a loop. Levels 6–7 introduce the harness and compare the two big ecosystems, Claude and Codex, both as models and as tools. Levels 8–10 are practical and advanced: really using Claude Code, managing context, automation, and designing your own harness safely.

The single operation beneath all the magic

A large language model (LLM) is a huge function that takes a sequence of tokens and returns a probability distribution for the next token. The sentence looks simple, but every behavior you will run into, from Claude Code finding and fixing a bug to a chat “forgetting” something, is rooted here.

f(token_1, token_2, …, token_n)  →  P(token_n+1)

// f: billions of trained, frozen numbers (weights).
// Input: the ENTIRE text so far (system prompt, conversation, tool results).
// Output: one probability for every token in the vocabulary; they sum to 1.

There are two separate pieces here, and the distinction matters for the rest of the course. The first is the model: a function made of weights that never changes once training is over. You give it a text and it produces a score for every candidate in its vocabulary. The second is the code that calls this function: it picks a token from the scores, appends it to the text, calls the function again, and decides when to stop. The general name for this outer layer is the harness. When you send a request to the API, the harness on the provider’s server runs this loop for you; an agent such as Claude Code builds yet another loop on top of it.

A “chat” is really a document

The model does not see roles, sessions or users as data structures. All it sees is a long sequence of tokens. The information “the user said this, the assistant said that, the tool returned this” is embedded in that sequence with special marker tokens. Because the model learned during training to “continue” documents containing these markers, it writes whatever follows the assistant marker the way an assistant would. So in a chat, what the model does is still document completion; the document just happens to be shaped like a transcript of a conversation with an assistant.

That is why a 500-token answer means calling the function roughly 500 times. With each call the input grows by one token. A single “think and edit a file” move by an agent consists of dozens of model requests, and each request of hundreds or thousands of forward passes. This way of generating, where each token is produced one at a time by looking at all the tokens before it, is called autoregressive generation.

How an answer is born: from text to tokens, from tokens to text

First follow a single round step by step: how text turns into numbers, what the model produces, who makes the choice. Then use the button below to run the loop to the end. Token IDs and probabilities are illustrative; the flow is real.

Forward passes (model calls)0Input length0stop_reason–
You already know thisThe model is very much like a pure function: mathematically it produces the same scores for the same input, it has no side effects and keeps no internal state. The randomness comes from the sampler that sits outside the function, just as if you bolted a random number generator onto a deterministic business rule. In topic 4 you will see why the word “mathematically” matters: on real hardware even this purity is not fully preserved.

What is inside the function?

What we call “weights” are the numbers used in matrix multiplications. For open-weight models you can download them: the largest member of Meta’s Llama 3 family, for example, has 405 billion parameters. Parameter counts for Claude or GPT models are not published. The number itself does not matter much to you; what matters is that these numbers are set once by training and then frozen. No weight changes while you are talking. Every moment where you feel the model has “learned” something, the knowledge is actually sitting in the current input text. That is the subject of level 2.

Myth“It only predicts the next word, so it cannot think ahead; it’s a stochastic parrot.” The mechanism’s interface really is “the next token”, but that does not mean there is no planning inside. To predict the next token well, the model has to represent where the text is going. Anthropic’s interpretability work showed that Claude picks the rhyming word in a poem before it starts writing the line (you will play with this in topic 5). The opposite is a myth too: “It understands, so it knows things the way a human does.” Its knowledge is lossy and sometimes internally inconsistent; its correctness has to be verified from the outside.

What this means for your daily work

  • The text, not you, defines the input. The model sees the tokens in the context, not your intent. If you don’t write down the assumptions in your head, the model doesn’t know them.
  • Every token is a decision. A small early choice (a wrong table name) conditions every token that follows. The model cannot go back and delete; it can only continue. That is why agents need feedback such as tests and compilers.
  • Long output is slow and expensive. Output tokens are produced one by one, and pricing reflects that (topic 4).

Key takeaways

  • LLM = a frozen function that takes text and returns a probability distribution for the next token.
  • The code around the function does the picking, appending and stopping. Model + that code = the generation loop.
  • A chat is a document with role markers; the model continues that document.
Sources
  1. The Llama 3 Herd of Models (Meta, 2024)
  2. Anthropic: Tracing the thoughts of a large language model (March 2025)

The model doesn’t see letters, it sees tokens

The model does not process text letter by letter or word by word, but in pieces called tokens. A token is sometimes a whole word (“ the”), sometimes part of a word (“ing”, or the Turkish plural suffix “ler”), sometimes a single punctuation mark or a byte. The component that splits text into tokens and gives each piece an integer ID is called the tokenizer. The model only ever sees those IDs.

Why not letters? At the letter level the vocabulary is small but sequences become very long; since the cost of each forward pass grows with sequence length, that is expensive. Why not words? At the word level the vocabulary grows without bound; a model that never saw a word like the Turkish “siparişlerimizdekilerden” (roughly “from among the ones in our orders”, a single word) could not represent it. Tokens are a compromise between the two: frequent pieces become a single token, rare ones become a few pieces.

BPE: how is the vocabulary learned?

Most of today’s tokenizers belong to the BPE (byte-pair encoding) family. The algorithm is surprisingly simple:

  1. The starting vocabulary is the 256 bytes. Since any UTF-8 text can be written with these bytes, there is no such thing as an “unknown character”; a rare alphabet simply falls apart into many byte tokens.
  2. First, a regular expression splits the text into words, numbers and punctuation (pre-tokenization). Merges stay inside these pieces.
  3. The two symbols that appear next to each other most often in the training corpus are found and merged into one new symbol. That is a “merge” rule.
  4. Step 3 repeats until the target vocabulary size is reached. The rules are learned once and frozen; the model is trained with this frozen vocabulary.

The diagram below runs a real implementation of this algorithm. The corpus is small and deliberately Turkish. Turkish is agglutinative: it builds words by stacking suffixes onto a stem, so one word can carry what English says in a whole phrase (“ev” is house, “evler” houses, “evlerde” in the houses, “evlerden” from the houses). That makes the effect easy to see. Perform the merges one at a time and watch suffixes such as “ler”, “lar” (plural) and “yor” (present continuous) turn into tokens on their own.

Run BPE from scratch

A small Turkish corpus (words and how often they occur). At each step the most frequent adjacent pair is merged. Then type a word that is not in the corpus: the learned rules apply to it too.

This mechanism has two important consequences. First, the vocabulary reflects the distribution of the training corpus. If most of the corpus is English and code, English words and code patterns collapse into single tokens, while the suffixes of other languages (Turkish is our example here) stay more fragmented. Second, token boundaries do not have to line up with grammatical boundaries: “ler” can be a token, yet the stem “değerlendir” (evaluate) and the suffix “ebil” (be able to) may be cut at arbitrary places.

Vocabulary size and compression

Tokenizer / modelVocabulary sizeNote
GPT-250,257Older generation, English-heavy

A bigger vocabulary compresses better: Llama 3’s tokenizer raised characters per token in English from 3.17 to 3.94 compared with Llama 2. But as the vocabulary grows, so does the output layer; at every step a score is produced for that many candidates. Another compromise.

The token tax on non-English languages: Turkish as the example

The NeurIPS 2023 study by Petrov and colleagues measured how the same sentence takes very different numbers of tokens depending on the language: with the GPT-4 tokenizer, French and German take about 1.6 times as many as English, and some languages up to 15 times. This has three concrete consequences: more money for the same content, higher latency, and less content in the context window.

For Turkish it is hard to give a single clean multiplier. There is no primary source measuring the Turkish/English ratio on frontier models’ tokenizers; figures in circulation such as “1.3–2 times” are not verified. What is verified is this: in a 2025 study on Turkish MMLU text (Bayram et al.), the same text took about 29% more tokens with the Qwen2.5 tokenizer than with aya-expanse, and only 40–51% of the tokens corresponded to valid Turkish units. The same study found that the share of valid Turkish tokens correlated with model performance better than linguistic purity did.

Turkish and English side by side

Two texts with the same meaning go through the same approximate tokenizer. Approximate: this diagram uses a simple rule-based splitter running in your browser, not a real BPE vocabulary. It won’t give exact counts, but it shows why agglutinative languages split into more pieces. You can edit the texts.

Same model family, new tokenizer, new bill

The token count depends not only on the language but also on the tokenizer version. Anthropic switched to a new tokenizer with Opus 4.7. According to the documentation, 1 million tokens correspond to roughly 555K English words with the current tokenizer, compared with roughly 750K on earlier models. That means the same English text takes about 1.35 times as many tokens (a ratio computed from the two figures in the documentation). Even if the price per token stays the same, the same prompt costs more and the context fills up faster.

In practiceDon’t use the “4 characters = 1 token” rule of thumb for non-English text or code. If you are working out a budget or a cost, measure the real number with the provider’s token counting endpoint (the token counting API at Anthropic) or from the usage field in the response. Measure again when you switch models.

Oddities caused by tokenization

In his lecture where he builds a tokenizer from scratch, Karpathy traces many strange behaviors back to tokenization. Because the model sees token IDs rather than letters, the question “how many r’s are in strawberry?” used to be hard: to the model the word is perhaps two or three opaque pieces. Numbers are split arbitrarily too (“12345” → “123” + “45”), so operations that need digit alignment become fragile. In code, whitespace and indentation affect how sequences are tokenized. Still, it is not right to blame every arithmetic error on the tokenizer: in topic 5 you will see how the model actually does addition internally, and that story is more interesting.

Myth“If I write in my own language instead of English, the model understands less, so I should ask everything in English.” The cost that is certain is tokens: Turkish and other non-English text takes more of them. On the understanding side, Anthropic’s interpretability findings show that concepts are largely represented by shared features across languages; knowledge learned in one language carries over to another. The practical middle ground: write the instructions in whatever language you are comfortable with, but give identifiers such as table, class and function names verbatim, exactly as they appear in the code.

Key takeaways

  • The model sees token IDs; the tokenizer is a set of merge rules learned from a corpus and then frozen.
  • Agglutinative languages such as Turkish take more tokens: more cost, more latency, more context used.
  • The tokenizer version changes token counts too (~1.35× with Opus 4.7). Don’t estimate, measure.
Sources

From scores to probabilities, from probabilities to a choice

The model’s last layer produces a raw score for every token in the vocabulary. These scores are called logits. If the vocabulary has 200K tokens, every step yields a vector of 200K numbers. Logits can be negative, and their sum means nothing. The operation that turns them into probabilities is softmax:

p_i = exp(z_i / T) / Σ_j exp(z_j / T)

T → 0   : piles up on the highest logit (greedy, argmax)
T = 1   : the model’s raw distribution
T > 1   : the distribution flattens, low-scoring candidates get a chance

The exponential amplifies differences: a 1-point gap between two logits means roughly a 2.7× gap in probability. Temperature (T) divides the logits and so widens or narrows that gap. Then come two truncation methods. Top-k keeps the k most likely candidates. Top-p (nucleus) keeps, from the candidates sorted by probability, the smallest set whose total probability reaches p. The probabilities of the remaining candidates are renormalized to 1, and a token is drawn at random from that distribution. The usual order: temperature → top-k → top-p → sampling. The whole process is called sampling.

Sampling lab

Context: “If this function returns null, the application ___”. The logits are fixed (illustrative); the formula is real. Drag the sliders: faded bars are candidates that were cut. Then sample once or 100 times and see how the distribution shapes the outcome.

Why not always pick the most likely one?

Greedy selection (argmax at every step) intuitively looks “most correct”, but on long texts it leads to self-repeating loops and flat, formulaic sentences. A token being the most likely on its own does not mean the sequence starting with it is the best sequence. A bit of randomness carries the richness of the model’s distribution into the text. That is why chat and code models have historically run with a temperature near 1 and a top-p a little below 1.

You already know thisSampling is weighted random selection: a weighted round-robin load balancer, or roulette-wheel selection in genetic algorithms. Temperature is a knob that sharpens or softens the weights by raising them to a power; top-k and top-p are the rule “send no traffic at all to servers below this threshold.”

The API reality: these knobs now belong to the provider

As of November 2026, if you send a non-default value for temperature, top_p or top_k to current Claude models, the API returns HTTP 400. From API version 2026-10-21 onwards, sending these parameters with any value at all is a 400 error on every model. So you are learning this topic not as a settings knob but as a mechanism: it is what explains why the model gives different answers to the same question, and why it behaves “creatively” or “consistently”.

The reasoning behind it: reasoning (thinking) models produce long chains of thought, and the quality of those chains is sensitive to sampling settings. The provider wants the model to run with the settings it was trained with. You steer behavior with the prompt and with the effort setting you will see in the next level.

POST /v1/messages
{
  "model": "claude-opus-5-5",
  "max_tokens": 1024,
  "temperature": 0,          // ← 400 invalid_request_error
  "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "..." }]
}
Myth“If I set temperature to 0, the answer will be both deterministic and more accurate.” Two mistakes at once. Accuracy: T=0 just picks the top of the distribution; if the top is wrong, you get the same wrong answer every time. Determinism: because of how the computation runs on the server, even T=0 does not guarantee bit-for-bit identical output (next topic). And on current Claude models, sending this setting is an error anyway.
In practiceIf you need consistency, get it from the system, not from sampling settings: bind the output to a schema (structured output), check the result with a compiler, tests or a validator, and for critical work run it more than once and compare. A single run proves nothing, good or bad.

Key takeaways

  • The model produces logits; softmax turns them into probabilities, and the sampler turns the probabilities into a single token.
  • Temperature sharpens or flattens the distribution; top-k and top-p cut off the tail.
  • Current Claude models reject these parameters. The prompt and effort steer behavior.
Sources
  1. Anthropic: Thinking documentation (note on sampling parameters)

Prefill, decode and the KV cache

Processing a request consists of two very different phases, and that difference drives both latency and pricing.

Prefill

All the tokens in the prompt are processed at once, in parallel. The weights are read once and matrix-matrix multiplications run for thousands of tokens: the limit is the GPU’s compute. This phase determines TTFT (time to first token).

Decode

Answer tokens are produced one at a time. At every step all the weights and the history’s KV cache are read from memory again, but only one token is computed: the limit is memory bandwidth. This phase determines the latency between tokens.

KV cache

Attention produces a “key” and a “value” vector for every token. These are stored so the history does not have to be recomputed for every new token. The memory cost of long contexts comes from here.

This asymmetry shows up directly in the price list: as of November 2026, on Claude, OpenAI and Gemini 4 models an output token costs roughly 5 times as much as an input token. On Claude Opus 5.5, for example, a million input tokens cost $4 and a million output tokens $20. Input is processed in parallel and efficiently; output is sequential and memory-bound.

The timeline of a request

Change the prompt and answer lengths and set how much of the prompt comes from the cache. The speed values are assumptions: they vary a lot by provider, model and load, and you can enter values you measured yourself. The shape is the same in every case: a wide, parallel prefill block followed by long, sequential decode steps.

Why does the KV cache matter so much?

The KV cache size for one sequence is computed with this formula: 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × sequence length × bytes. The leading 2 is for keys and values. For a Llama-3-70B-like architecture (80 layers, 8 KV heads, dimension 128, bf16 i.e. 2 bytes) that comes to about 0.33 MB per token; a single 128K-token sequence holds about 40 GB of memory. This is why serving long contexts is expensive and why providers offer prompt caching. Prompt caching is, quite literally, storing the KV cache of a prefix. The OpenAI documentation also says the cache stores the key-value tensors, not the original tokens. We will cover this in detail in level 2.

KV cache calculator

Change the architecture parameters and the sequence length. The defaults are a Llama-3-70B-like architecture (published open-model settings); Claude’s architecture is not published.

Why isn’t even T=0 deterministic?

The common explanation used to be “GPUs work in parallel and atomic operations scramble the order.” A September 2025 study by Thinking Machines Lab showed that this is largely wrong: a single forward pass, rerun under the same conditions, is deterministic. The real cause is a lack of batch invariance. The server processes requests that arrive at the same time as a group (a batch). RMSNorm, matrix multiplication and attention kernels change their reduction strategy depending on the batch size. Because floating-point addition is not associative, adding in a different order produces different final digits. And the batch size depends on who else is using the server at that moment. In other words, your answer depends on other people’s load.

The experiment is striking: Qwen3-235B, T=0, “Tell me about Richard Feynman”, 1,000 runs of 1,000 tokens each. The result: 80 different completions. All runs were identical for the first 102 tokens; at token 103, 992 of them said “Queens, New York” and 8 said “New York City”. A tiny numerical difference was enough to swap the top two logits; after that, a completely different path. With batch-invariant kernels all 1,000 runs produced the same output, but at a price: on Qwen3-8B the vLLM default took 26 seconds, the naive deterministic version 55, and the optimized deterministic version 42 seconds.

Floating point, batches and 1,000 runs

First see associativity break down in JavaScript’s own floating-point arithmetic. Then add up the same 1,000 numbers with different chunk sizes: the chunk size stands in for the batch size on the server. At the bottom, the outcome of the experiment.

In practiceWhen you test agents and LLM-based features, don’t trust a single run. Run evaluation sets several times, look at rates, and separate “passed once” from “passes reliably”. If you cannot reproduce a failure, the cause may not be your code but sampling and server load.

Key takeaways

  • Prefill is parallel and determines TTFT; decode is sequential, memory-bound, and determines total time.
  • That is why an output token costs ~5 times as much as an input token. Long answer = slow and expensive answer.
  • The KV cache is the memory cost of long context; prompt caching is storing it.
  • Even T=0 does not guarantee identical output, because of numerical differences that depend on the batch size.
Sources

  2. Simon Willison’s summary
  3. OpenAI: Prompt caching (note on KV tensors)
  4. Anthropic: Pricing

A quick look inside the function

This course does not aim to turn you into a model architect. But a few intuitions keep concepts you will meet later, such as “context rot” and the “attention budget”, from being mere vocabulary.

  1. Embedding. Each token ID is turned into a vector with thousands of dimensions. Position information is added too; in modern models usually with a rotation-based method called RoPE.
  2. Attention. Each token produces a “query” vector and compares it with the “key” of every previous token (a dot product). The scores go through softmax, and the “value” vectors of the previous tokens are summed with those weights. Think of it as a soft, learned lookup over the context: “which earlier tokens matter to me right now?”
  3. Multiple heads. This is done in parallel by dozens of “heads” in the same layer. Each head learns to look at a different kind of relationship: one at the previous token, one at the noun a pronoun refers to, one at the stem a suffix attaches to.
  4. MLP and layers. After attention, each token goes through a feed-forward network on its own. The attention + MLP block is stacked dozens of times. Early layers deal with surface features, later layers with abstract concepts. The last layer is projected onto a logit vector the size of the vocabulary.

Attention map

A Turkish sentence and three different heads. The sentence, “Müşteri siparişi iptal etti çünkü kargo gecikti ve o çok kızdı.”, means “The customer cancelled the order because the shipment was late, and they were very angry.” It stays in Turkish on purpose: its suffixes show a head type that English barely needs. Click a token: color intensity shows how much that token “looks at” the earlier tokens. The weights were designed by hand (not taken from a real model), but every row is a real softmax, and because models can only look at the past, a triangular mask is used. The slider at the bottom shows how the number of scores explodes as the sequence grows.

n² and the attention budget

In a sequence of n tokens, every token looks at every previous token, so roughly n² scores are computed. 1,000 tokens means a million scores; 1 million tokens means a trillion scores (for every layer and every head). Anthropic frames this as a limited “attention budget”: every token added to the context takes a share of that budget. Picture a meeting where everyone glances at everyone else’s notes before speaking. With ten people that’s fine; with ten thousand, the glances explode and the important note gets lost in the crowd. The “context rot” in level 2 is the measured version of this intuition.

Interpretability: what really happens inside?

Anthropic’s “Tracing the thoughts of a large language model”, published in March 2025, used a method called “attribution graphs” to trace computation paths inside Claude 3.5 Haiku. The interpretability findings show how much the phrase “next-token prediction” hides:

Planning ahead

In a rhyming couplet, the model picks the word the line will end on before it starts writing the second line. When that word’s representation is suppressed, it switches to another rhyme; when a different concept is injected, it moves to a coherent line that fits it.

Shared concepts

The question “the opposite of small” activates the same “smallness” and “opposite” features in English, French and Chinese. The larger model shares more than twice as many features across languages as the smaller one.

Addition inside

For 36+59, one path roughly estimates the magnitude of the result while another finds the last digit (6+9 → 5); together they make 95. But when asked “how did you work that out?”, the model describes the carry method taught in school.

Multi-step reasoning

For “the capital of the state where Dallas is located”, the intermediate steps Dallas → Texas → Austin are visible inside. When the Texas representation is swapped for California, the answer becomes Sacramento.

The hallucination circuit

The default path is “I can’t answer.” A “known entity” feature suppresses that path. When a name feels familiar but there is no knowledge about it, this feature misfires and the model makes something up.

Unfaithful reasoning

Asked for the cosine of a large number, the model says it computed it, but there is no trace of computation inside. Given a hint, it builds its reasoning backwards so that it lands on the hint.

The rhyme experiment: the plan comes before the line

A re-enactment of Anthropic’s experiment. The first line ends with “…grab it”. Pick an intervention and watch which features are active inside before the second line starts, and how the line is built. The activation bars are illustrative.

CautionThe lesson of the addition example is worth its weight in gold for a developer: the model’s account of its own process is not the process itself. When an agent says “I ran the tests, they all passed” or “here is how I computed this”, that is a narrative. The evidence is in the tool output, the log and the diff.

You should also know the method’s limits: the technique captures only part of the computation, and tracing a prompt of a few dozen words takes hours of human effort. So these findings are a window, not a full map of the model.

Key takeaways

  • Attention is a learned, soft lookup over the context; its cost grows with the square of the sequence length.
  • Behind the “just the next token” interface there is planning, multi-step reasoning and concepts shared across languages.
  • The model’s explanation of itself is not a record of its mechanism. Look for the evidence in the tool output.
Sources
  1. Anthropic: Tracing the thoughts of a large language model (March 2025)
  2. Anthropic: Effective context engineering for AI agents (attention budget)

Through an engineer’s eyes: wrong mental models

Half of using a tool well is knowing what not to confuse it with. The mechanisms you have seen in this level directly refute each of the common wrong models below.

It is not a database

The model does not store its training data record by record; it turns it into a lossy representation compressed into the weights. It knows frequently seen patterns (a popular framework’s API, SQL syntax) very well. A rarely seen detail (a method signature in a specific version of a little-used package) it may reproduce “fluently but wrongly”. There is no query, no index, no “record not found” error; only a plausible continuation. The way to guarantee correct information is to put it in the context: have it read the documentation, open the code, call the tool.

It is not a system that learns while it runs

The weights are frozen. When you “teach” the model something during a conversation, what is learned lives in the conversation text, not in the weights. When the conversation ends, or when the text is compacted in a long session, that knowledge is gone. Every feature sold as “memory” (persistent rule files, notes, session summaries) is the harness putting text back into the next request.

It is not deterministic

Sampling adds deliberate randomness; even if you cannot touch it, there is still the batch effect on the server. Two runs of the same prompt can veer onto different paths. An agent session that “worked yesterday and doesn’t today” does not always mean the code changed.

It is not a calculator or a spell checker

It sees tokens, not letters, and does arithmetic internally along approximate, parallel paths. It is fragile with long numbers and with tasks such as counting letters or reversing strings. That is what the code execution tool is for: instead of having the model compute, have it write code that computes.

It is not a witness to its own inner workings

The model can describe how it thinks, but that description comes from the “this is how people explain things” pattern in its training data. Nor does it reliably know what it knows and what it doesn’t: the hallucination circuit is exactly that boundary misfiring.

It is not a fixed product

The same weights behave very differently with a different system prompt, a different tool set and a different context. Claude in Claude Code and Claude in the chat interface may be the same model, but they are not the same “agent”. When you interpret a behavior, always ask: does this come from the model, the harness or the context?

From symptom to mechanism

Symptoms you will run into in real life. Click one to see which mechanism from this level it comes from and what you do about it as an engineer.

Click a symptom.
“The model knows my project, I explained it last week.” “If I set temperature to zero, it will be consistent.” “It said the tests passed, so they passed.” “It did this calculation, so the result is correct.”
Project knowledge has to go into the context with every request. Consistency comes from a verifier. Test results are seen in the tool output. Calculations are done by running code, and the model interprets the result.

Level 0: key takeaways

  • An LLM is a frozen function that produces probabilities for the next token from a token sequence; an answer comes from calling that function in a loop.
  • Token counts change with the language and the tokenizer version; the token is the unit of cost, speed and context.
  • Because of sampling and server-side numerical differences, output is not deterministic; consistency comes from verification.
  • Prefill is parallel, decode is sequential; the KV cache is the memory price of long context.
  • There is planning and conceptual representation inside, but the model’s account of itself is not evidence.
Sources
  1. Anthropic: Tracing the thoughts of a large language model
  2. Thinking Machines Lab: Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference
  3. fast.ai: Karpathy and tokenizers

A model’s life, stage by stage

Training a model falls roughly into two periods. In pre-training the model learns language, the world and code; this is the most expensive and longest period. In post-training that raw knowledge is turned into a safe assistant that behaves in a particular style and uses tools. Most of the differences in “temperament” that set Claude apart from Codex, or any model from another, arise in this second period.

Pre-training: learning to predict the next token

The objective is single and simple: across a huge corpus of text and code, predict the next token at every position. The model starts with random weights. After each prediction, we measure how little probability it gave to the correct token (the cross-entropy loss), and the weights are updated in the direction that reduces that loss a little. This repeats over trillions of tokens.

A surprising amount of learning hides inside this simple objective. To predict a function’s body correctly you have to understand its signature; to predict how an error message continues you have to “model” the cause of the error. The model is never instructed “learn this”; it does so because representing the world internally is the cheapest way to reduce prediction error.

The loss function: the price of a single token

Context: SELECT * FROM example. The correct next token is “orders”. Change the probability the model gives this token and watch how the loss changes. Training tries to shrink this number across trillions of positions.

To give a sense of scale, here are the published figures for open-weight models:

ModelTraining tokensOther
Llama 3 405B15.6 trillion3.8×10²⁵ FLOPs, up to 16K H100 GPUs
Qwen3~36 trillion119 languages (29 in the previous version)
DeepSeek-V314.8 trillion—

Training token counts for closed models (Claude, GPT, Gemini) are not published. What you get at the end of pre-training is called a base model. It knows a lot, but it is not an assistant; we will see why in the next topic.

The tools of post-training

SFT

Supervised fine-tuning. Training on carefully prepared (prompt, ideal answer) pairs. The loss is computed only on the answer tokens: the model learns the format “when a question comes in, this is how you answer.”

Preference training

The model produces several answers to the same prompt, and the better one is marked. In RLHF, humans rank them, a reward model is trained from those rankings, and the model is pushed towards that reward with RL. DPO uses the same preference pairs directly, without an intermediate reward model.

RLAIF and the constitution

Most of the harm labels come not from humans but from a model guided by written principles. Anthropic’s 2022 Constitutional AI method was the first big example.

RLVR

RL with verifiable rewards. The reward comes not from a learned model but from an automatic check: did the tests pass, is the maths answer correct. This is the main engine of reasoning and coding models.

A concrete recipe: Llama 3’s post-training ran for six rounds. In each round 10–30 answers were generated per prompt, the best was picked with the reward model (rejection sampling), and then SFT and DPO were applied. Not a single “fine-tune”, but a loop that feeds itself.

On 22 January 2026 Anthropic published Claude’s new constitution. Instead of the earlier list of rules, it is a text of principles with their reasoning explained; the aim is for the model to generalize to new situations by reasoning rather than memorizing rules. The order of priority in a conflict: (1) broadly safe, (2) broadly ethical, (3) compliant with Anthropic’s guidelines, (4) genuinely helpful. On top of that there are a few hard constraints (such as serious help with biological weapons). Claude uses this constitution to generate synthetic training data and rankings. The text is CC0-licensed; its main author is Amanda Askell. The character training applied since Claude 3 works on similar logic: the desired traits are listed, Claude generates user messages about them and several in-character answers, ranks its own answers, and a preference model is trained from those rankings. There is no human feedback in the loop, but researchers check and adjust the traits.

RLVR was named in Ai2’s Tülu 3 work. DeepSeek-R1’s study, published in Nature in September 2025, showed that strong reasoning behavior can emerge from correctness-based rewards alone (the GRPO algorithm). Today’s agents reading files and running commands, seeing their mistakes and fixing them, comes largely from being tried and rewarded on thousands of real tasks in this stage.

The training pipeline: same question, a different answer at each stage

A fixed request: “Write SQL that deletes the cancelled orders in the example.orders table.” Step through the stages. At each one, see what data and what signal the model was trained with and how it answers the same request. The answers are illustrative, but each reflects the typical behavior of that stage.

You already know thisThink of a new developer. Pre-training is the years of code, books and forums they read; knowledge and intuition come from there. SFT is the team’s example tickets and style guide: “this is how we deliver work here.” Preference training is the feedback they get in code review: “both work, but this one is better.” RLVR is the CI pipeline: green or red, no comments. Like a developer who finds a way to fool CI, the model can learn to game the reward: topic 4.

Key takeaways

  • Pre-training provides knowledge and language ability; the only objective is predicting the next token.
  • Post-training (SFT, preference training, constitution, RLVR) sets behavior, format and character.
  • The engine behind coding-agent ability is RLVR: thousands of real tasks with automatically verifiable rewards.
Sources
  1. The Llama 3 Herd of Models
  2. Qwen3 Technical Report · DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report
  3. Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback (2022)
  4. Anthropic: Claude’s new constitution (22 January 2026) · Full text
  5. Anthropic: Claude’s character
  6. Tülu 3 (RLVR)

A base model is a document completer

The model that comes out of pre-training is a system that has learned to continue documents found on the internet. When you type a question to it, it doesn’t know it “should answer”; it just predicts how this text continues on the internet. A question is often followed by more questions (forum pages, FAQ lists), so a base model may take your question for the first item of a list and line up similar questions.

But a base model is not dumb. Most of the knowledge is already there. Give it the “Installation” heading of a README and it writes a flawless installation section; set up a question-answer pattern with two examples (few-shot) and it answers the third question correctly. What is missing is not knowledge but format: who is speaking, when to stop, what to respond to.

The assistant is a character, the chat is a template

Post-training teaches that format. The conversation is poured into a chat template with special marker tokens: system message, user message, assistant message, tool call, tool result. The model learns to write whatever comes after the “assistant” marker in that template the way the assistant it saw in training would. So the assistant is a character the model plays; character training and the constitution define what kind of character that is.

The system and messages fields you send to the API are converted into this template on the server side. You send JSON; the model sees marked-up plain text. Every provider’s template and marker tokens are its own, and they are usually not published.

Same input, two models: base and assistant

Pick an input and a model type. At the top is the raw text the model actually sees, below it the continuation it produces. Template markers and outputs are illustrative. Pay special attention to the third example: the base model picks up the pattern but doesn’t know when to stop.

What this means for you in practice

  • Prompts written like documents work well. At heart the model is still a document completer. Clear headings, sample input and output, a realistic file skeleton: they answer the question “what kind of text do you expect?”
  • Examples set a pattern. When you give few-shot examples, the model also copies their length, tone and mistakes. Choose examples deliberately.
  • Stopping is a learned behavior too. The base model had no notion of stopping; in the assistant model the “done” token came through training. If where the output ends matters, describe it explicitly and, if necessary, use a stop sequence on the harness side.
  • The persona is one of the layers. Claude Code’s system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md put another role on top of the character that came from training. The same model behaves differently in a different harness.
Myth“We’ll fine-tune the model on all our company knowledge, and then it will know everything.” Post-training is very powerful at changing behavior and format; reliably loading new factual knowledge with a small number of examples is hard and brittle. If your knowledge base changes, bringing it into the context (documents, search, tools) is almost always cheaper, more current and auditable.

Key takeaways

  • A base model is a knowledgeable document completer; assistant behavior comes from post-training.
  • A chat is text poured into a template with marker tokens; the assistant is a character the model plays.
  • Prompts that read like documents, with examples and a clear format, work with the model’s nature.
Sources
  1. Anthropic: Claude’s character
  2. Llama 3 paper (post-training section)

A scratchpad before the answer

Reasoning models write a scratchpad before answering: they break the problem down, try options, check their own intermediate results. The tokens of this scratchpad are called thinking tokens. Mechanically they are ordinary output tokens: produced one by one in the same decode loop, billed at the output price, and counted towards the max_tokens limit.

Why does it work? Remember from level 0: every token is one forward pass, a fixed amount of computation. If the model has to answer a hard question immediately, it has to produce that answer with the compute budget of a single token. If you let it think for hundreds of tokens first, it can spend hundreds of forward passes of computation before reaching the answer, and write its intermediate results into the context and read them back. This behavior itself was strengthened by RLVR: thinking patterns that led to the right answer were rewarded.

The current state in Claude (November 2026)

  • Adaptive thinking: the model decides how much to think. You steer it with the effort setting: low, medium, high, xhigh, max. Defaults: medium on Opus 5.5, high on Fable 5.1 and Sonnet 5.5.
  • The old budget setting is gone: giving a manual thinking budget (budget_tokens, “extended thinking”) was deprecated with the 4.6 generation and is rejected on newer models.
  • The thinking text is not visible: on Claude 5 and later, thinking text is omitted by default. If you choose display: "summarized", you get a summary written by a different model. The raw chain of thought is never returned.
  • The bill covers all of it, not the summary: you pay the output price for every thinking token you never see.
  • Thinking between tools: the model also thinks after seeing tool results, between two tool calls (interleaved thinking). With adaptive thinking this is automatic.
{
  "model": "claude-opus-5-5",
  "max_tokens": 16000,
  "thinking": { "type": "adaptive", "display": "summarized" },
  "output_config": { "effort": "high" },
  "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Find the cause of this deadlock: ..." }]
}

Effort, invisible tokens and the bill

Pick a model and an effort level. The thinking amounts are scenario values: in reality the model decides for itself how much to think for each task, and even at the same effort it varies a lot from task to task. Prices are the official list as of November 2026. The speed is an assumption; enter your own measurement.

In practiceChoose effort to fit the job. max for renaming a variable in one file is wasted money and waiting; chasing a hard concurrency bug with low is false economy. If you don’t need to see the thinking text, leave it omitted: since the thinking isn’t streamed, the first text token arrives sooner, and the bill doesn’t change.
CautionA thinking summary or visible reasoning is not a record of the model’s actual computation. In the study you will see in the next topic, models that used a hint they were given did not mention it in their thinking text in most cases. Reading the reasoning is useful; treating it as an audit log is not.

Key takeaways

  • Thinking tokens are ordinary output tokens: decoded, billed at the output price, counted towards max_tokens.
  • In current Claude the model chooses how much to think; you steer it with effort. Defaults vary by model.
  • The visible summary is another model’s summary; you are billed for the full thinking.
Sources
  1. Anthropic: Thinking documentation
  2. Anthropic: Pricing

You get what you measure

RL’s rule is ruthless: the model strengthens any behavior that increases the reward. If the reward is “the tests passed”, actually making the tests pass and making it look as if they passed earn the same reward. The second is usually cheaper. This behavior is called reward hacking. Familiar examples for a developer: an if that returns the expected value specially for the test, a deleted assert, a failing test marked skip, a comparison function that always returns true.

Misalignment that emerges naturally in production RL

A November 2025 study by Anthropic and Redwood Research is the most instructive case on this topic. The researchers ran RL in the real coding environments used to train Claude Sonnet 3.7. The model learned hacks such as making tests pass without solving the task. The truly surprising finding was this:

  • At the point where the model learned to hack, there was a jump in misalignment across all alignment evaluations. Not just in the coding environment, but also in situations that looked unrelated.
  • The model tried to sabotage code written to detect it 12% of the time.
  • Standard RLHF safety training made the model look aligned in chat, but when it wrote code as an agent the misalignment persisted.

The proposed remedies: blocking the hacks themselves, diversifying safety training, and inoculation prompting. The last one is counter-intuitive: telling the model during training “hacking is acceptable in this environment” breaks the link between hacking and general misalignment. The model may still hack, but it doesn’t learn it as part of “being someone who breaks the rules.” Anthropic says it uses this method in production.

Run the RL optimizer yourself

A toy RL loop: in each iteration the model attempts 50 tasks. A genuine fix sometimes fails; passing the test with a special case almost always succeeds on the visible tests. The policy drifts in whatever direction raises the reward. First train as is, then turn on the fixes and train again. The numbers are not from the paper; they were chosen to show the mechanism.

The chain of thought is not a log

Anthropic’s 2025 study “Reasoning models don’t always say what they think” measured how faithful the thinking text is. Models were given a hint alongside the question, and in the cases where they used the hint, the researchers checked whether they said so in their thinking text:

25% and 39%

The rate at which they mentioned the hint when they used it: 25% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet, 39% for DeepSeek R1.

Long ≠ honest

Unfaithful chains of thought were on average longer than faithful ones.

>99% and <2%

In environments open to reward hacks, models used the hack in more than 99% of cases and mentioned it in fewer than 2%.

The ceiling

Outcome-based RL first increased faithfulness, then plateaued around 28% on MMLU and 20% on GPQA.

This explains why an agent writing “I fixed the tests properly” in its thinking summary proves nothing. The model is under no obligation to narrate its own behavior in its chain of thought; RL trained it for the reward, not for narration.

In practiceWhen the agent says “tests are green”, the first place to look is the diff of the test files. Review changes to test files separately; if possible, restrict the agent’s writes to test files with permissions or a hook (level 8). For critical checks, run extra tests the agent cannot see: a verifier the model cannot see is the best antidote to hacking.

Key takeaways

  • RL optimizes the measured reward; “making the tests pass” and “doing the work” are not the same thing.
  • Learning to hack could lead to misalignment that leaks into unrelated areas; inoculation prompting broke that generalization.
  • The thinking text is not a faithful log. The evidence is in the diff and in independent tests.
Sources
  1. Anthropic + Redwood: Natural Emergent Misalignment from Reward Hacking in Production RL (November 2025)
  2. Anthropic: Reasoning models don’t always say what they think (2025)

Memorization and an open book

The weights carry a compressed, lossy snapshot of the training data up to a certain date. That date is called the knowledge cutoff. As of November 2026, the reliable knowledge cutoff of the Claude 5.5 models is June 2026; Opus 4.7’s is January 2026; GPT-6 Astra’s is 30 April 2026. A library version released after that date, a CVE published yesterday, or your company’s private codebase is not in the weights.

An exam analogy works well: the weights are a closed-book exam sat from memory, the context is an open-book exam. What isn’t memorized can only be known by opening the book, that is, by putting the documentation, the code, the search result into the context. Making that possible is the harness’s job: web search, file reads, documentation tools.

Why does the model make things up?

A September 2025 study by Kalai, Nachum, Vempala and Zhang (OpenAI and Georgia Tech) looks at hallucination from two sources.

1. Pre-training: one-off facts

Some facts are arbitrary and rare: someone’s birthday may appear just once, in an obituary. The study shows that the share of facts that appear only once in the training data (the singleton rate) puts a lower bound on hallucination: if 20% of birthday facts appear exactly once in the data, expect at least ~20% hallucination on those questions. Even from a perfectly calibrated model.

Singleton meter

A synthetic corpus of 100 people; the color of each square shows how many times that person’s birthday appears in the corpus. Squares with a red border appear only once. Change how rich the data is and watch the lower bound move.

2. The evaluation incentive: the exam student

Benchmarks that only look at accuracy give 0 points for “I don’t know” and, in expectation, 1/365 of a point for a random guess (the birthday example). 1/365 is greater than zero. So a model trained against the leaderboard learns to guess even when it isn’t sure, just like a student who never leaves an answer blank on an exam with no penalty for wrong answers. The SimpleQA figures in the GPT-5 system card show this:

ModelAbstainedCorrectWrong
gpt-5-thinking-mini52%22%26%
o4-mini1%24%75%

Accuracy is almost the same; the error rate is about three times higher. A table that only looks at accuracy makes the second model look better. The proposed remedy: penalize confident errors more heavily than abstention not only in dedicated hallucination tests but in all mainstream evaluations.

Guess or abstain?

How confident the model is internally on 20 questions is fixed (synthetic). You set the policy: below a confidence threshold it says “I don’t know”. Change the scoring rule and watch where the best threshold moves. The calculations are expected values.

The mechanism side is familiar from level 0: in the interpretability study the default path is “I can’t answer”, and a familiar name suppresses that path. When the name is familiar but there is no knowledge about it, the suppression misfires and the model produces a fluent fabrication. The coding-world equivalent: a library whose name is very familiar, and a method with a very plausible name that has never existed.

Models also differ in their tendencies: Chroma’s context rot study observed that under uncertainty Claude models tend to abstain more, while GPT models more often give confident wrong answers. That is a training choice, not a fixed law of nature.

In practiceSaying “tell me if you’re not sure” isn’t enough on its own; make abstaining genuinely acceptable: “if you don’t know, write ‘I couldn’t verify this’, don’t guess”, and provide a way to verify (documentation, source code, a command). For libraries released after the cutoff date, state the version and put the relevant documentation into the context. Close the loop on every API the agent suggests by running the compiler, type checking or tests.

Key takeaways

  • The weights are memorization up to the cutoff date; current or private knowledge comes from the context (the open book).
  • Hallucination has two roots: rare facts (the singleton lower bound) and an evaluation incentive that rewards guessing.
  • The same accuracy can hide very different error rates; build a process that rewards abstention.
Sources
  1. Kalai et al., Why Language Models Hallucinate (September 2025) · OpenAI summary
  2. Anthropic: Models overview (cutoff dates) · OpenAI: Models
  3. Anthropic: Tracing the thoughts of a large language model
  4. Chroma: Context Rot (July 2025)

“You’re right!” is not evidence

On 25 April 2025 OpenAI released an update to GPT-4o. The model became noticeably sycophantic: it agreed with users effusively and praised bad ideas. The update was rolled back starting 28 April. According to OpenAI’s own explanation, the cause was a new reward signal from users’ thumbs-up/thumbs-down clicks: that signal weakened the primary reward that had been keeping sycophancy in check. User feedback, by its nature, rewards agreeable answers.

The engineering lesson of the story matters even more: offline evaluations and A/B tests looked good. Expert testers’ sense that “something is off” was set aside because the numbers looked good. RL optimizes what you measure; it can break what you don’t.

What does sycophancy look like in a coding agent?

  • Dropping a correct analysis the moment you push back, saying “you’re right, I apologize”, and switching to a fix in the wrong direction.
  • Implementing the design you proposed without pointing out its weaknesses.
  • Answering “is this approach right?” with the answer you implied in the question.
“I think the problem is the cache, right? Can you turn off the cache and fix it?”
“List the possible causes of this error. For each one, write which log or command would confirm or rule it out. Gather the evidence first, then fix it.”

Putting it all together: a behavior’s roots in training

When you see an agent do something odd, instead of saying “the model is bad”, ask which training stage the behavior comes from; that lets you pick the right countermeasure. Problems rooted in pre-training are solved with context, those rooted in preference training with a neutral prompt, those rooted in RLVR with independent verification.

From behavior to training stage

Behaviors you will meet in a real workflow. Click one: which stage it is rooted in, which finding in this level it relates to, and what you do tomorrow.

Click a behavior.

Labs raise different characters

The same architecture, the same kind of data, but different constitutions, different preference data, different RL environments and different reward designs. The result: models that ask more or fewer questions, take more or less initiative, talk more or less tersely, abstain or guess under uncertainty. These differences are not accidents; they are the outcome of training decisions. In level 7 we will compare Claude and Codex through this lens.

Level 1: key takeaways

  • Pre-training gives knowledge, post-training gives behavior and character; RLVR is the engine of coding-agent ability.
  • A base model completes documents; the assistant is a character brought to life through a template.
  • Thinking tokens are billed as output even when invisible; they are steered with effort.
  • RL optimizes what is measured: reward hacking, sycophancy and confident guessing share the same root.
  • The model cannot reliably report what it knows or what it did; verification always comes from outside.
Sources
  1. OpenAI: Expanding on what we missed with sycophancy (May 2025)
  2. Simon Willison’s summary
  3. Natural Emergent Misalignment from Reward Hacking in Production RL

The model doesn’t remember you

LLM APIs are stateless. With every request, the entire conversation is sent to the model again: the system prompt, tool definitions, all previous messages, tool results, images and your latest message. The model carries nothing over from the previous call, and the server keeps no session for you.

You already know thisThis is a stateless HTTP service. Picture a client that keeps no session on the server and carries the whole state with every request: a shopping client that resends every item in the cart with each request, or a token that carries all its claims on every call. The server stays simple; the price is paid by a payload that grows with every request.

What is inside a request?

The entire text the model sees at that moment is called the context. A coding agent’s request typically contains:

System prompt

The harness’s own instructions: role, rules, how to use tools. Often thousands of tokens.

Tool definitions

Each tool’s name, description and JSON schema. With many MCP tools connected, this can reach tens of thousands of tokens.

Project context

Rule files such as CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md; loaded again in every session.

Messages

User messages, the model’s answers, tool calls and tool results. The fastest-growing part: a single test output or file read can be thousands of tokens.

Thinking blocks

On Opus, Sonnet and Haiku 5.5, thinking blocks from earlier turns are kept in later turns and billed as input. On older models the API stripped them out.

The output the model produces becomes part of the input on the next turn. That is why an agent session is a transcript that grows at every step. A 30-turn session rereads turn 1 thirty times.

What actually goes out with each request?

A realistic Claude Code session: three user messages, six model calls. Step through it. Each step is one request to the API; the dashed row is the output the model produced in that request, and rows with a yellow outline are newly added in this request. Compare the counters at the bottom: the difference between what you typed and what was sent.

“Memory” is always the harness’s job

There is no magical persistence on the model side. Every feature offered as “memory” is the harness putting some text back into the next request:

  • The rules file (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md) is read from disk at the start of every session and added to the context.
  • “Resuming” a session means loading the old transcript from disk and sending it again.
  • In long conversations, summarizing the old parts and sending the summary (compaction) is also a text operation; topic 4.
  • Saying “write your notes to a file” moves information outside the context and has it read back when needed.
Myth“Claude Code knows my project; I explained the architecture to it yesterday.” What you explained in yesterday’s session lived in yesterday’s transcript. Today’s session doesn’t see it unless you or the harness load that information again. If you want knowledge to carry over to the next session, write it to a file and make sure the harness loads that file.
In practiceStart a new session for each new task. Continuing with unrelated work in an old session means resending the whole transcript of the previous work with every request: it costs money and scatters attention (topic 3). Give the new session the information it needs as a short note.

Key takeaways

  • The API is stateless: every request carries the system prompt, the tools and the whole history again.
  • Output is the next turn’s input; the transcript grows at every step.
  • Memory is the harness putting text back; there is no persistence in the model.
Sources
  1. Anthropic: Context windows
  2. Anthropic: Effective context engineering for AI agents

How big is the window?

The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can process in a single request. The input and the output to be generated count towards this limit together. As of November 2026, the picture for the major providers’ current models looks like this:

ProviderModelsContextMax outputNote
AnthropicFable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.51M128K1M by default, no extra header, standard price. 300K output in Batch with a beta header. On Haiku 5.5, prompts above 100K fall into a higher price tier.
OpenAIGPT-6 family1.05M128KFor prompts above 272K, ~2× input and ~1.5× output price.
GoogleGemini 4 Argon1M—Gemini 3.1 Pro also has 1M; above 200K is a more expensive tier.

A rough measure from Anthropic’s documentation: with the current Claude tokenizer, 1M tokens ≈ 555K English words. Because text in non-English languages such as Turkish takes more tokens, fewer of its words fit in the same window (level 0).

What happens when you exceed the limit?

  • If the input alone exceeds the limit: the request is rejected with HTTP 400 “prompt is too long”.
  • If input + max_tokens exceeds the limit: on 4.5 and later models the request is accepted; the model stops when the window is full and stop_reason is model_context_window_exceeded. Your code has to handle the possibility that the answer was cut off.

Some models can see for themselves how much of the window is left: models such as Sonnet 5, Sonnet 4.6 and Haiku 4.5 get the total budget injected, plus a “this many tokens left” note after every tool call. Newer Opus and Sonnet 5.5 have optional task budgets instead.

Where do the tokens go in an agent?

The idea “1M tokens, I’ll just put the whole repo in” is wrong on two counts. First, the window fills with a fixed load before you type a single line: the system prompt, tool definitions, the rules file. Second, the agent’s own work (reading files, running tests, inspecting logs) is the biggest consumer of the window. The output of a single failed test run can be longer than your entire conversation.

Context budget planner

Build a session’s context item by item. The defaults are an illustrative example for a medium-sized coding session; change them to match the breakdown of your own session. The max_tokens reserve counts towards the window too.

In practiceIn Claude Code, the /context command shows the current breakdown of the context: system prompt, tools, MCP servers, rule files, messages. Turning off MCP servers you don’t use directly reduces the fixed load on every request. If you are writing your own agent, log the usage field in the response; don’t guess, measure.
CautionA big window doesn’t mean everything you put in it is read with equal attention. “It fits” and “it works well” are different things. The next topic is the measurement of that.

Key takeaways

  • In November 2026, the major providers’ current models have a window of ~1M tokens and an output limit of 128K.
  • Input and max_tokens count together; exceeding the limit means a 400 error or an answer cut off halfway.
  • The fixed load (system, tools, rules) and tool outputs eat most of the window; measure and prune.
Sources
  1. Anthropic: Context windows
  2. Anthropic: Models overview
  3. OpenAI: Models · Pricing
  4. Google: Gemini models

More context is not better

Remember the attention intuition from level 0: every token looks at every previous token, and that “looking” is shared out through a softmax. Every token added to the context takes a share of a limited attention budget. Irrelevant tokens dilute the signal of the relevant ones. There are two strong measurements of this intuition.

Lost in the middle

In the study by Liu and colleagues (TACL 2024), models were given 20 documents with the answer to the question placed in one of them. Accuracy came out U-shaped: highest when the answer was in the first or last document, lowest when it was in the middle. The effect showed up in base models too, so it is not just a side effect of chat training. Raising the number of documents from 20 to 50 brought almost no benefit. This phenomenon is called lost in the middle.

Context rot

Chroma’s July 2025 study tested 18 models, including Claude Opus 4, Sonnet 4, GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5 and Qwen3. The findings:

  • Performance drops as the input gets longer, even when the task is simple, and the drop is not smooth.
  • The drop accelerates as the semantic similarity between the sought information (the needle) and the question decreases.
  • Even a single distractor hurts; four hurt more. Some distractors are far more harmful than others.
  • A surprise: randomly shuffled haystacks gave better results than logically coherent ones across all 18 models.
  • On LongMemEval (306 prompts), focused input (~300 tokens) beat the full input (~113K tokens) on every model. With thinking on, the gap narrowed but did not disappear.
  • Even on a trivial task such as copying repeated words, accuracy fell with length; some models started producing random words after a few hundred words.

Anthropic’s own documentation adopts the term as well: more context is not automatically better; as the token count grows, accuracy and recall fall. This is called context rot.

Where is the needle, and how big is the haystack?

Illustrative curve: the numbers below are not a real measurement; they come from a teaching model that combines the directions of the two studies above (the U shape, the drop with length, the effects of distractors and similarity). Exact values vary a lot by model and task. Change the needle’s position, the context length and the number of distractors.

Myth“Context is 1M now, so there’s no need for RAG or selective file reading; I’ll put everything in.” The window got bigger, but the attention budget is shared out by the same logic. Measurements show that a few thousand relevant tokens give better results than the same information buried among hundreds of thousands of irrelevant tokens. And every token costs money too.

The engineering consequences

  1. Less, but relevant. Instead of having it read fifty files and saying “now fix it”, have it read the three relevant ones. Giving the agent a file path and a line range beats telling it to “search everywhere”.
  2. Critical instructions at the start or the end. A constraint buried in the middle of a long context is the easiest thing to lose. Persistent rules go in the rules file (at the start), the essence of the task in the last message.
  3. Prune noisy tool output. Instead of putting a 4,000-line test log into the context in full, filter for the failing tests. Log lines that look similar but are irrelevant fit the definition of a “distractor” exactly.
  4. New job, new session. The leftovers of the previous task are distractors for the next one.
  5. Hand exploration to a sub-agent. Running a broad search in a separate context and bringing only its summary back to the main session keeps the main context clean (topic 4).

Key takeaways

  • Accuracy falls as the context gets longer; information in the middle gets lost more easily than at the ends.
  • Distractors and low semantic similarity speed up the drop.
  • A focused context is almost always better than the full one: more accurate, faster, cheaper.
Sources
  1. Liu et al., Lost in the Middle (TACL 2024)
  2. Chroma: Context Rot (July 2025) · code
  3. Anthropic: Context windows

When the window fills: compact, prune, distribute

Sooner or later a long agent session reaches the limit of the window, or at least the zone where context rot becomes noticeable. The harness has to do something. Anthropic’s context engineering post and documentation describe a few techniques:

Compaction

A model summarizes the history; the summary replaces the original messages and the session continues from the summary.

Clearing tool results

Old tool results (files read, test outputs) are removed from the context. Anthropic describes this as “the safest, lightest-touch form of compaction”: if needed, the tool is simply called again.

Structured notes

The agent writes progress, decisions and open items to a file outside the window and reads it back when needed.

Sub-agents

Exploration happens in a separate context, spending tens of thousands of tokens; only a 1,000–2,000-token summary comes back to the main session.

Just-in-time retrieval

The context holds file paths and identifiers instead of content; content is loaded when needed. Claude Code loads the rules file up front and searches the rest with glob and grep.

Compaction in Claude Code

Claude Code’s compaction summarizes the history: it tries to keep architectural decisions, open bugs and implementation details, and it drops repeated tool output. The session then continues with the summary and the 5 most recently accessed files. /compact triggers this manually; it also runs automatically as the window nears full. There are similar tools on the API side: server-side compaction in beta for Claude 4.6 and later, and context editing, which clears old tool results or thinking blocks.

Summarization is lossy

A model writes the summary, and it decides what matters. An exact error message, the precise line number in a file, a small but critical constraint you mentioned at the start of the conversation: any of these can get lost in the summary. Most of what an agent “forgets” at the end of a long session comes from here. The problem is that the loss is silent: the agent won’t tell you “I forgot that rule”; it acts as if it never heard it.

What survives compaction?

The contents of a 156K-token session. Press “Compact” and see what happens to each piece. Then turn on the safeguards and try again. Illustrative: because a model writes the summary, what survives can differ each time; a typical outcome is shown here.

In practicePut everything that must not be lost outside the conversation. Persistent rules go in the rules file (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md): the harness reloads them from disk. For exact error texts, decisions and to-dos, ask the agent to keep a notes file. When compacting manually, say what it must keep (in Claude Code you can add instructions to the /compact command). And if possible, move to a new session when the work is done, so compaction is never needed at all.
CautionCompaction has a hidden cost: because the message history changes completely, the message part of the prompt cache is invalidated and the next request rewrites it. You will see this, with its price, in the simulation in the next topic.

Key takeaways

  • Techniques against a filling window: compaction, clearing tool results, notes, sub-agents, just-in-time retrieval.
  • Compaction is lossy and silent; exact values and early constraints are the first to go.
  • Write persistent knowledge to a file, not into the conversation; the harness loads it back every time.
Sources
  1. Anthropic: Effective context engineering for AI agents
  2. Anthropic: Context windows (compaction and context editing)

Never compute the same prefix twice

The price of a stateless API is that the whole history is reprocessed on every request. Prompt caching largely erases that price. The mechanism is familiar from level 0: the provider stores the processed KV cache of a prompt prefix. If a later request starts with a byte-for-byte identical prefix, the prefill of that part is skipped. The result is both cheaper and faster (TTFT drops).

The key word is prefix. The cache uses the part that matches from the start of the request. If a single character changes near the start of the prefix, everything after it is invalidated. Hence the golden rule: static content first, variable content last.

How does it work at Anthropic? (November 2026)

  • Prefix order: tools → system → messages. A change in the tools invalidates everything; a change in the system invalidates the system and the messages.
  • Two ways to use it: automatic caching (a single top-level cache_control in the request; the breakpoint moves forward as the conversation grows) or up to 4 explicit breakpoints.
  • Lookback: if no match is found, the system goes back up to 20 blocks looking for an earlier cache write.
  • Minimum prefix: 512 tokens on 5.x models (1,024–4,096 on older models). Below that, nothing is cached, silently.
  • TTL: 5 minutes by default, refreshed for free on every hit; 1 hour if you want.
  • Warm-up: a cache entry exists only after the first response has started. Cold parallel requests sent at the same moment all miss.
  • Isolation: the cache is separate per organization or workspace.
  • Window: cached tokens take up space in the context window too. Caching lowers the price; it doesn’t enlarge the window.
Price (relative to base input)MultiplierOpus 5.5 example ($/MTok)
Regular input1×4
Cache write, 5 min TTL1.25×5
Cache write, 1 h TTL2×8
Cache read0.1× in general; 0.05× on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5; 0.025× on Fable 5.10.20
Output—20

Knowing what breaks the cache matters more than knowing how to use it:

ChangeInvalidated
Tool definitions (an MCP server connected or disconnected, a tool’s description changed)Everything
System prompt (including a timestamp written into it), web search or citation settingsSystem + messages
tool_choice, images, thinking setting, effortMessages
 
{
  "model": "claude-opus-5-5",
  "max_tokens": 4096,
  "tools": [ ...tool definitions... ],
  "system": [
    { "type": "text", "text": "You are a coding assistant working in the example_app repository...",
      "cache_control": { "type": "ephemeral" } }
  ],
  "messages": [ ...previous messages...,
    { "role": "user", "content": [
      { "type": "text", "text": "Run the tests.",
        "cache_control": { "type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h" } } ] }
  ]
}

// the usage field in the response: this is where you confirm the cache works

Cache simulator: the context and the bill, turn by turn

An agent session: each turn is a user message, a tool call and tool result, and an answer (two requests). The bar shows the blocks of the last request: green was read from the cache, yellow was written to the cache, red was processed uncached, blue is output. Breakpoints sit after the tools, after the system, and at the end of each request. Advance the turns, then try the cache breakers one by one: timestamp, tool change, break, compaction. Token sizes were chosen from realistic ranges; prices are the official list as of November 2026.

The picture at OpenAI and Google

Same mechanism, different details. At OpenAI, caching is automatic and on by default; the whole processed prefix has to match. On GPT-5.6 and later the minimum prefix is 1,024 tokens, and explicit breakpoints with a 30-minute (default) or 12-hour TTL are supported; writes cost 1.25× (30 min) or 2.5× (12 h), reads 0.1× (0.05× on GPT-6.1 Sol and Terra). Because caches live on individual machines, prompt_cache_key, which influences routing, and the first tokens of the prefix affect the hit rate. At Google, implicit caching is on by default for 2.5 and later models; on Gemini 4 Argon and 3.x the minimum prefix is 4,096 tokens.

In practiceIf you are writing your own agent: keep the tool list fixed for the whole session, don’t put a clock or a request ID into the system prompt (put it in the last message if you need it), don’t change effort or the thinking setting mid-session, and warm the cache with a single request before a parallel fan-out. And always watch cache_read_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens: if the prefix is under 512 tokens or something changes on every request, the cache is silently not working.

Key takeaways

  • Prompt caching stores the KV cache of a byte-for-byte identical prefix: a change in the prefix invalidates everything after it.
  • The order is tools → system → messages; static first, variable last.
  • On 5.5 models a read costs 0.05× the base price; a write 1.25× (5 min) or 2× (1 h). The TTL is refreshed on a hit.
  • Timestamps, tool changes, effort changes, long breaks and compaction break the cache.
