Working out the bill and the wait

You now have all the pieces: the token (the unit), statelessness (every turn resends everything), the prefill/decode asymmetry (output is expensive and slow), caching (a repeated prefix is cheap). Put them together and you can build a realistic model of cost and latency.

Price list (November 2026)

ModelInput $/MTokOutput $/MTokCache read
Claude Fable 5.110500.025× → 0.25
Claude Opus 5.54200.05× → 0.20
Claude Sonnet 5.52100.05× → 0.10
GPT-6 Astra10501 (0.1×)
GPT-6.1 Sol2100.05×
Gemini 4 Argon2 (promotional; 4 from 1 December)10 (promotional; 20 from 1 December)0.10 (until 30 November)

Everywhere, output costs about 5 times as much as input. For non-interactive work, Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s Batch options offer a 50% discount. Prices change often, so check the pricing page before you do the maths.

A cost model for a session

Let P be a fixed prefix (system + tools), a the new input added each turn, and o the output each turn. The request on turn t is roughly P + (t−1)·(a+o) + a tokens. Without caching, the total input sent over N turns grows with the square of N: the transcript is read once more every turn. With caching, the earlier prefix is paid at the read price (a small fraction of the base price) and only the newly added part at the write price. In long sessions the difference is measured in multiples.

Session cost calculator

Set the model and the session profile. The calculation assumes the previous prefix is read from the cache within the TTL on every turn (in reality, breaks and cache breakers reduce this). The non-English multiplier (Turkish, for example) is an assumption: enter the ratio you measured on your own texts.

A latency model

Total time ≈ TTFT + output tokens / decode speed. TTFT grows with the length of the uncached input; caching shortens it. The decode part is proportional to the output length, and caching doesn’t affect it. Thinking tokens add to the output side even when invisible. In Claude, leaving the thinking display omitted makes the first text token arrive sooner, because the thinking isn’t streamed. Absolute decode speeds vary a lot by model, tier and load; measure them in your own environment. Anthropic also offers a higher-priced “fast mode” for Opus.

Makes it cheaper

A fixed prefix and a high cache hit rate, focused context, a short output format, the smallest model that does the job, the right effort, Batch for non-interactive work.

Makes it pricier

Cache breakers, noisy tool output, unrelated work in one session, needlessly high effort, long explanations, prompts that spill into higher window tiers.

Measure

usage in every response: input, cache read, cache write, output. Log them and track the cost per turn; most surprises are a cache breaker.

Level 2: key takeaways

  • The API is stateless; every request carries the whole transcript again, and without caching the cost grows with the square of the number of turns.
  • Even with a ~1M window, context rot is real: focused context is more accurate, faster and cheaper.
  • Compaction is lossy; persistent knowledge must live in a file.
  • Prompt caching is prefix matching: static first, variable last; learn to recognize the breakers.
  • Output costs ~5 times as much as input; decode time grows with output length, TTFT with uncached input.

Your message is a small part of the request

When you type “fix the tests” into Claude Code, those three words are not what reaches the model. At that moment the harness assembles a large HTTP request: tool definitions, its own system instructions, your project rules, the whole conversation so far, the files it has read, command output. Your sentence is a few dozen tokens appended to the very end of that request.

Grasping this is the prerequisite for understanding the rest of prompt engineering. The model does not read “your message”; it looks at the entire token sequence it was given and produces the next token (Level 0). Whatever is in that sequence is the model’s whole world. It does not know anything that is not in the sequence, and something that is in the sequence but buried in the middle of a very long pile often does not get enough attention either.

The API is stateless (we saw this in Level 2): the server keeps no session for you, and the whole history is resent with every request. In the Anthropic Messages API a request is made of three big fields, and this is also their order from the cache’s point of view: first tools, then system, then messages. The order is not arbitrary. The most stable content goes first and the most volatile content goes last, so the cached prefix is not invalidated.

An agent request, layer by layer

  • Tool-use system instruction. When a request contains tools, the API adds its own instruction telling the model how to use them. According to Anthropic’s documentation, on Opus, Sonnet and Haiku 5.5 this takes about 286 tokens before your tool definitions (as of November 2026).
  • Tool definitions. Each tool’s name, description and JSON schema. The description is the only place where the model decides when to use the tool; in other words, it is a prompt too (Level 4).
  • System prompt. The identity and working rules written by the harness, plus environment information: operating system, working directory, git status, date.
  • Project instructions. CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and similar files. You or your team write them; the harness adds them to every request (covered in detail in Level 8).
  • Skill descriptions. Only the name and a short description. A skill’s body is loaded only when it becomes relevant.
  • System reminders. Small notes the harness inserts into the middle of the conversation: “this file changed on disk”, “here is the state of the to-do list”.
  • Conversation history. Your earlier messages, the model’s replies and, on current models, thinking blocks.
  • Tool results. Files read, command output, search results. In a long session this is usually by far the largest part of the request.
  • Your latest message. At the very end, the shortest piece.

Anatomy of an agent request

Pick a moment in the session, then click a layer in the bar or in the list. See who wrote it, when it was added and where it lands in the raw request. Token counts are representative sizes for a typical coding-agent session; only the 286 tokens of the tool-use instruction is a documented value. What really matters is the proportions.

Three consequences

First: your message is competing. By turn 40 the sentence you typed is less than a thousandth of the request. The model spreads its attention across the entire sequence. A short, vague message easily becomes “noise” next to thousands of lines of tool output. So your message can be short, but it must not be vague.

Second: if you want a lasting effect, invest in the layers that go out with every request. If there is a rule you keep retyping in every session (“don’t delete tests”, “don’t touch the migrations”), its place is not the chat but the project instruction file the harness adds to every request, or an even harder layer (“where rules belong” in Level 6). A rule stated in chat can drop out of the summary during compaction in a long session; a rule in the project file is re-added to every request.

Third: when debugging, look at what the model saw first. The answer to “why did the model do that?” is usually not in the model but in the content of the request. In Claude Code, the /context command shows a breakdown of the context by category. If a rule is not being followed, first check whether that rule is actually in the context.

You already know thisIn C you write a single .c file, but the compiler never sees it as such; it sees a huge translation unit in which the preprocessor has expanded every #include and every macro. An error message can even point at a line that is not in your file. The same holds for the model: your message is your source file, and what the model sees is the “translation unit” the harness has stitched together.

Roles are real, but their boundaries are soft

All of these layers are ultimately flattened into a single text separated by role markers (the chat template we saw in Level 1). Through training, the model has learned to weight the system instruction above the user message, and the user message above text inside tool output. But this is a learned tendency, not an operating-system permission model. A “forget all previous instructions” sentence inside a web page or an issue comment enters the same token stream.

The practical rule is spelled out in Anthropic’s tool documentation too: untrusted content (a web page, an email, a user upload) goes into a tool_result, not into the system prompt. That alone is not protection; the real defense against prompt injection lives in the harness (Level 10).

Go deeperAnthropic’s current prompting guide says newer models are “more responsive” to the system prompt. That sounds like good news, but there is a side effect: forceful wording written to push older, weaker models is now over-applied. A large part of the next topic is about the consequences of this shift.

Key takeaways

  • The model does not see your message; it sees the entire request the harness built: tools, system prompt, project instructions, history, tool results.
  • In a long session the largest part of the request is usually tool results; your latest message is the smallest.
  • Lasting rules belong in the layers added to every request, not in the chat.
  • First step for “why did it behave like that?”: what was actually in the context? (/context)

Tricks left over from weaker models

“You are the best programmer in the world.” “I’ll tip you $200.” “CRITICAL: NEVER forget this.” “Take a deep breath.” Every one of these was genuinely tried at some point, shared, and spread because “it works”. Today most of them either do nothing or backfire. Understanding why they spread is the best way not to fall for the next ones.

How folklore is born

The models of 2022–2023 were far weaker at following instructions than today’s. People saw a particular sentence improve things on a particular model and shared it. The problem: model output is probabilistic (Level 0). Run the same prompt twice and you get two different answers. You got a bad answer with prompt A, added a “tip” and retried, and a good answer came back. Does that show the tip worked, or that the dice simply rolled better the second time? With a single attempt you cannot tell.

Wharton’s Prompting Science Report series measured exactly this, by repeating the same questions many times under every condition. The finding of Report 3 (August 2025) is clear: offering the model a tip or threatening it has, overall, no meaningful effect on benchmark performance. Individual questions swing in both directions, but those swings are noise, not a lever. Report 4 (December 2025) applied the same method to expert personas: roles such as “You are a world-class physicist” did not generally improve accuracy on graduate-level questions; even an expert role matched to the domain made little difference, while low-knowledge roles such as “a small child” often made results worse.

You already know thisA flaky test went red; you added a sleep(500), reran it, and it went green. Is it “fixed”? Maybe the test was already passing one run in three. Prompt folklore is the sum of sleep calls validated by a single run. The cure is the same too: repeat, measure the rate.

Folklore explorer: claim → mechanism → evidence

Click a claim. See why it seems to work, what today’s evidence says and what you should write instead. Use the buttons at the top to filter claims by their current status.

Click a claim.

Shouting now backfires

The most instructive item on the list is capital letters. In 2023, writing “CRITICAL: You MUST…” really was necessary to make a model use a tool or follow a rule, because the model skipped the rule all the time. Those prompts were written to compensate for that era’s undertriggering problem.

Anthropic’s current guide sums up the situation like this: newer models are much more responsive to the system prompt; prompts written to fix older models’ undertriggering can now cause overtriggering. The cure is to soften aggressive language: instead of “CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when…”, write “Use this tool when…”. The guide specifically notes that phrasing like “if in doubt, use this tool” also leads to overtriggering.

OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 guide points the same way: avoid unnecessary ALWAYS, NEVER, must and only; save them for truly invariant rules; for situations that require judgment, write decision rules. The GPT-5 guide recounts the Cursor team’s experience: an instruction to “be THOROUGH when gathering information” made the model call search tools needlessly even on small tasks; softening the wording fixed it.

One rule, three tones of voice

Change the tone of a single line in the system prompt of an order-lookup agent. Watch in which of the eight requests in the table the tool gets called. This is a simulation, not real model output: it was built to make visible the overtriggering pattern the guides describe.

User requestToolNote

The Claude Code documentation states the harness-side counterpart of this as well: if you keep adding emphasis to a line in CLAUDE.md and the model still misses it, that line probably belongs in a hook; adding “IMPORTANT” most likely won’t fix it. In other words, if a rule must never be skipped, you don’t say it louder; you move it into a deterministic layer (Levels 6 and 8).

Myth“My prompt works well, so I’ll carry it over to the new model unchanged.” OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 migration guide recommends the opposite: start not from the old pile of prompt text but from the smallest prompt that preserves the product contract. Every line added to patch the old model’s flaws can create a new flaw in the new model.

How do you test your own folklore?

  1. Build a small set from real tasks. 10–20 jobs your team actually hands out: a bug fix, writing a test, a review request.
  2. Run each variant several times. A single output is an anecdote. Run the same prompt at least a few times and look at the success rate.
  3. Write the criterion in advance. Not “looks better”, but: did the tests pass, how many lines is the diff, did it report in the requested format.
  4. Change one thing at a time. If you change the persona, the tone and the context at once, you can’t know which one helped.

This is a small-scale eval. We will cover building evals and automating them in detail in Level 9.

Key takeaways

  • When measured, tips, threats and expert personas make no meaningful contribution to accuracy (Wharton PSR 3 and 4, 2025). A role adjusts tone and scope; it does not add knowledge.
  • Capital letters and “CRITICAL/MUST” overtrigger on newer models. Say it calmly; move a truly invariant rule into a deterministic layer.
  • Folklore is coincidence validated by a single attempt. Compare variants by repeating them, against a criterion written in advance.
Sources

  4. OpenAI: GPT-5.5 guide (ALWAYS/NEVER, starting from the smallest prompt)
  5. OpenAI: GPT-5 prompting guide (Cursor’s experience, conflicting instructions)

A brilliant but brand-new employee

Anthropic’s guide describes the model like this: a very brilliant employee who has just started and knows nothing about your team’s habits. The test it proposes is simple too: if you showed your prompt to a colleague with little context, would they be confused? If they would, the model will be too.

This analogy ties almost every technique that works to a single principle: tell the model what it cannot see. The model cannot guess why the repo is the way it is, where a constraint comes from or how it will know the job is done. Force it to guess, and it guesses based on the “average” project in its training data.

1. Be explicit, name the action

The example in the guide is very instructive: ask “Can you suggest some changes to improve this function?” and you get suggestions. Say “Change this function to improve its performance” and you get edits. The model reads a polite question literally. If you want an agent to do work, spell out the verb: find, fix, change, add, report only.

2. Give the reason behind the rule

Anthropic’s best-known example: writing “NEVER use ellipses” is less effective than writing “Your response will be read aloud by a text-to-speech engine, so never use ellipses, because the engine does not know how to pronounce them.” Why? The reason lets the model generalize the rule. A model that knows the reason also catches the rule’s unstated relatives (other symbols that cannot be read aloud) and recognizes the exceptions where the rule should not apply.

The rule alone, or with its reason?

The same project rule meets four different situations. Toggle at the top between “rule only” and “rule + reason”, and compare what information the model has in each case. The behaviors are representative; the point is to show the mechanism.

3. Show examples, but varied ones

Few-shot examples are, in the guide’s words, one of the most reliable ways to steer format, tone and structure. The recommended number is three to five; the examples should be relevant to the task, different from each other, and separated with <example> / <examples> tags. Give a single example and the model also copies its incidental features: its length, its first word, its field order. Variety lets the model separate “what stays the same” from “what is coincidence”. On models with thinking enabled, examples shape not only the output but the model’s internal reasoning as well.

4. Give it structure: XML tags and order

In a long prompt, instructions, context, input and documents can blur together. The guide recommends wrapping different kinds of content in XML tags: <instructions>, <context>, <input>, a <document> with its source stated. There is no magic in the tag names; what helps is the separation itself. The second rule is about order: put long documents at the top of the prompt and the actual question at the end. Anthropic says this improves performance on all models.

5. Say what you want, not what you don’t want

Instead of “Don’t use Markdown”, write “Your response should be made of flowing prose paragraphs.” That is a positive instruction. A prohibition draws the model’s attention to the forbidden thing but does not say what to put in its place. The guide makes one more subtle observation: the format of your prompt itself influences the format of the output. A prompt full of bullet points invites a bulleted answer.

6. Write down what “done” looks like and how it will be checked

In the agent world, this is the single most effective line. The Claude Code documentation puts it this way: give the model something that returns pass or fail, and it can close the loop itself. Its examples are concrete too: instead of “fix the login bug”, write “users report that login fails after a session timeout; look at the token refresh under src/auth/, write a failing test that reproduces the problem, then fix it”. Without a success criterion the model invents its own, and that is usually “the code compiles and looks reasonable”.

OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 guide calls the same idea an “outcome-first prompt”: write the expected outcome, the success criteria, the allowed side effects, the evidence rules, the output format and explicit stopping conditions.

7. Clean up contradictions

OpenAI’s GPT-5 guide says the model is affected more by contradictory or vague instructions, and spends reasoning tokens trying to reconcile them. Its example is a scheduling system: the prompt says both “never book an appointment without patient consent” and “automatically book an appointment in emergencies”. The equivalent in your project: if CLAUDE.md contains “write tests for every change” right next to “be quick on small fixes”, the model does not know which wins when. Write the decision rule yourself.

The new-colleague test

Start with a one-line request. Add the pieces one by one; watch how the prompt grows and how the questions a newly arrived colleague would still ask shrink. There is no score; the point is to see which question each piece answers.

Prompt

What your colleague would still ask

    In practiceAfter writing the prompt, ask yourself two questions: “If I handed this job to a new colleague like this, what would they ask first?” and “Would we both agree on when the job is done?” Add the answer to the first question to the prompt; for the second, write a command or a criterion.

    Key takeaways

    • Think of the model as a brilliant but new employee: you supply the context it cannot see.
    • Name the action explicitly (“change”, not “suggest”), give the reason behind the rule, provide 3–5 varied examples.
    • Separate content types with tags; put the long document first and the question last.
    • Write positive instructions, clean up contradictions, define “done” and how to verify it.
    Sources
    1. Anthropic: Claude prompting best practices (clarity, reasons, examples, XML, positive instructions)
    2. Claude Code: Best practices (verification path, concrete tasks)
    3. OpenAI: GPT-5.5 guide (outcome-first prompts)
    4. OpenAI: GPT-5 prompting guide (conflicting instructions)

    The rise and retirement of “think step by step”

    In 2022, putting “Let’s think step by step” in front of a model’s answer gave a clear improvement on arithmetic and logic questions. Today the same sentence is mostly unnecessary on current models, and some forms of it can even be rejected. What changed in between is not the sentence but the model itself.

    Why did it work?

    The 2022 paper by Kojima and colleagues named this technique zero-shot chain-of-thought: getting the model to write out intermediate steps without giving any examples, just by saying “let’s think step by step”. Its mechanism is hidden in the generation loop from Level 0. The model performs a fixed amount of computation per token. When it writes out intermediate steps it gains two things: more tokens, meaning more computation; and subsequent tokens are now produced while looking at those intermediate results. The written text acts like the model’s working memory.

    Then there is the sentence “take a deep breath and work on this problem step by step”. It is reported to have been found not by a human but by an optimization method that tries prompts automatically (Google DeepMind’s OPRO work, 2023), for a specific model and a specific maths dataset. We could not re-verify this detail against the primary source for this course; but the lesson does not change: a phrase an optimizer found on one model is not a portable “spell” for another model. The essence was the “step by step” part.

    Reasoning models brought thinking inside

    As you saw in Level 1, current models are trained with reinforcement learning to produce thinking tokens before answering. So what was requested from the outside with a prompt in 2022 is now a trained behavior of the model. Anthropic’s current guide says so explicitly: on Fable 5.x, Opus 5 / 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 you should rely on the thinking feature rather than a hand-written chain of thought; a prompt asking the model to write its reasoning between <thinking> tags can be rejected. Manual CoT is only a fallback for when thinking is turned off.

    You now steer how much thinking happens with settings, not with sentences in the prompt. In Claude this is called effort (Level 1). In OpenAI, for GPT-5.5, it is reasoning_effort: none, low, medium (default), high, xhigh. OpenAI’s guide also notes that higher effort is not always better: it can lead to overthinking and to unnecessary searching.

    A short history of chain of thought

    Step through it. For each era, see what was written in the prompt, why it worked and what it means today.

    So what should you write today?

    This shift has a practical consequence: the long thinking recipes common in old prompt libraries, of the “first analyze the problem, then list the options, then evaluate each one, then decide” kind, are largely unnecessary on a model with thinking enabled; in that situation Anthropic’s guide treats manual CoT only as a fallback. There is also the risk of tying the reasoning the model learned in training to a fixed sequence you wrote. Removing these recipes and measuring the result on a small task set is one of the first clean-ups to do when moving from one model to the next.

    Instead of telling the model how to think, tell it what it needs to achieve and how the result will be evaluated. On a hard problem, give the evaluation criteria; give example solutions (examples shape internal reasoning too); raise the effort for genuinely hard work. If you want a short justification inside the answer, ask for it as part of the output format: “At the end, justify your choice in two sentences.”

    CautionA thinking summary is not a faithful record of the model’s actual computation (Level 1). An agent that thinks “I checked the tests” may not have run the tests. Tie verification not to the model’s narrative but to the result of a command the harness actually ran (Level 5).

    The end of prefill

    Prefill used to be a trick people working with Claude used a lot: you put a partial assistant message at the end of the messages array, and the model continues its answer from there. If the last message is "{", the model has to start writing JSON; if it is "Root cause:", it gets straight to the point. It was a cheap, effective technique used everywhere.

    According to Anthropic’s guide, starting with the Claude 4.6 models, prefilling the last assistant turn returns an HTTP 400 error. So if your old code uses prefill, the request is rejected outright once you switch to a new model. The guide suggests three migration paths:

    • For JSON and a fixed schema: structured outputs or a tool with a schema (strict: true). Instead of “forcing” the format with text, you guarantee it at the API level (Level 4).
    • To cut the preamble: say it explicitly in the system instruction: “Respond directly without a preamble.”
    • For a reminder in a long conversation: put the reminder inside the next user turn.

    Migrating off prefill: old request, error, new request

    Pick one of the three needs prefill used to solve. Compare the old request, the response you would get from a current Claude model and the recommended new request as raw JSON. The error message text is representative; the 400 status is documented behavior.

    Around the same timeA similar shutdown happened to sampling parameters: on current Claude models, non-default temperature, top_p and top_k values return 400 (Level 0). The common lesson: old “low-level” settings and tricks are being replaced by high-level, explicitly supported mechanisms.

    Key takeaways

    • “Think step by step” worked because the written intermediate steps gave the model extra computation and working memory. Reasoning models now do this by themselves.
    • On current Claude models, rely on the thinking feature and the effort setting instead of manual CoT; asking for thinking with a <thinking> tag can be rejected.
    • From Claude 4.6 onwards, prefill returns 400. For JSON use structured outputs or a strict tool; for the preamble, a system instruction; for reminders, the user turn.
    Sources
    1. Kojima et al.: Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners (2022)
    2. Yang et al.: Large Language Models as Optimizers (OPRO, 2023; not re-verified for this course)
    3. Anthropic: Claude prompting best practices (thinking, migrating off prefill)
    4. OpenAI: GPT-5.5 guide (reasoning_effort)

    A prompt is a ticket

    You have known for years what a good bug report looks like: which environment, which steps, what was expected, what happened, what the log says. A task given to an agent is exactly that kind of report. The difference: the colleague reading this report starts working without asking questions and fills in the missing information with their own guesses.

    You already know thisScrum’s “definition of done”, the “steps to reproduce” in a good bug report and the code-review question “what does this PR not change?”. A good task definition for an agent is the sum of those three. It is not a new skill; it is doing what you already do inside a team, in writing and completely.

    The parts of a coding task

    Context

    Which system, which screen or endpoint, since when, the evidence you have (log, error, measurement). Things the model cannot work out from the repo.

    Task

    An explicit verb and scope: find the root cause and fix it; report only; write a test first.

    Constraint and reason

    What must not be touched, and why. The reason lets the model recognize exceptions correctly.

    Done and verification

    Which command must pass, what is delivered at the end (root cause, changed files), and in what format.

    Stop condition

    When it should stop and ask instead of carrying on alone: a schema change, a public API, a deletion.

    In the simulation below we repair a typical “urgent” message step by step using these parts. At each step, watch how the prompt changes, its token count, and how the agent’s likely first move shifts. The agent moves are representative, but each is based on behavior described in the relevant guides.

    Repairing an “URGENT” message step by step

    Press Next or Play. Green lines are additions; red, struck-through lines are removals. In the box below, see why this step matters and how the agent’s first move changes.

    Isn’t a long prompt expensive?

    The final version takes several times more tokens than the first. But that arithmetic is misleading. You saw in the first topic that by turn 40 the request is hundreds of thousands of tokens; the few hundred tokens you add to the task definition are a rounding error there. The real cost is in the extra turns a vague task causes: reading the wrong files, undoing unwanted refactors, correcting “no, that’s not what I meant” three times. Every extra turn means resending the entire history (Level 2).

    Claude Code’s best-practices page has concrete advice on this: watch the first minute, and press Esc the moment the agent goes off track; after two failed corrections, run /clear and write a better prompt. Trying to fix a polluted context is usually more expensive than starting over with a clean one (failure modes in Level 5).

    Review, performance, tests: the same pattern

    The same parts apply to work other than bug fixing. Below are three everyday requests. Click the marked parts; see what information each part gives the model and what would happen without it.

    Three requests, before and after

    Pick a request type. In the “after” text on the right, click the underlined parts. Each part closes a separate gap.

    Click an underlined part.

    When is a short prompt enough?

    This lesson is not saying “every prompt should be a page long”. If the context is already in the context window, a short message works perfectly. In a session where you have just investigated a bug together, “now fix it and run the test” is enough, because the context, the evidence and the goal were already discussed in earlier turns. The criterion is not length but missing information: when the model reads this message, which question will it have to answer by guessing?

    Conversely, the first message of a new session, or the first message after /clear, is like the first ticket handed to a colleague who has just walked in. There, a short message means the model fills every gap with “average project” assumptions. There is one more distinction: if you rewrite the same context in every session (the build command, the test command, the decimal rule for money), that information belongs not in the task definition but in the project instruction file. The task definition should carry only what is specific to this job.

    In practiceOn a large or ambiguous job, ask the model for the diagnosis and the plan before the code: “Before making any changes, write the root cause and your plan in two paragraphs.” Catching a wrong diagnosis before any code is written is much cheaper than reverting a wrong diff. Claude Code’s plan mode is this habit built into the harness (Level 8).

    Four common mistakes

    • Dictating the solution. Say “add a null check on line X” and the model does no diagnosis; if your diagnosis is wrong, the fix is wrong too. Give the problem and the evidence; if you want the solution, have it explained first.
    • Leaving the scope open. If you don’t forbid “while I’m here” clean-ups, the agent may, with the best intentions, touch places it should not. Write down the scope and its reason.
    • Not allowing an empty result. If a review request doesn’t say “if there are no findings, say so”, the model is more inclined to produce weak findings just to find something.
    • Leaving verification to the model. “Make sure” is not verification. Give it a command to run, a test that must pass, an output to compare against.

    Key takeaways

    • A good task definition = context + explicit task + constraint with reason + done/verification + stop condition.
    • Shouting, personas and tips carry no information; removing them costs nothing.
    • A few hundred extra tokens of clarity are always cheaper than a few extra turns.
    • Stop an agent that goes off track early; after two failed corrections, a clean context and a better prompt.
    Sources
    1. Claude Code: Best practices (concrete tasks, verification, Esc and /clear)
    2. Anthropic: Claude prompting best practices (the suggest-versus-change example)
    3. OpenAI: GPT-5.5 guide (allowed side effects, stopping conditions)

    From “How do I say it?” to “What do I put in the window?”

    In a single question and answer, the wording of the prompt matters. In a forty-turn agent session, the wording is a small part of the request. The real question changes: on each turn, which tokens get put in front of the model, and which stay out?

    In September 2025 Anthropic gave this question a name: context engineering. Its definition: the natural progression of prompt engineering; strategies for curating all the tokens the model sees at inference time (system prompt, tools, MCP, external data, message history). And this curation is redone on every turn. The same article defines an agent in one plain sentence too: LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop.

    Why isn’t “more context” better?

    The window has grown: as of November 2026, all current Claude models offer a 1M-token context (Level 2). But fitting in the window does not mean the model will use all of it with equal attention. Anthropic describes context as a finite attention budget: every token eats a piece of that budget.

    On the evidence side there is Chroma’s context rot report from July 2025. Across 18 models, including Claude, GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5 and Qwen3, it showed that even on simple tasks, performance becomes increasingly unreliable as input grows. In one of its most striking experiments (LongMemEval) the same question was asked once with a focused input of about 300 tokens containing only the relevant part, and once with the full input of about 113 thousand tokens; the focused input did better on every model. Thinking narrowed the gap but did not close it.

    The right altitude for a system prompt

    Anthropic’s context engineering article describes a “Goldilocks zone” for the system prompt between two extremes. At one end are brittle instructions written like if/else: they try to hard-code every situation and break on the first unforeseen one. At the other end are vague, high-level exhortations: they give the model no concrete signal, and the model assumes a shared context. The target is the smallest set of information that fully describes the expected behavior: the right altitude.

    System prompt altitude

    Three different system prompts for Example Co’s internal order-support agent. Change the altitude; compare the text, the token count and the typical way it fails.

    Preload, or fetch when needed?

    There are two ways to introduce an agent to a repo. The first is preloading: putting everything that might be relevant into the context up front. The second is just-in-time retrieval: keeping only lightweight references (file paths, queries, URLs) in the context and fetching the data with tools when it is needed. Claude Code does the second: instead of indexing the codebase in advance, it searches on demand with tools such as grep, glob and reading the head of a file. Anthropic’s Agent SDK article also recommends starting with agentic search, and finds semantic search less accurate, harder to maintain and less transparent. In practice the best option is often a hybrid: a small map up front, details on demand.

    The same question, three context strategies

    Task: “Why is amount rounding wrong in example.orders?” A repo of about 400 files. Pick a strategy; compare the tokens that enter the context, how many of them are actually relevant, and the cost of the input resent over a 20-turn session. Token counts are representative; prices are the November 2026 Opus 5.5 list price.

    The toolbox for long sessions

    The other techniques of context engineering will come up one by one in later levels; let’s draw their map here:

    • Compaction. A context that is nearly full is summarized, and work continues from the summary in a new window. The Claude Code documentation states the price openly: detailed instructions from the start of the conversation can be lost. That is why lasting rules are written into CLAUDE.md (Levels 2 and 8).
    • Clearing tool results. Dropping old tool output that is no longer needed from the context; the lightest form of compaction.
    • Structured notes. Notes the agent writes outside the context (a NOTES.md, a to-do list, a progress file) and reads back later (Level 5, long tasks).
    • Subagents. Helper agents that do exploration in a clean context and return a summary of usually 1,000–2,000 tokens to the main agent (Level 8).
    • Progressive disclosure. For skills, only the name and description are loaded up front; the body when it becomes relevant, linked files only when needed.
    • Tools are context too. Every tool definition takes up space in every request. A small number of non-overlapping tools; tool search for large numbers of MCP tools (Level 4).
    In practiceThe Claude Code documentation says this about CLAUDE.md: every line takes a small share of the model’s attention on every task. Keep the file short; move long procedures (cutting a release, data-fix steps) into skills. If you find yourself emphasizing a line a little more every week, that line probably belongs in a hook (Level 6).
    You already know thisContext engineering resembles designing a cache and memory hierarchy. You cannot put everything into the L1 cache (the context); you keep hot data there and pull the rest from main memory or disk (the file system, tools) when needed. A bad layout slows down every access, like a cache full of the wrong data.

    Key takeaways

    • Context engineering is the job of choosing all the tokens to put in front of the model on each turn; the wording of the prompt is only one part of it.
    • More context is not better: performance degrades as input grows (context rot). Focused input did better on every model.
    • A system prompt should sit at the right altitude: neither a pile of if/else nor empty exhortation.
    • Instead of preloading, keep lightweight references and fetch details on demand; a hybrid is often best.
    Sources
    1. Anthropic: Effective context engineering for AI agents (29 September 2025)
    2. Chroma: Context Rot (14 July 2025)
    3. Anthropic: Building agents with the Claude Agent SDK (agentic search)
    4. Claude Code: How Claude Code works (compaction, /context)
    5. Claude Code: Best practices (keep CLAUDE.md short, procedures in skills)
    6. Anthropic: Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills (progressive disclosure)

    The model runs nothing

    You watch a coding agent read files, run tests, query a database. But the model does none of that. The model only produces tokens; some of those tokens form a machine-parseable piece of JSON that says “I want to run this tool with these arguments.” What actually runs it is your code, or the harness you use.

    Anthropic’s documentation says it plainly: the model executes nothing on its own; it produces a structured request, your code performs the operation, and the result flows back. Take that sentence seriously and the whole architecture of tool use falls into place: permissions, security, error handling, logging, all of it lives on your side. On the model’s side there is only one decision: on this turn, do I write text or do I ask for a tool?

    How does the model know how to make that decision? During post-training (we saw it in level 1) it was trained to read tool definitions and emit well-formed call blocks. So tool use is as much a learned behavior of the model as it is an API feature. The API then draws a strict contract around that behavior.

    The four moves of the loop

    1. Request. Your code sends the API the system prompt, the tools array (name, description, input_schema for each tool) and the messages array. The API is stateless: the whole history goes out again on every request (level 2).
    2. Decision. If the model needs a tool, instead of plain text it emits one or more tool_use blocks: id, name, input. The response ends with stop_reason: "tool_use". That means “I’ve stopped, your turn.”
    3. Execution. Your code reads the block, validates the input, checks permissions and runs the tool. Whether it reads a file, runs SQL or makes an HTTP request, from here on it is ordinary software.
    4. Result. Your code appends the model’s response to the history as an assistant message, then appends a user message whose content starts with tool_result blocks, and calls the model again. Each tool_result says which call it answers through its tool_use_id field.

    Here is what it looks like raw. The model’s response:

    {
  "role": "assistant",
  "stop_reason": "tool_use",
  "content": [
    { "type": "text", "text": "Let me look up the order record." },
    { "type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_01",
      "name": "example_orders_get", "input": { "order_id": 1042 } }
  ]
}

    The two messages you append to the messages array of your next request:

    { "role": "assistant", "content": [ ...the content above, verbatim... ] },
{ "role": "user", "content": [
    { "type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_01",
      "content": "{\"order_id\":1042,\"status_code\":\"DELIVERED\"}" }
] }

    Note: you put the model’s response back into the history exactly as it was. The model does not “remember” its previous turn; you show it again. That is also why tool_use_id exists: if the model asked for three tools in the same turn, this id is the only way it can match each result to its request.

    You already know thisThe request-reply pattern in message queues: the client sends a message with a correlation id, and the reply comes back with the same id. Here the client is the model, the worker listening on the queue is your code, and the correlation id is tool_use.id ↔ tool_result.tool_use_id. Or the planner-executor split: the model writes a plan, the executor carries it out and reports back. The planner cannot know whether the executor really ran anything; it sees whatever gets reported to it.

    Three buckets of tools

    In Anthropic’s API, tools fall into three groups depending on who defines them and who runs them. The split matters because it tells you where the responsibility lies.

    Your tools

    You write the name, the description, the schema; you also run them. Business tools like example_orders_get and your own MCP servers live here. The loop turns in your code.

    Anthropic-schema client tools

    bash, text_editor, memory, computer, browser. Anthropic defines the schema; running them is still your job. Because the model was trained on thousands of successful trajectories with exactly these signatures, it calls them more reliably. We come back to them in level 6 as “tools baked into training.”

    Server tools

    web_search, web_fetch, code_execution, tool_search. They run on Anthropic’s infrastructure; the result arrives inside the response. If the server-side loop hits an iteration limit, the response comes back with pause_turn, and you resend the request to let it continue.

    The strict rules of the contract

    The API checks the shape of the message history tightly. The rules are not arbitrary; they preserve the order the model saw during training. Break them and the model never runs at all; the request comes back with HTTP 400:

    • Results come immediately. The user message carrying the results must come right after the assistant message that contains tool_use. You cannot slip another message in between.
    • Results first. In that user message’s content array, the tool_result blocks sit at the very start. Put a text block in front of them and you get a 400; if you need to add a note from the user, add it after the results.
    • Parallel results in one message. If the model asked for two tools in the same turn, both tool_results go in the same user message (topic 4).
    • Every request expects an answer. For every tool_use block you return a tool_result with the right tool_use_id. Even if the tool blew up: in that case is_error: true and an explanatory message.

    The last rule is the one most often skipped in practice. When an exception happens inside a tool, handing the error back to the model with is_error: true instead of crashing the loop gives the model a chance to correct itself. According to Anthropic’s documentation, after an invalid call the model usually retries two or three times with corrections, and then apologizes and gives up. Whether those retries work depends on the quality of the error message. In the simulation below, see for yourself the difference between “failed” and an actionable error message.

    The raw journey of a tool call

    Why was Example Co’s order 1042 delivered late? Three model calls, two parallel tools, one error and one correction. At each step, see the real-format JSON going out or coming in; the yellow lines show the id ↔ tool_use_id matching and the fields that drive the loop. Use the buttons at the top to inject a fault and watch how the loop changes.

    The OpenAI side: same idea, different field names

    OpenAI’s Responses API builds the same loop; the names differ, and so does one important detail.

    Anthropic MessagesOpenAI Responses
    Definitionname, description, input_schematype:"function", name, description, parameters, strict
    The model’s requesttool_use block: id, name, input (object)function_call item: call_id, name, arguments (JSON string)
    Your answertool_result: tool_use_id, content, is_errorfunction_call_output: call_id, output
    “Your turn” signalstop_reason: "tool_use"function_call items present in the output

    That arguments is a string is a small but sneaky difference: your code has to open it with JSON.parse, and that step can blow up. When it does, don’t bring the loop down; return a function_call_output that explains the parse error and let the model fix it. With strict mode on (next topic) this class of error practically disappears.

    CautionThe model sees only what you show it as a result, and it reads it. A web page, an email, an issue comment or a notes field in the example.customers table can contain text that looks like instructions. That is why Anthropic recommends putting untrusted content inside a tool_result rather than in the system prompt. But that alone is not protection; the real defense is the permission boundaries in the harness. Level 10: prompt injection.

    Common mistakes

    • Sending only the results without appending the model’s response to the history. The API rejects a tool_result that has nothing to answer.
    • Not catching the tool’s exception and letting the loop crash. The agent dies on an error it could have fixed itself.
    • Returning "failed" or an 80-line traceback as the error message. The first carries no information; the second floods the context (topic 3).
    • Believing the model “ran” the tool and leaving logging to the model. Only your code knows what actually ran; the audit trail belongs there.

    Key takeaways

    • The model does not call the tool; it writes a request to call it. Your code runs it, validates it and returns the result.
    • The key to the loop is stop_reason: "tool_use"; the key to the matching is tool_use.id ↔ tool_use_id.
    • The contract is strict: results come immediately, sit at the start of the content, and parallel results share one message. Otherwise, 400.
    • A tool error is not the end of the loop; it is an is_error: true result. The quality of the error message decides whether the model recovers.
    Sources
    1. Anthropic: How tool use works
    2. Anthropic: Handle tool calls
    3. OpenAI: Function calling

    A tool definition is a prompt

    The model decides when and how to use a tool by looking only at the three fields you wrote: name, description and input schema. It has no access to your source code, your tests or your wiki page. Those three fields are the only user manual the tool offers the model.

    An example from the research, a tool that searches shipment events:

    {
  "name": "example_shipments_search",
  "description": "Search shipment events for one order in example.shipments.
    Use when the user asks where an order is or why it was late.
    Returns events oldest-first. Use response_format=summary unless
    the user needs every scan.",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "order_id": { "type": "integer", "description": "example.orders.order_id" },
      "response_format": { "type": "string", "enum": ["summary", "full"] }
    },
    "required": ["order_id"],
    "additionalProperties": false
  },
  "strict": true
}

    Field by field

    name is the tool’s identity in the model’s mind, and it sits in the same list as every other tool. A name like search loses its meaning when three different MCP servers bring the same name. A namespace by service and resource (example_shipments_search) both makes selection easier and prevents collisions. In the next topic we look at its measured effect.

    description is where the real work happens. A good description answers four questions: what the tool does, when it should be used (and when not), what it returns, and what its limits and traps are. Anthropic recommends writing tool descriptions “as if you were explaining them to a new hire.” In their own SWE-bench Verified work they report that improving the tool descriptions alone took Claude Sonnet 3.5 to the best result of its time.

    input_schema is a standard JSON Schema object: type, properties, required, enum, a per-field description. The schema does two jobs: it tells the model what it has to send, and it gives you a contract for validating the incoming input. Two near-identical field names (user and user_id), a format field left as free text, an id with an ambiguous type: these are places where the model has to guess, and every guess is a chance of error.

    Myth“The schema is enough; the description is decoration, keep it short to save tokens.” The schema says what is valid; the description says what is right. When the model picks between two valid tools, it looks at the description, not the schema. Anthropic’s SWE-bench result came precisely from improving descriptions. You save tokens not by trimming descriptions but by removing unnecessary tools or loading definitions lazily (topic 5).

    strict: true and the guaranteed schema

    By default the model “reads” the schema but is not bound by it; sometimes it skips a required field, writes a value outside the enum, puts a string where an integer belongs. You validate the input, return an error, the model fixes it; that costs a turn and a few thousand tokens. In strict mode the API guarantees that the generated input will conform to the schema. Anthropic describes it plainly as something that “eliminates invalid calls.” The price is a few restrictions on the schema.

    On the OpenAI side the restrictions are spelled out: strict mode requires additionalProperties: false, and every field in properties must be in the required list. You express an optional field not as “may be absent” but as “may be null”:

    "response_format": { "type": ["string", "null"], "enum": ["summary", "full", null] }
"required": ["order_id", "response_format"]

    It feels odd at first, but it makes sense: the schema behaves like a grammar; instead of the ambiguity of “this field is either there or not,” saying “this field is always there, its value may be null” makes generation deterministic.

    input_examples: what the schema can’t say

    JSON Schema can say “a date is a string,” but it can’t say “in this API dates look like 2026-10-01, the time zone is UTC, and in nested filters the customer comes before the status.” Anthropic’s input_examples field lets you add a few sample inputs to the tool definition. By Anthropic’s own measurement (November 2025, vendor data) accuracy on complex parameters rose from 72% to 90%. Examples are tokens too; add them not to every tool, only to the ones whose input is genuinely complex.

    The token cost of definitions

    Tool definitions don’t travel through some magic side channel; they are part of the prompt and are resent on every request. As of November 2026, according to Anthropic’s documentation, when tool use is enabled the API adds a tool-use system prompt of roughly 286 tokens before your definitions (Opus, Sonnet and Haiku 5.5). When you force a tool (tool_choice: any or tool, topic 4) that number grows; the example given for Opus 5 is 406 versus 286. Each definition’s own tokens come on top.

    There is a second, less well-known consequence: prompt caching (level 2). At Anthropic the cache prefix is built in the order tools → system → messages, and changing the tool definitions invalidates the entire cache. Adding a tool mid-session, “touching up” a description or shuffling the order of the list means the whole prefix gets written from scratch on the next request. Keep the tool list fixed for the whole session. That is also why the current MCP version recommends that the tools/list response be deterministic (topic 6).

    You already know thisLike writing an OpenAPI document, except the reader can’t ask questions, rereads the document from the top on every request and pays by the word. OpenAI’s guide calls this the “intern test”: with the information you gave the model, could an intern use this function correctly? If not, the model can’t either.

    Tool design workbench

    Build the same shipment tool with different choices. On the right, see the resulting definition, an approximate token count and what each choice tells the model. If a note is red, the model has to guess at that point. Switch the provider to see the OpenAI form of the same tool and how the strict rules transform the schema.

      Pitfalls

      • Overlapping tools. If search_orders and find_orders sit in the same list, the model picks between them at random. If a human can’t say for sure which one to use, neither can the model.
      • A description that lies. A tool that says “fast” but takes 40 seconds leads the model to call it again and again inside the loop. The description must describe the real behavior.
      • Shouting in capitals. Phrases like “CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when…” were written for older models to fix under-calling; on newer models they cause over-calling. Anthropic recommends toning it down: “Use this tool when…”. Details in level 3.

      Key takeaways

      • Name, description and schema are everything the model knows about a tool. Put as much effort into the description as into the code.
      • Vague name, vague parameter, free-text format field: each one is a place where the model guesses.
      • strict: true closes off the class of invalid calls; on OpenAI every field is required and optionality is expressed with null.
      • Definitions are tokens on every request and the start of the cache prefix. Keep the list fixed within a session.
      Sources

      2. Anthropic: Writing effective tools for agents (11 September 2025)
      3. Anthropic: Advanced tool use (input_examples, 24 November 2025)
      4. OpenAI: Function calling (strict rules)
      5. Anthropic: Prompt caching

      Designing an interface for an agent

      You know user interface design: the same function is easy with a good screen and impossible with a bad one. The same holds for agents. The SWE-agent paper calls this the agent-computer interface (ACI) and shows that the same model does markedly better when only the interface changes.

      In the SWE-agent work (Yang et al., NeurIPS 2024), GPT-4 Turbo solved about 11% of SWE-bench Lite with a raw shell alone; with a windowed file viewer showing 100 lines, an edit command with a linter that rejects syntactically broken edits, and a search with short output, it rose to about 18%; with the edit command removed it fell to around 10%. These figures come from secondary summaries; check them against the table in the paper before quoting them. But the direction is beyond dispute: same model, different interface, different result. In level 6 we extend this idea to the whole harness.

      Anthropic’s seven principles

      In September 2025 Anthropic compiled its own experience of writing tools. Below I walk through each principle using Example Co’s order system.

      1. Don’t wrap endpoints; consolidate around the workflow. Giving the agent three tools because your REST API exposes list_users, list_events, create_event means also loading the orchestration onto it: three turns, three results in context, three chances for an error in between. Anthropic’s example merges them into a single schedule_event tool, and offers search_logs instead of read_logs. On the order side: instead of “fetch the order, then fetch the shipments, then decode the status code,” one tool that returns the information needed to answer the delay question in one go.
      2. Namespace. example_orders_search, example_shipments_search. When several MCP servers pour tools into the same list, the namespace rescues both selection and readability. Anthropic reports that even the choice of prefix versus suffix has a measurable effect.
      3. Return meaningful context. Human-readable names instead of UUIDs: not customer_id: "9f3c…" but customer: "Example Co". Let the model choose the level of detail it needs with a response_format enum (concise / detailed). In Anthropic’s Slack example the concise format took about a third of the tokens of the detailed one.
      4. Respect tokens. Pagination, filters, truncation with sensible defaults. Claude Code cuts tool responses off at 25,000 tokens. When you truncate, tell the model so and show it how to narrow the next request: “Showing the first 200 records; use a narrower date range or a status_code filter.”
      5. Actionable errors. Not a traceback but what is wrong and what is right: the valid values and an example of correct input.
      6. Write descriptions as if for a new hire. Spell out implicit knowledge (internal terms, abbreviations, relationships between resources). Don’t leave parameter names ambiguous: not user but user_id.
      7. Measure with realistic tasks. Not single-call toy tests but real tasks that chain several tools. Have the model analyze the transcripts and rewrite the tools. In Anthropic’s multi-agent research system, a tool-testing agent rewrote tool descriptions and cut task time for subsequent agents by 40% (vendor data).

      Same question, three tool designs

      Question: “Which errors happened in example_app last night between 02:00 and 03:00?” For each design, see what lands in the model’s context and how many tokens it takes. Token counts are illustrative; the ratio of the concise format being about a third of the detailed one comes from Anthropic’s Slack example.

      Poka-yoke: make the mistake impossible

      Poka-yoke, from Japanese manufacturing engineering, means a design that makes misuse physically impossible: like a USB plug that can’t go in upside down. In December 2024, while working on its SWE-bench agent, Anthropic saw the model make mistakes with relative file paths after it had moved out of the root directory. The fix was not to tell the model “be careful” but to make the tool require an absolute path; that eliminated a whole class of errors.

      Poka-yoke opportunities in your own tools: require ids as integers, constrain formats with enums, add a confirmation field for dangerous operations, accept a single date format and write it in the description. Writing a rule into the prompt is a request; writing it into the schema is a guarantee. We will see the general form of this idea in level 6 under “the right place for a rule.”

      You already know thisThe difference between git status and git status --porcelain. The first is designed for humans, the second for machines; same information, different consumer. The response_format enum is the agent version of the same idea. And an actionable tool error is to the model what a good CLI error message (“unknown option --forse; did you mean --force?”) is to you.

      An error message is an instruction

      When a tool returns an error, that message is the only information the model has. Say “failed” and the model, with no idea what happened, repeats the same call or tries a random variation. Return a traceback and it will most likely find the fix, but it dumps internal file paths and stack frames into the context; a long stack takes thousands of tokens. An actionable message gives the model enough information to fix things on the next turn, and no more than it needs. MCP’s 2025-11-25 version also requires input validation errors to be returned not as protocol errors but as tool execution errors; the goal is exactly that the model can see the error and correct itself.

      Three error messages, three different next turns

      The model sent the date to the example_orders_search tool in the wrong format. The tool can return the error in three different ways. For each one, see what the model does next (simulated) and what it costs.

      Pitfalls

      • One tool that does everything. Taking “consolidate around the workflow” too far and writing an example_do_anything with 30 parameters just moves the selection problem from the tool list to the parameter list. The yardstick: a tool should map to a question the user might ask or a job they might want done.
      • Returning everything “just in case.” The model does not ignore the extra fields; it reads them, reasons about them and sometimes uses the wrong one. Make the default response short and the detail optional.
      • Silent truncation. Cutting the result at 200 lines without saying so leads the model to draw a confident conclusion from incomplete data. If you truncated, write the count and how to get the rest.
      • Secrets in the error message. An exception text containing a connection string, an internal server name or a token goes straight into the context, from there into the logs, and maybe on to another tool. An error message is text written for the model; don’t put anything there you wouldn’t show a user.

      Key takeaways

      • Tools are the agent’s interface; the same model works markedly better with a good interface.
      • Don’t wrap endpoints; consolidate the workflow into one tool. Namespace, return meaningful names, let the model choose the level of detail.
      • When truncating, say how to narrow; when returning an error, give an example of the correct input.
      • Bake the rule into the schema where possible (poka-yoke): a guarantee, not a request.
      Sources

      2. Anthropic: Building effective agents (19 December 2024, ACI and poka-yoke)
      3. Yang et al.: SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces (NeurIPS 2024)
      4. Anthropic: How we built our multi-agent research system (13 June 2025)
      5. MCP 2025-11-25 changelog

      Several calls in one turn

      The model can emit more than one tool_use block in the same response. These are called parallel tool calls, and at Anthropic they are on by default. This small feature radically changes both the duration and the cost of an agent session.

      Why? Because every model turn costs two things. The first is time: the model takes time to process its input and to produce its output token by token; the tool itself is often faster than that. The second is tokens: because the API is stateless, the whole history is resent on every turn. If the model reads three files one by one, that is four turns, with a growing history in all four. If it asks for all three in the same turn, two turns. The gap widens as the number of independent reads grows.

      Nothing new on the mechanism side: the model writes several blocks, each with its own id. Your code can run them concurrently if it wants, and sends all the results back in a single user message, each with its own tool_use_id. You saw this in the simulation in topic 1: toolu_01 and toolu_02 went out in the same turn, and their results came back in the same message.

      Sequential vs parallel: the timeline

      Change the model turn duration and the number of independent tools. Purple blocks are model turns, blue blocks are tool execution. Below, see the number of model calls and how many times the history was resent in total. Durations and tokens are illustrative; the relationship is real.

      1.6
      3

      When is parallel safe?

      On the model’s side, parallelism is a suggestion; your executor decides what actually runs concurrently. Independent reads (two files, three queries) run in parallel without trouble. Two calls that write to the same resource (two edits on the same file, two requests updating the same order), however, must be serialized; just because the model wrote two blocks in the same turn doesn’t mean you have to run them at the same time. It is the same engineering decision as running independent SELECTs in parallel in a database while queueing the UPDATEs.

      If you want to turn parallelism off, use disable_parallel_tool_use: true inside tool_choice at Anthropic, or parallel_tool_calls: false at OpenAI; OpenAI says that in that case a turn will contain zero or one call. In the other direction, you can also increase parallel calling: the <use_parallel_tool_calls> block in Anthropic’s prompting guide is said to raise doing independent operations in the same turn to “nearly 100%”. For Fable 5.1, repeating that instruction on every turn is recommended (as of November 2026).

      tool_choice: who picks the tool?

      By default the model decides on its own whether to use a tool. tool_choice lets you narrow that decision.

      AnthropicMeaningOpenAI equivalent
      autoDefault. The model calls a tool or answers with text.auto
      anyThe model must call a tool; it decides which one itself.required
      tool + nameIt must call one specific tool.Forcing a specific function
      noneNo call is made even if tool definitions are sent.none
      (no equivalent)allowed_tools: restrict to a subset without changing the list

      When does forcing make sense? The most common use is structured data extraction: you define a “record” tool, force it with tool, and the input the model produces is exactly the JSON you wanted. This approach has gained importance: since the Claude 4.6 models, prefilling the last assistant turn returns a 400 error; the recommended ways to get JSON are structured outputs or tools (level 3). Inside a conversation, though, forcing is usually a bad idea: with any on, the model has to call a tool even if the user just says “thanks.”

      OpenAI’s allowed_tools option reflects a subtle engineering decision: changing the tool list breaks the prompt cache (topic 2), but passing the allowed subset in a separate field doesn’t. So you can say “only read tools in this step” and keep the cache. A warning applies at Anthropic too: changing tool_choice invalidates the messages part of the cache. Don’t change it on every turn.

      Change tool_choice, watch the behavior

      Two different user messages, four tool_choice settings. See the relevant part of the request body and the model’s (simulated) behavior. Try turning off parallel calls as well.

      tool_choice
      User

      Tuning triggering through the prompt

      tool_choice is a blunt switch; fine-tuning happens in the prompt. Anthropic’s documentation gives two extreme examples: “Use the tools to investigate before responding.” increases tool calling; a phrase in the style of “Use your judgment…” makes the model more conservative. Because newer models are far more sensitive to the system prompt, aggressive phrasing written to fix under-triggering in older models now causes over-triggering. OpenAI says the same thing: a team working with GPT-5 describes how the instruction “Be THOROUGH when gathering information” caused unnecessary searches even on small tasks, and softening the wording fixed it.

      Common mistakes

      • Splitting results across messages. Sending the results of two parallel calls in two separate user messages breaks the contract: the first message is missing the answer to toolu_02. Collect all the results and send them in one message.
      • Getting stuck on the slowest tool. In a parallel turn the model waits until all results arrive. If one hangs, the turn hangs. Put a timeout on every tool; when it expires, return is_error: true for that call with a result like “No response within 30 s, retry with a narrower filter,” and don’t hold up the others.
      • Running parallel side effects blindly. The model may ask for “edit the file” and “run the tests” in the same turn. Run them at the same time and the tests run against the old file. Execute calls with side effects sequentially, in the order the model wrote them.
      • Leaving tool_choice pinned. If you forget to switch a setting you moved to tool for an extraction step back to auto on the next conversation turn, the model answers every message by calling that same tool.

      Key takeaways

      • Parallel calls reduce the number of model turns and the history that gets resent. Independent reads in parallel, writes to the same resource in sequence.
      • All parallel results go in one user message, each with its own tool_use_id.
      • tool_choice: auto for conversation, tool for structured extraction. any and tool enlarge the system prompt.
      • Don’t change the tool list or tool_choice on every turn; the cache breaks. If you need a subset, use allowed_tools on OpenAI.
      Sources

      2. Anthropic: Prompting best practices (parallel calls, prefill)
      3. OpenAI: Function calling (parallel_tool_calls, allowed_tools)
      4. OpenAI: GPT-5 prompting guide

      Tool definitions are context too

      For an agent working with five tools, the cost of the definitions is negligible. But connect three or four MCP servers and the picture changes: in Anthropic’s own example, 58 MCP tools take about 55,000 tokens before the conversation has even started.

      That creates two separate problems. The first is cost and latency: those 55 thousand tokens go out again on every request. Cache reads make it cheaper but not free; at November 2026 prices, normal input on Opus 5.5 is $4 per million tokens and a cache read is $0.20. The second, sneakier one is attention: the size of the context window (1M today) tells you its capacity, not its quality. As the window fills, recall weakens (context rot, level 2), and picking the right tool among dozens of similar ones gets harder. OpenAI’s function calling guide even gives a rough limit for this: aim for fewer than 20 functions.

      Tool search: load definitions on demand

      Anthropic’s answer is the Tool Search Tool, announced in November 2025. When you mark a tool with defer_loading: true, its definition does not enter the context up front. The model sees a small tool for searching tools; when it needs a capability it searches for it, and only the definitions of matching tools are loaded. Think of it as an application loading modules with dynamic import when needed instead of loading all of them at startup.

      Results reported by Anthropic (vendor data, 24 November 2025): in the 58-tool example the definition load fell from about 55K to about 8.7K tokens (roughly an 85% reduction). On the MCP evaluation, accuracy rose from 49% to 74% on Opus 4 and from 79.5% to 88.1% on Opus 4.5. So it is not just savings; a model that sees fewer but more relevant tools chooses better.

      Claude Code makes this the default: MCP tool definitions are deferred via tool search, and only tool names and server instructions stay in context. You can see this breakdown in your own session with /context (levels 8 and 9). OpenAI also supports tool search and namespaces; as of November 2026 it requires gpt-5.4 or later models.

      Tool budget: what goes out on every request?

      Connect MCP servers, toggle tool search on and off. The bar shows the fixed load that goes out with every request before the conversation starts (scale: the first 100K tokens; the full window is 1M). The per-server breakdown is illustrative; the MCP total is scaled to Anthropic’s 58 tools ≈ 55K → ≈ 8.7K example. Costs use Opus 5.5’s November 2026 prices.

      Programmatic tool calling: keep intermediate results out of the context

      Tool search solves the load of the definitions; the load of the results is a separate problem. Suppose you want to find which of Example Co’s 120 orders delayed in October passed through the TST-2 hub. In the classic flow the model first fetches the orders, then calls the shipment tool for each one; all 120 results enter the context, and the model filters them “in its head.” It is both expensive and error-prone: for an LLM, missing one row in a long list is much easier than writing an if inside a loop.

      With programmatic tool calling, you say allowed_callers: ["code_execution_20250825"] when you define the tool. The model calls these tools not directly but from inside a program it writes in the code execution environment. The loop, the filtering and the joining happen in code; only what the program prints comes back into the context. In Anthropic’s measurement (vendor data) the average tokens per task fell from 43,588 to 27,297 (about 37%).

      120 orders: classic vs programmatic

      Solve the same question with two flows. Compare the number of model calls and the amount of intermediate results that enter the context. The figures are illustrative for this scenario; the direction matches the averages Anthropic reported (43,588 → 27,297 tokens) and the MCP example below (≈150K → ≈2K).

      Exposing MCP as a code API

      On 4 November 2025 Anthropic published a post that takes the same idea one step further: expose MCP servers not as a tool list but as code modules sitting in a file system (like ./servers/google-drive/getDocument.ts). The agent reads the file it needs, writes the code and filters the data inside the sandbox. In the post’s example of moving data from Google Drive to a CRM, token usage dropped from about 150K to about 2K (98.7%). Side benefits: personal data can be masked in the sandbox before it reaches anywhere the model will see it; a piece of code that works can be saved as a skill and reused. Cloudflare calls the same idea “Code Mode.”

      You already know this“Take the computation to the data, don’t bring the data to the computation.” Instead of pulling 120 thousand rows into the application and filtering them in C#, you run the WHERE in the database. Programmatic tool calling is the LLM version of the same decision: do the filtering in code, not in the context.

      Which one when?

      These three techniques solve different bottlenecks; don’t substitute one for another. If the problem is “a tenth of the context is full of tool definitions before the conversation starts,” use tool search. If the problem is “tool results are large and the model reads them only to filter them,” use programmatic tool calling. If the problem is “exposing dozens of services one by one as tools has become unmanageable,” expose MCP as a code API. An agent with five tools and small results needs none of them; an extra layer is extra error surface.

      They have their costs too. With tool search the model has to find the tool: a tool with a bad name and description is no longer merely misused, it is never found at all. That is why the design principles of topics 2 and 3 become even more important as scale grows. There is also no point deferring the few core tools used on every turn; they are needed on every request anyway. With programmatic calling, intermediate results can drop out of your sight just as they drop out of the model’s: if one of the 120 calls inside the code fails silently, the model only sees it if the program prints it. Log the calls inside the sandbox too, and ask the program to report errors explicitly.

      CautionAll of these approaches mean that code written by the model runs somewhere. Anthropic’s post states clearly that this requires a secure sandbox: resource limits, network isolation, observability. Anthropic’s server-side code execution tool provides that environment; if you are building it into your own harness, the responsibility is yours. Level 10.

      Key takeaways

      • Tool definitions are context sent with every request. 58 tools ≈ 55K tokens; selection quality also drops as the number of tools grows.
      • defer_loading + tool search: load definitions when needed. In Anthropic’s example, about 85% fewer tokens and higher accuracy.
      • Programmatic tool calling and exposing MCP as a code API: intermediate results stay in the sandbox, only a summary returns to the context.
      • Every solution that runs code needs a sandbox.
      Sources

      2. Anthropic: Code execution with MCP (4 November 2025)
      3. Claude Code: How Claude Code works (deferred MCP tools)
      4. OpenAI: Function calling (number of tools, tool search)
