      Why a protocol?

      If every AI application writes its own integration with every service, you need N applications × M services worth of integrations. Model Context Protocol (MCP) exists to bring that down to N + M: a service writes an MCP server once, and every MCP-capable application can use it.

      You already know thisLanguage Server Protocol. Editors used to need a separate plugin for every language; with LSP a language writes a server once, and both VS Code and Vim speak to it. MCP makes the same move for tools and data sources; underneath, like LSP, it uses JSON-RPC 2.0.

      Three roles: host, client, server

      The host is the AI application the user works in: Claude Code, an IDE, a desktop app. It is the one that talks to the LLM API, manages user approval and makes the security decisions. The host creates a separate client for each server it connects to; each client holds a one-to-one connection with a single server. The specification’s deliberate design decision: servers must not be able to read the whole conversation, and must not see into one another. Only the host combines the context.

      This also means MCP does not talk to the model directly. The model still writes a tool_use block as in topic 1; the host knows it belongs to an MCP tool, sends a tools/call to the server through the corresponding client, and hands the answer back to the model as a tool_result. MCP is the cable between the harness and the outside world; the contract between the model and the harness stays the same.

      One host, three clients, three servers

      Click the boxes. See what each part knows, what it doesn’t, and which transport it connects over.

      Click a box.

      Primitives: who controls what?

      PrimitiveSideControlled byExample
      ToolsServerModel (it decides whether to call)example_orders_cancel
      ResourcesServerApplication (the host chooses what goes into context)A schema dump addressed by URI
      PromptsServerUser (usually picks it as a slash command)An “Order delay report” template
      Sampling, RootsClientThe server asks, the host fulfilsDeprecated in the current version (below)
      ElicitationClientThe server asks the user for information/approval“Cancel 1042?”

      This “who controls it” column is the least-read yet most important part of MCP. The model can call a tool on its own; that is why, when operations with side effects are exposed as tools, the approval layer must live in the host. A resource, on the other hand, enters the context only when the application or the user selects it.

      Transport: stdio and Streamable HTTP

      With stdio, the host starts the server as a child process and sends JSON-RPC messages line by line over standard input/output. Simple and fast for local tools; credentials come from environment variables and the process runs with your user permissions. With Streamable HTTP, every message is POSTed to a single endpoint; the response comes back as plain JSON or as a request-specific SSE stream. In the current version requests carry the MCP-Protocol-Version, Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers, so a gateway can see which tool is being called without opening the body.

      2026-07-28: the protocol goes stateless

      As of November 2026 the current specification version is 2026-07-28. Compared with the previous version (2025-11-25) it brings a major architectural change; if you learned MCP from an older guide, most of what follows will be new to you.

      Topic2025-11-252026-07-28
      Connection setupinitialize handshake, sessionNo handshake. Every request carries the protocol version and client capabilities in _meta; new and mandatory server/discover
      SessionMcp-Session-Id headerRemoved. A server that needs state issues an explicit handle and passes it around as a tool argument
      Server asking the clientThe server sends its own request (elicitation/create, sampling/createMessage, roots/list)MRTR: the server returns resultType: "input_required", the client resends the request with inputResponses
      DeprecatedRoots, Sampling, Logging (use a tool parameter, call the LLM API directly, log to stderr/OTel), the old HTTP+SSE transport, Dynamic Client Registration
      Long-running workExperimental tasksMoved to the io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks extension
      Cache friendlinesstools/list SHOULD be deterministic; ttlMs, cacheScope on list results

      Why statelessness? In a session-based protocol, requests from the same client have to go to the same server instance; scaling horizontally behind a load balancer gets hard. In the stateless model each request carries its own context, and any instance can answer. MRTR follows from the same logic: the server can no longer ask the client a question over an open channel; it returns a result saying “to do this I need the following information,” and the client adds the answer and repeats the request. It resembles getting a 401 over HTTP and retrying with a token.

      A tool call under 2026-07-28: cancellation with user approval

      The model wants to cancel order 1042; the server first asks for the user’s approval. At each step, see the HTTP headers and the JSON-RPC body. Method names, resultType, inputResponses, ttlMs and the headers come from the specification; some field names inside _meta and in the approval request are simplified and illustrative. See the specification for the exact schema.

      Authorization

      stdio servers take their credentials from the environment. For servers running over HTTP the specification defines OAuth 2.1, and it is quite strict:

      • The MCP server is a resource server and MUST publish Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728); that is where the client learns which authorization server to go to.
      • When requesting a token the client MUST send the resource indicator (RFC 8707); the server MUST verify that the token was issued for it (audience).
      • Token passthrough is forbidden: the server may not accept any other token, and may not forward a token it received to an API behind it. Otherwise the authority you grant one server leaks into everything it talks to.
      • PKCE and iss validation (RFC 9207) are mandatory. With insufficient scope the server returns 403 and a step-up scope flow begins.
      • Dynamic Client Registration is deprecated; Client ID Metadata Documents replace it.
      CautionAdding an MCP server is adding a dependency, and one that can write text straight into your context. Tool descriptions and tool results are text the model reads; a malicious or compromised server can plant instructions there. A stdio server runs with your user permissions; a remote server sees every piece of data you send in tool arguments. Who wrote it, which tools it exposes, which permissions it runs with: review these the way you would review a NuGet or npm package. Details in level 10.
      In practiceAfter connecting a new MCP server, check how much room it takes in Claude Code with /context; gate tools with side effects behind approval using permission rules (level 8). If you are writing your own server, the tool design principles of this level apply unchanged: namespacing, a concise response format, actionable errors, a deterministic tools/list.

      Key takeaways

      • MCP is LSP for tools and data sources: the host opens a separate client for each server, and only the host combines the context.
      • Tools are under the model’s control, resources under the application’s, prompts under the user’s. Approval for tools with side effects lives in the host.
      • With 2026-07-28 the protocol is stateless: no handshake and no session, but there is server/discover; to ask a question the server returns input_required.
      • HTTP servers are protected with OAuth 2.1; token passthrough is forbidden. Every MCP server is a dependency and an attack surface.
      Sources
      1. MCP: Architecture
      2. MCP: Versioning (current version)
      3. MCP 2026-07-28 changelog
      4. MCP 2026-07-28: Transports
      5. MCP 2026-07-28: Authorization
      6. MCP 2025-11-25 changelog

      A one-sentence definition, ten lines of code

      The word agent has been stuck onto so many things in the last two years that its meaning has gone blurry. The definition that is useful to an engineer is short: an agent is a model that runs tools in a loop until it reaches a goal.

      In September 2025 Simon Willison boiled this down to one sentence: “An LLM agent runs tools in a loop to achieve a goal.” Anthropic’s context engineering post says the same thing: an agent is an LLM autonomously using tools in a loop. Both definitions have three parts: tools (we covered them in level 4), the loop (the subject of this level) and the goal, the thing that decides when the loop ends. Take away any one of the three and you no longer have an agent: a loop without tools is just a chat talking to itself, a tool without a loop is a one-off function call, and a loop without a goal is an infinite loop that burns money.

      The canonical loop

      The loop in Anthropic’s tool use documentation works like this. The harness sends the messages and tool definitions to the model. As long as the response’s stop_reason field is "tool_use", the harness runs the requested tools, appends the model’s response (the assistant message) to the history, then appends a user message carrying the tool results, and calls the model again. When stop_reason has any other value, the loop exits. At the heart of every coding agent, no matter how many layers are stacked on top, this loop is beating.

      messages = [user(task)]
for turn in range(MAX_TURNS):                  # hard stop condition
    resp = llm(system, tools, messages)        # PURPLE: the single probabilistic line
    messages.append(assistant(resp.content))   # the response enters the history
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":         # end_turn / max_tokens / refusal
        break
    results = [run(t) for t in resp.tool_uses] # TEAL: deterministic execution
    messages.append(user([tool_result(r) for r in results]))
    if tokens(messages) > BUDGET:              # context management
        messages = compact(messages)
else:
    raise MaxTurnsExceeded()                   # limit reached, controlled failure

      Spend two minutes on this code, because the rest of the course is built around these lines. In the diagram below you can click each line to see what it does, which layer it belongs to and what would break without it.

      What does each line of the loop do?

      Click a line. The color on the left edge shows the line’s layer: purple model, teal harness, amber context. Notice how many lines the intelligence lives in.

      Click a line.

      The intelligence is in one line

      The only “smart” place in the code is the llm(...) call. The model decides what to read, which command to run and whether the work is done. Every other line is ordinary, deterministic, testable software: appending to a list, comparing a field, calling a function. This split is the most solid frame for thinking about agent systems. When something goes wrong, the first question should be: did the model make the wrong decision, or did the harness fail to give it the information, tool or feedback it needed to make the right one? The second case comes up far more often than you would think, and it is also much easier to fix, because that side is the one you write.

      You already know thisThink of the reconcile loop in Kubernetes: the controller observes the current state, compares it with the desired state, takes an action and observes again. It stops when it reaches the desired state. The agent loop has the same skeleton. The difference is that “the gap between desired and current state” is computed by a model, not by a deterministic diff function. That is why neither the stop condition nor the correctness of the action is guaranteed; you have to put fuses around the loop.

      stop_reason: the loop’s steering wheel

      A single field decides where the loop goes. Each stop_reason value means something different to the loop, and harnesses that do not tell them apart break silently. The most common bug is treating everything other than tool_use as “work done”. A response cut off by max_tokens is not finished; it is truncated. refusal is not a finished job but a refused one, and it should be shown to the user as such. In server-side tool loops (such as web search), pause_turn means “I hit the iteration limit, resend the request to continue”; a harness that mistakes it for completion abandons the work halfway.

      stop_reason explorer

      Pick a value. See a trimmed JSON of the model’s response, what the loop should do at that moment and the typical mistake.

      The same loop in the other ecosystem

      The OpenAI Agents SDK loop is a slightly more abstracted version of the same idea. The SDK calls the model; if the output is “final”, meaning there is text output of the requested type and no tool call, it stops. If the output is a handoff, it passes control to another agent. If there are tool calls, it runs them, appends the results and calls again. When the max_turns limit is exceeded it raises MaxTurnsExceeded; if you defined an error handler, you can return a controlled final output instead. So both big providers guarantee the same three things: append tool results to the history, recognize the final answer, set a limit.

      Where did it come from?

      This loop did not appear overnight. The 2022 ReAct paper popularised the idea of having the model write “Thought / Action / Observation” lines in turn and executing the Action line by parsing it out of plain text. Back then the harness caught a line like Action: search[...] with a regular expression; if the model bent the format a little, the loop broke. Toolformer in 2023 showed that a model could learn to insert API calls into its own text. Today’s native tool calling APIs are the productised descendants of those ideas: the model no longer produces free text but a structured tool_use block that matches a schema, and it learns this specifically in post-training (levels 1 and 4).

      CautionDo not write an unbounded loop. An agent built on while True, with no turn or budget limit, can repeat the same failing command until morning, and because it resends the whole history every turn, the cost grows with every turn. The limit belongs on the loop’s first line; it is not an improvement to add later.

      Key takeaways

      • Agent = a model that runs tools in a loop until it reaches a goal. The harness writes the loop.
      • The loop’s steering wheel is stop_reason. Every value other than tool_use has its own meaning; do not call them all “done”.
      • The intelligence is in one line; the rest is deterministic code. When debugging, ask first: “model or harness?”
      • Give every loop a turn and budget limit from day one.
      Sources

      2. Anthropic: Effective context engineering for AI agents (29 September 2025)
      3. Claude Docs: How tool use works
      4. Claude Docs: Context windows (model_context_window_exceeded)
      5. OpenAI Agents SDK: Running agents
      6. Yao et al. ReAct (2022) · Schick et al. Toolformer (2023)

      An agent fixing a red test, in the raw

      What you see in the UI is a few lines of summary: “Ran 3 commands, edited 2 files, tests pass.” Behind the curtain there is a message array that grows every turn, seven model calls and, at one point, a harness that rejects the model’s “done” decision. In this lesson we lift that curtain.

      Here is the scenario: example_app is an ASP.NET Core API backed by PostgreSQL. After this morning’s deploy, one of the OrderMapper tests is red: Map_NullStatus_ReturnsUnknown. When an order’s status_code comes in as NULL, the mapper throws InvalidCastException. The user types one sentence to the agent: “The OrderMapper test in example_app is red, fix it.” The harness has a Stop hook that runs the tests; the moment the agent says “done”, the harness will run the tests itself.

      The simulation below replays this session event by event. At each step watch three things: which station of the loop we are at, what was appended to the messages array, and the total number of tokens the model has to read on the next call. The token counts are illustrative, but the ratios resemble real sessions.

      An agent session, message by message

      Step through with Next or press Play. The strip on the left shows the loop’s stations, the middle shows the growing message array, and below is the raw JSON exchanged at that step. The orange row is the message appended at that step.

      What did you see in the simulation?

      The model did not run anything. Every model call produced either plain text or a tool_use block. It was always the harness that ran dotnet test, read the file and applied the edit. On the next step the model only saw the text the harness put back as a tool_result. That is why how clear and how short the tool output is directly determines the quality of the model’s next decision (which is exactly what good tool design in level 4 is for).

      Every call re-read the whole history. On the first call the model saw roughly nine thousand tokens of system prompt and tool definitions plus a sixty-token user message. On the last call it saw all of that plus every tool result, its own earlier responses and the hook feedback. Because the API is stateless (level 2), this is unavoidable. The result: total processed input grows not linearly with the number of turns but roughly quadratically. The “total processed input” counter at the bottom right of the simulation shows this. Prompt caching cuts the price of that load considerably, but it does not reduce the space it takes in the context window.

      Tool results filled most of the context. What the model wrote itself is a few hundred tokens; the test output and file contents are thousands. In real sessions the ratio is even more extreme: a single log dump or a whole large file can take tens of thousands of tokens. That is why Claude Code capping a single tool output at 25,000 tokens is a harness decision.

      The critical moment: where the model says “done”

      On the fourth model call the model said “Fixed it” and stopped with end_turn. But the fix was incomplete: it assigned "UNKNOWN" in the NULL case, yet a normalization a few lines below lowercased that value. Because the model finished without rerunning the test, it never saw this. This is the most common failure mode of agents: premature completion. From the inside, the model has no signal that could show it the difference between “I made a sensible fix” and “the fix works”; only a verifier can produce that signal.

      This is where the harness stepped in. The configured Stop hook ran the tests when the model wanted to stop; because the test was red, it exited with code 2. In Claude Code that means the hook’s error output is passed back to the model and the loop continues. The model saw “1 test failed: expected UNKNOWN, got unknown” as a new message and solved the problem in two turns. The user probably did not even notice this extra round.

      You already know thisA Stop hook works like a CI gate placed inside the loop. When a developer says “merge it” and the pipeline is red, nothing gets merged; when the agent says “done” and the test is red, the turn does not end. The difference is that CI reports to a human, while the hook reports straight to the model. That makes the hook output a prompt too: a short, actionable message that says which test broke and why gets a fix far faster than a long stack dump.

      What you do not see in the UI

      Had you watched this session in a terminal, you would most likely have seen a few tool lines, a “Fixed it” message, a short hook notice and the final summary. The real message array lives in the harness’s session log. Claude Code writes sessions to JSONL files, and resuming or forking a session works from that log; we will open it up in levels 6 and 8. When you are trying to understand an agent’s behavior, looking at this raw log is always more instructive than looking at the summary in the UI. The model decided based on what it saw; you cannot judge its decision without knowing what that was.

      In practiceWhen an agent makes a strange decision, first ask “what was in the context at that moment?” In Claude Code, /context shows what the context is filled with. If you are writing your own harness, logging the full request body of every model call is half of debugging.

      Key takeaways

      • A session is a single messages array that grows every turn; every model call re-reads all of it.
      • Tool results fill most of the context. Short, clear tool output is both cheaper and leads to better decisions.
      • When the model says “done”, the work may not be done. A harness that puts a verifier at the loop’s exit catches this.
      Sources
      1. Claude Docs: How tool use works
      2. Claude Code Docs: Best practices (Stop hook, verification)
      3. Claude Code Docs: How Claude Code works
      4. Anthropic: Writing effective tools for agents (25K token limit)

      Not every LLM application needs to be an agent

      Once you learn the loop, you want to build a loop for everything. Yet for many jobs the best solution is a flow where your code decides the steps and the model is only called at specific points.

      Anthropic made this distinction explicit in “Building effective agents”, published in December 2024. It calls both “agentic systems” but splits them in two. In workflows, LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths: the order, the branching and the stop condition are written in your code. In agents, the model directs its own process and tool use: the model decides how many steps to take, which tool to call and when to stop. The first is a pipeline; the second is an employee with a goal.

      Both share the same building block: the augmented LLM, a single model call enhanced with retrieval, tools and memory. Workflows wire these blocks together with code; an agent puts the block in a loop.

      Five workflow patterns

      The post lists five patterns that show up often in production. Knowing all of them pays off, because being able to look at a problem and say “this is a routing problem” saves you from building an agent you did not need.

      1. Prompt chaining. The work is split into sequential steps; each step’s output is the next one’s input. You can put programmatic gates between steps: if the output is not in the expected format, the chain stops. Example: extract the changes from commit messages, categorize them, write the release notes.
      2. Routing. A classifier recognizes the input and sends it to a specialized handler. Each branch runs with its own prompt, and if needed with a cheaper or a stronger model. Example: sorting incoming support tickets into billing, technical bug and feature request.
      3. Parallelization. It comes in two forms. Sectioning: the work is split into independent pieces that run in parallel, and the results are merged. Voting: the same task is run several times and the decision is made by a vote or a threshold. Example: reviewing a PR separately for security, performance and readability; or checking a security suspicion with three independent runs.
      4. Orchestrator-workers. An orchestrator model dynamically breaks the work into subtasks, hands them to workers and merges the results. The difference from parallelization is that the subtasks are not known in advance. Example: a change where you cannot tell up front how many files it will touch.
      5. Evaluator-optimizer. One model generates, another call evaluates against criteria and gives feedback, and the generator tries again. It works for tasks with clear evaluation criteria where iteration genuinely improves the result. Example: a translation that must follow a terminology glossary.

      Same boxes, six different wirings

      Pick a pattern, then step through to watch a sample request flow between the boxes. Purple boxes are model calls, teal boxes are your deterministic code.

      When is it an agent?

      Anthropic’s advice is surprisingly conservative: start with the simplest solution and add complexity only when you see a measurable benefit. Most of the time the simplest solution is a single model call enriched with retrieval and a few examples. Workflows give predictability and consistency for well-defined tasks. Agents are for open-ended problems where the number of steps cannot be known in advance and the path cannot be hard-coded. “Find and fix this bug” is exactly that kind of job: nobody can know how many files will be read or how many times the tests will run.

      The price of an agent is just as clear: you trade flexibility for higher cost and latency, and errors compound. Even if each step has a 95 percent chance of being right, the chance that 20 independent steps all go right is 0.9520 ≈ 36 percent. This simple calculation treats the steps as independent, and in reality the picture is not that grim because agents can see and correct their mistakes; but it explains well why a long agent chain without a verifier is fragile. If you are going to use agents, the post itself recommends testing in a sandbox and setting up guardrails from the start.

      Multi-agent systems cost even more. In Anthropic’s research system (June 2025), single-agent runs used about 4 times the tokens of a chat, and multi-agent runs about 15 times. The same post notes that most coding tasks, which need shared context, are not a great fit for multi-agent parallelism. That is why subagents in Claude Code are used mostly for “explore in a clean window and bring back a summary”; more on that in level 8.

      You already know thisA workflow is like a CI pipeline or a DAG: the steps are written in YAML, each step’s input and output are known, and when a step breaks you know where it broke. An agent is like an engineer you hand a job to and tell “let me know when it’s done”. You use both, but not for the same job. Nobody hands the release pipeline to an intern with “you decide how to do it each time”.
      Myth“Agents are here, workflows are obsolete.” Even Anthropic’s current prompting guide says the opposite: although the model handles multi-step reasoning well on its own, explicit prompt chaining is still useful when you need to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a specific pipeline structure. For work that needs an audit trail, compliance and reproducibility, a workflow is often the right answer.

      Look at the scenarios

      The cards below are typical jobs you might run into at work. Click a card to see the suggested setup, why, and when that setup will fall short. There is no single right answer here; when the context changes, the suggestion changes too. The point is to see the reasoning.

      Which setup for this job?

      Click a card. The suggestion and its reasoning open below.

      Click a card.

      Key takeaways

      • Workflow: your code draws the path. Agent: the model draws the path. Both use the same building block (the augmented LLM).
      • Five patterns: chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer.
      • Start with the simplest. Save agents for open-ended work where the number of steps cannot be predicted; cost, latency and compounding errors are their price.
      Sources
      1. Anthropic: Building effective agents (19 December 2024)
      2. Claude Docs: Prompting best practices (note on prompt chaining)
      3. Anthropic: How we built our multi-agent research system (13 June 2025)

      How does the loop break, and what holds it together?

      Agent failures are not random; they fall into a few familiar patterns. Once you recognize the pattern, the cure is largely known too, and most cures live in the harness, not in the prompt.

      1. Premature completion

      The model says “done” before the work is done. As you saw in the previous lesson, from the inside the model has no signal that shows the difference between “I made a sensible change” and “the change works”. Long tasks have another variant: a freshly started session looks around, sees that a lot of code has been written and decides the project is finished. The cures are layered. In the prompt, give a verifiable definition of “done” (level 3). For long jobs, keep a structured feature list where every item starts with "passes": false; let the agent change only that field, and state explicitly that deleting or editing tests is unacceptable. On the harness side, put a verifier at the loop’s exit: in Claude Code, if a Stop hook returns exit code 2, Claude is sent back to work. This is not infinite either: if the hook blocks 8 times in a row, Claude Code disregards the hook and ends the turn. As an alternative, the /goal command has a separate model check every turn whether the condition has been met.

      2. Doing everything at once

      An agent that tries to finish a big task in one go leaves three half-built features and a broken build in the middle of its context. The cure from Anthropic’s long-running agent experiments is simple: work on one feature per session and end the session in a clean, committable state. We will see this in detail in the next lesson.

      3. Looping and thrashing

      The model retries the same failing command over and over with small variations. Every attempt adds another error output to the context, and as the context grows the model loses focus even further. There is a harness version of this too: thrashing. If a large tool output refills the context right after compaction, the harness keeps trying to compress; Claude Code gives up on automatic compaction after a few attempts. The cure is always a hard limit: maximum turns, maximum tokens or maximum time. Claude Code’s auto mode has something similar: if the classifier blocks 3 actions in a row (or 20 in total), Claude Code drops out of auto mode and goes back to asking you.

      4. Drift

      Drift is the agent slowly wandering away from the task: while fixing a null bug it thinks “while I’m here” and starts fixing naming in six files. The resulting diff is harder to review and carries unwanted changes. Claude Code’s advice is practical: watch the first minute and press Esc as soon as you see it veer; if two correction attempts fail, clear with /clear and write a better prompt. Trying to repair a polluted context is usually more expensive than starting over with a clean one.

      5. Overeager or too timid

      Some models and prompts push the agent to call a tool for every little thing; others make it stop at the first ambiguity and ask the user a question. OpenAI’s GPT-5 guide shows both directions are tunable: to curb eagerness, a tool call budget and an escape hatch along the lines of “proceed even if you are not sure”; to increase persistence, an instruction telling it not to hand back on uncertainty. Anthropic also provides two opposing example blocks: one says to take action by default, the other says not to act until instructed. Which one you choose depends on the risk of the work.

      6. Destructive shortcuts

      An agent locked onto its goal may pick the shortest way to remove an obstacle: skipping the pre-commit hook with --no-verify, force pushing, deleting the red test, dropping and recreating a table. Anthropic suggests an example prompt block that says to ask for confirmation before hard-to-reverse actions and not to use destructive actions as shortcuts. But a prompt is a request, not a guarantee. Real protection lives in permission rules, hooks and the sandbox (levels 6, 8 and 10).

      7. Stopping early near the context limit

      Models that can track their remaining token budget may start wrapping up in a hurry when they notice the window is about to fill. If the harness is going to compact, you need to say so in the prompt; otherwise the model finishes early when it could actually have kept going.

      Loop simulator with failure injection

      The task is the same: fix the red test in OrderMapper. Inject failures in the top row, switch defenses on or off in the bottom row, then press Run. Look at how the session ends and how many turns it takes. Try different combinations; especially “premature completion + looping + Stop hook” together.

      Go deeperIn the simulator, pay attention to the “flaky test + Stop hook” combination. When the verifier is unreliable, the agent finds the shortest way to turn red into green, and sometimes that is skipping the test. The stronger the verifier, the more important it becomes to protect the verifier itself: that is why you block edits to the test folder with a hook, or read the test diff separately in review.

      Key takeaways

      • Seven familiar patterns: premature completion, everything at once, looping/thrashing, drift, too much or too little eagerness, destructive shortcuts, stopping early near the limit.
      • Most cures live in the harness: turn limits, a Stop hook or /goal, permission rules, starting over with a clean context.
      • Intervene early when you see drift; after two failed corrections, /clear.
      • If the verifier is unreliable, the agent will find a way around it. Protect the verifier too.
      Sources

      2. Claude Code Docs: How Claude Code works (compaction)

      4. Claude Docs: Prompting best practices (action and destructive-action blocks)
      5. OpenAI Cookbook: GPT-5 prompting guide (agentic eagerness)
      6. Anthropic: Building effective agents (compounding errors)

      Work that does not fit in one context window

      As of November 2026, all current Claude models have a 1M-token context window. That is a lot of room, but it is not unlimited; and as you saw in level 2, the model’s recall quality drops as the window fills. That is why work that takes hours is spread across several sessions, that is, several clean windows.

      The problem is that every new session starts with no memory. It does not know what the previous session did, what it left half-finished or which approach did not work. There are two ways out. The first is compaction: summarize the conversation that is about to overflow and continue from the summary. The second is restarting from the file system: keep the state on disk rather than in the model’s memory, and open every session from scratch by reading those files. Anthropic’s current guidance recommends the second wherever possible.

      Anthropic’s recipe for long-running agents

      In November 2025 Anthropic described the harness it used to have an agent build an application across many sessions. The recipe rests on two kinds of session.

      1. Initializer session. Sets up the project: an init.sh that brings up the development environment, a JSON feature list that lists every feature to build and marks all of them as failing, a progress file (claude-progress.txt) where progress is recorded, and the first git commit.
      2. Coding sessions. Each one opens the same way: read the progress file and the recent git log, bring up the environment with init.sh, check that the basic functionality still works, pick one failing feature from the list, implement and test it, set its passes field to true only if the test passed, commit, and update the progress file.
      [
  { "id": "F2",
    "description": "The order list can be filtered by the status_code field",
    "steps": ["call GET /api/orders?status=DELIVERED",
              "only delivered orders should be returned"],
    "passes": false }
]
      Session 3 — F2 done (commit 4c1e9a2). Added a status filter to OrderQuery.
Note: example.orders.status_code is stored upper-case; use ToUpperInvariant in the filter.
Next: F3 CSV export. The seed data in init.sh loads 120 orders.

      A small but important observation: according to the post, the model was less inclined to overwrite JSON inappropriately than Markdown. The model happily “reorganises” a free-text to-do list; in a strict JSON structure, changing a single boolean field feels more natural. Likewise, it was stated explicitly that deleting or editing the tests in the feature list was unacceptable. That is a direct fuse against the premature completion from the previous lesson.

      You already know thisThe context is RAM, the file system is disk. When a database crashes, it does not try to rescue the state in RAM; it reads the WAL and the last checkpoint on disk and rebuilds. Here the git log plays the WAL, the progress file plays the checkpoint, and init.sh is the recovery procedure. Or think of an on-call handover: without a good handover note, the night shift has to rediscover everything from scratch.

      Cross-session handover simulator

      A five-feature job for example_app. Every session starts with an empty context. Switch parts of the recipe on or off with the toggles, then press “Next session” to advance session by session. Feature chip colors: green passed, amber half-done, grey not started.

      When compaction, when a clean start?

      Compaction is not bad; it is practical for work on a single problem that needs a short break. But a summary is lossy. The Claude Code documentation says so plainly: automatic compaction preserves requests and key code, but detailed instructions from early in the conversation may be lost. That is why persistent rules go into CLAUDE.md, because that file is reloaded on every request (covered in level 9 together with the context budget). Restarting from the file system, on the other hand, is lossless, because you decide what is kept: the progress note, the feature list, the commit history.

      One more detail: some models track their remaining token budget. If the harness is going to compact, or the work is going to span several windows, you need to say so in the prompt. Otherwise the model may notice the window filling up and try to close the work in a hurry. In Claude Code you can also use /goal for a long objective: a separate model checks every turn whether the condition has been met.

      Tasks are getting longer

      This recipe matters more and more. According to METR’s measurement, the length of tasks (measured in human time) that models can complete with 50 percent success doubled roughly every 7 months between 2019 and 2025. More recent estimates suggest that period is getting shorter; however, we could not verify those figures against a primary source, so we do not give them here. The trend is clear enough: as the work handed to agents gets longer, designing the handover between sessions becomes a harness responsibility.

      In practiceWhen you start a job that will take several sessions, dedicate the first session to setup only: create a script with the run and test commands, a JSON to-do list and a short progress file, and commit. Make the first message of every later session the same: “read the progress file and the last 10 commits, pick one failing item from the list.”

      Key takeaways

      • On long jobs, keep the state on disk, not in the context: a progress file, a JSON feature list, git history, a setup script.
      • One feature per session; every session ends in a clean, committable state.
      • Compaction is lossy; where possible, prefer a clean start from the file system.
      • If the harness will compact, tell the model; otherwise it may wrap up early as it nears the limit.
      Sources
      1. Anthropic: Effective harnesses for long-running agents (26 November 2025)
      2. Claude Docs: Prompting best practices (multi-window work, context awareness)
      3. Claude Code Docs: How Claude Code works (compaction)
      4. Claude Code Docs: Best practices (/goal)
      5. METR: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks (arXiv 2503.14499, 2025)

      What closes the loop: the verifier

      The answer to why the agent loop works so well is one word: feedback. Writing correct code in one shot is hard, for humans too. But writing it, running it, seeing the error and fixing it is much easier. The loop gives the model that opportunity; the verifier determines the quality of that opportunity.

      In its post introducing the Claude Agent SDK, Anthropic describes an agent’s working rhythm with four verbs: gather context, take action, verify the work, repeat. The Claude Code documentation puts the same idea more sharply: give the model something that reports pass or fail, and it can close the loop itself. This may be the most practical sentence in the whole course. An agent’s quality is bounded by how verifiable the environment it works in is.

      Kinds of verifier

      Rules

      Compiler, type checker, linter, unit and integration tests. Deterministic, fast, cheap. The agent’s best friend. The Agent SDK post puts this first.

      Visual feedback

      Take a screenshot and have the model look at it. In UI work it catches the alignment and overflow bugs that tests miss; but the interpretation is still up to the model.

      LLM-as-judge

      Another model call evaluates the output against criteria. For work that cannot be reduced to rules it may be the only option; Anthropic describes it as “generally not very robust”.

      Human

      Business rules, product decisions, architectural fit. The most expensive and slowest verifier; so everything a machine can catch should be caught before it gets there.

      These kinds form a ladder: the further down you go, the wider the range of bugs that can be caught, but speed, cheapness and reliability drop. A good setup puts the cheap, deterministic ones inside the loop and the expensive ones at the loop’s exit. The compiler and focused unit tests can run after every edit; the full test suite when the agent says “done”; human review when the PR is opened.

      Which verifier catches which bug?

      There are eight realistic bugs the agent could introduce in OrderMapper and the order screen. Select the verifiers you put in the loop; see which bug is caught, which is partly noticed and which slips silently all the way to the PR. Click a bug to see why.

      Why are models so good in the loop?

      In level 1 you saw reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR): the model writes code, the tests run, and passing solutions are rewarded. Today’s coding models were trained heavily in exactly these environments, that is, on reading a test output and deciding the next move. When you give it a test command, you put it back in the environment it was trained in. When you do not, the model flies blind and when it says “done” nobody knows whether it really is.

      Three places to put the verifier in the loop

      1. In the prompt. Tie the definition of “done” to a command: “first write a failing test that reproduces the bug, then fix it; finish when dotnet test passes.” Claude Code’s own example is the same: instead of “login is broken, fix it”, a task that includes the symptom, the relevant folder and the instruction “write a failing test first” (level 3).
      2. In the harness. Stop hook, /goal, automatic format and lint after edits. These do not depend on the model remembering; they run every time. Detailed setup in level 8.
      3. In the environment. Fast, focused test commands and readable error messages. A test suite that takes twenty minutes means only a handful of iterations per session. Being able to run a single class with a filter improves the agent’s speed and accuracy together.

      The verifier’s output is a prompt too

      A verifier does not just say pass or fail; what it says when it fails determines the model’s next move. Between an output that says “1 test failed” and one that says “Map_NullStatus_ReturnsUnknown: expected UNKNOWN, got unknown (OrderMapperTests.cs:42)” there is a difference of one or two turns for the agent. The reverse holds too: a stack dump hundreds of lines long fills the context and buries the line that matters. When you write your own Stop hook or test script, remember that the model will read the output: which test, which expectation, which file and line. A short, actionable, reproducible error message is the verifier-side counterpart of good tool design (level 4).

      Then there is speed. The agent waits on every verification round, and every wait is real time. Instead of running the whole suite after every edit, running the relevant class with a filter inside the loop and saving the full suite for the “done” point makes room for far more iterations in the same session.

      You already know thisThis is TDD’s red-green cycle. The difference: humans practise TDD through discipline, while for an agent you can make it mandatory. The “show me the red test first” step is also a diagnostic check: if the test really reproduces the bug you saw, you can be sure the fix fixes the right thing.
      CautionGoodhart’s law applies to agents too: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. An agent fixated on passing the tests may loosen an assertion, skip the test or set the expected value to the actual output. Read the diff of the test files separately; if possible, block edits to the test folder with a hook or require approval for them.

      Key takeaways

      • An agent’s quality is bounded by the verifiability of its environment. Fast, deterministic verifiers are the best investment.
      • Cheap verifiers inside the loop, expensive ones at the exit: the compiler on every edit, the test suite at “done”, a human at the PR.
      • LLM-as-judge is for work that cannot be reduced to rules; on its own it is not a reliable gate.
      • Protect the verifier too: read the test diff, lock the test folder.
      Sources
      1. Anthropic: Building agents with the Claude Agent SDK
      2. Claude Code Docs: Best practices (verification, Stop hook)
      3. Claude Code Docs: How Claude Code works
      4. Anthropic: Effective harnesses for long-running agents

      Everything outside the model

      Remember the equation from the Getting started page: Agent = Model + Harness. From level 3 through level 5 we built the pieces of that equation one by one: we wrote the prompt, defined tools, and put the tools in a loop. In this level we step back and look at the whole picture. What surrounds that loop, why is it there, and how much of an agent’s success does it decide?

      The clearest definition of the term as it is used today is Vivek Trivedy’s post at LangChain, “The Anatomy of an Agent Harness”, dated 10 March 2026. The definition is deliberately broad: the harness is every piece of code, every configuration and every bit of execution logic that is not the model itself. The line that sticks is this one: “If you’re not the model, you’re the harness.” In other words, everything that touches the agent apart from the model’s weights sits on this side.

      Trivedy groups the components into five buckets:

      • System prompts. The text that tells the model who it is, what environment it runs in, and how to use its tools.
      • Tools, skills, MCP servers and their descriptions. The model’s hands reaching into the world, and the way those hands are described.
      • Bundled infrastructure. File system, sandbox, browser: the place where commands actually run.
      • Orchestration. Subagents, handoffs from one agent to another, model selection by task type.
      • Hooks and middleware. Code that steps in at specific points of the loop, such as compaction, “keep going” logic and lint checks.

      The vendors speak the same language

      This is not just a framework company’s marketing frame. Anthropic’s Claude Code documentation describes Claude Code with exactly this word: the layer around the model that provides the tools and manages the context, in other words an agentic harness. There is a more concrete signal too: in 2025 the Claude Code SDK was renamed the Claude Agent SDK. The reason was simple: the same harness was running agents that do not write code. File system, bash, search, permissions and context management are not “coding” features; they are the infrastructure any general-purpose agent needs.

      LangChain founder Harrison Chase made the same point in his “Deep Agents” post: what makes Claude Code so capable is not only the model, but a general harness made of a planning tool, a file system, subagents and a very detailed system prompt. Put those four pieces around a different model and you also get an agent that works “deep”.

      You already know thisThink of the relationship between an operating system and a program. When a program wants to write to a file, it does not do it itself; it makes a system call, the kernel checks permissions, carries out the operation and returns the result. The program does not know how the disk works; it only sees the result of the call. Here the model is the program, the tool call is the system call, and the harness is the kernel plus the runtime. Another analogy: the model is the business logic, the harness is the framework, the DI container, the middleware chain and all the infrastructure. However good the business logic is, it runs badly in a misconfigured framework.

      How much does the model actually produce in one turn?

      The best way to see why this distinction matters is to take a single agent turn apart. The diagram below shows the pieces that flow behind the scenes when you tell Claude Code “fix the red test”. Click each piece and see who produced it. Then pick the “Model only” filter: you will see what a small share of the whole the model’s output really is, a few sentences of text and a few JSON objects.

      Anatomy of an agent turn: who produced it?

      Simplified pieces from a Claude Code session, in the order they flow. Click a piece to see who produced it, what it is for, and what you can control. Use the filter to highlight only the model’s share or only the harness’s.

      Click a piece.

      Three things in the diagram deserve your attention. First, everything the model produces is a request: “I want to run this command”, “I want to change this file like so”. Every step that turns that request into reality, rejects it, truncates it, formats it and feeds it back belongs to the harness. Second, the things you write (your message and CLAUDE.md) reach the model not where and how you want, but where and how the harness chooses. Third, some pieces, like the compaction summary, are mixed: a model writes the text, but the harness decides when it is written, what is kept and where it goes.

      What does this distinction change in practice?

      1. Debugging. When the agent does something bad, the first question should be: “Did the model make the wrong decision, or did the harness fail to give it the information, tool or feedback it needed to make the right one?” The second is surprisingly common. If it ignored an important file, look at the context; if it ran the wrong command, look at the tool description and the permissions; if it keeps repeating the same mistake, look at the feedback the environment gives it.
      2. Selection decisions. “Which model is best?” is an incomplete question. As you will see in lesson 3 of this level, the same model gives very different results in different harnesses. The right question is: “Which model and harness pair is best for my work?”
      3. Security. You cannot guarantee what the model will produce. You can, however, control exactly what the harness will execute. Because the harness is the only place where a guarantee is possible, security is built there too (level 10).
      Myth“The harness is just an interface; the real work happens in the model.” The interface is the outermost and most visible layer of the harness, but not the most influential one. The Claude Code documentation says that the terminal, IDE, desktop, web and CI surfaces all run the same loop. The surface changes; the tool set, permissions, context management and hooks stay the same. Those inner layers are what shape the behavior.
      CautionThe most expensive reflex is this: when the agent breaks a rule, add one more sentence to the prompt, then one more “IMPORTANT”. If the rule is the kind the harness can enforce (do not read a file, do not run a command, make the tests pass before finishing), the prompt is the wrong layer. Lesson 5 of this level is about exactly that decision.

      Key takeaways

      • The harness is everything that touches the agent apart from the model’s weights: prompts, tools, infrastructure, orchestration, hooks.
      • The model only produces requests. The harness turns a request into reality, rejects it, and feeds the result back.
      • The Claude Code SDK becoming the Claude Agent SDK shows that a good coding harness is really a general-purpose agent infrastructure.
      • When an agent fails, ask first: was the decision wrong, or was the information, tool or feedback needed for the decision missing?
      Sources
      1. LangChain, Vivek Trivedy: The Anatomy of an Agent Harness (10 March 2026)
      2. Claude Code docs: How Claude Code works
      3. Anthropic: Building agents with the Claude Agent SDK

      The nine layers of a coding harness

      The while loop in level 5 was the skeleton of the harness. A real coding harness wraps that skeleton in layers, each of which closes off a specific way agents fail in the real world. We use Claude Code as the reference because its documentation describes these layers explicitly; Codex CLI and the others have their equivalents (level 7).

      The list below is based on the Claude Code documentation as of November 2026. Names and details may change from release to release; the concepts last.

      1. System prompt and system reminders

      The instructions the harness puts at the start of every request: identity, working rules, environment information (operating system, working directory, git status). On top of that there are system reminders inserted into the conversation: the contents of CLAUDE.md, the selected output style, “this file changed after you read it” notes, the attribution lines to add to commits. The harness writes and places all of them; you control part of the content, not where it goes.

      2. Tools, MCP and skills

      The built-in tools cover groups such as file operations, search, command execution, web and code intelligence. Tools from the MCP servers you connect are loaded deferred by default: thanks to tool search, only the tool names and server instructions sit in the context, and the full definition arrives when it is needed (level 4). Skills work the same way: first just the name and description, the content when needed.

      3. Permissions and sandbox

      Which tool runs without asking, which needs approval, which never runs at all. Claude Code has several permission modes: Auto, where a classifier decides; Manual, which asks about everything; Accept edits, which accepts edits on its own; and Plan, which produces a plan without changing anything. Above these sit allow and deny rules, and at the very bottom the sandbox, which limits commands’ file system and network access at the operating system level.

      4. Checkpoints and the session log

      The harness snapshots the files it edits; you can rewind with Esc Esc. The whole session is stored as a JSONL file; resume and fork are built on top of it. The checkpoint is the layer that gives the agent freedom to make mistakes: you supervise something you can undo more loosely.

      5. Context management

      Automatic compaction as the window nears full, the breakdown you see with /context, and the cap placed on tool output. In Claude Code a tool result can be at most 25,000 tokens; anything beyond is truncated. We saw the mechanism of this layer in level 2; what matters here is that all of these are harness decisions, not model decisions.

      6. Memory

      CLAUDE.md (project instructions shared with the team), CLAUDE.local.md (personal, never committed to the repo) and MEMORY.md, the automatic memory file Claude maintains itself. According to the documentation, the first 200 lines or the first 25 KB of automatic memory are loaded at session start. Memory is the harness’s answer to the model’s statelessness: the model starts every session from scratch, the files do not.

      7. Hooks

      Points where your code runs at specific events of the loop (before a tool call, after it, at session start, when the model says “done”). Tell two kinds apart: command and http hooks are deterministic, meaning a script or an HTTP endpoint decides. In prompt and agent hooks, a model makes the decision again. That difference is decisive when you choose where to put a rule (lesson 5). The syntax is in level 8.

      8. Subagents

      Helper agents that run in a separate context window and return only a summary when they finish. They can start with a clean window or with a copy of the current conversation (fork). Their real value is context isolation more than parallelism: the dozens of files read during exploration never enter the main window.

      9. Interfaces

      Terminal, IDE extension, desktop app, web, Slack, CI. The documentation stresses that they all run the same loop. Changing the interface should not change the behavior; if it does, a different permission mode or a different settings file is usually in play.

      The harness onion

      Click the rings or the labels below (Tab and Enter work from the keyboard too). The model sits at the center, with layers closer to the outside world further out. The “Who decides?” view colors the rings as deterministic or model-decided.

      Pick a layer.

      Each layer exists to close off a specific way agents fail in the real world.

      The line between deterministic and model-decided

      The onion’s “Who decides?” view shows the most important idea of this level. Some layers are deterministic: a deny rule, the sandbox, a command hook, the tool output cap. They give the same response to the same input every time; they can be tested and audited. Others ultimately come down to the model’s interpretation: CLAUDE.md, skill descriptions, prompt hooks, the classifier in Auto mode. The Claude Code documentation says so plainly: CLAUDE.md is guidance, and Claude may decide that a line does not apply in a given situation. Hooks, deny rules and managed settings, on the other hand, are enforced by the harness.

      You already know thisIt is the difference between a “let’s do it this way” comment in code review and a required check in CI. The comment is guidance; a developer may ignore it for a good reason. A branch protection rule asks nobody. CLAUDE.md is like the review comment; hooks and deny rules are like branch protection.
      In practiceWhen you wonder what an agent is working with, do not guess; ask the harness. In Claude Code, /context shows the context breakdown, /permissions the active rules, /hooks the registered hooks. Codex CLI has similar status commands. It is the fastest way to find where a behavior comes from.

      Key takeaways

      • The nine layers of a coding harness: instructions, tools, permissions and sandbox, checkpoints, context management, memory, hooks, subagents, interfaces.
      • Each layer closes off a specific failure path. If a layer is missing, that failure will happen sooner or later.
      • Some layers are deterministic (enforced), others are model-decided (guidance). Critical rules belong on the deterministic side.
      Sources
      1. Claude Code docs: How Claude Code works
      2. Claude Code docs: Best practices
      3. LangChain: The Anatomy of an Agent Harness

      Same model, different harness, different result

      The claim that “the harness matters” feels intuitively right, but how much does it matter? We have a few measurements on this. None of them is flawless, so we will read each one together with its source, its method and its weak spot.

      Evidence 1: pin the model, change only the harness

      LangChain pinned the model to gpt-5.2-codex in its own open-source coding agent, deepagents-cli, and changed only the prompt, the tools and the middleware. The Terminal-Bench 2.0 score went from 52.8% to 66.5%. Two changes stand out. The first is adding an explicit plan, build, verify, fix structure to the loop: the agent has to pass through a verification step before it may say it is done. The second is what the post calls the “reasoning sandwich”: high reasoning effort for the planning and verification steps, medium for the implementation steps. The result is a vendor measuring its own product, in other words vendor-reported. Still, the direction is clear: same weights, a gap of roughly 14 points.

      Evidence 2: change only the edit tool

      Can Bölük’s post of 12 February 2026 measures an even narrower variable: the file edit format. 16 models, 180 tasks. A “hashline” format, in which lines are tagged with short content hashes, beat apply_patch in 14 of the 16 models by roughly 15 points on average. The most extreme case is Grok Code Fast 1: from 6.7% to 68.3%. This is a single-author company blog vendor blog, single author; we have not seen an independent replication. But the mechanism is plausible and we will examine it in the next lesson: the format changes the surface on which the model can make mistakes.

      Evidence 3: interface design as an academic result

      The SWE-agent paper (Yang et al., NeurIPS 2024) named the interface between the agent and the computer the “ACI”. A file viewer with a 100-line window, an edit command with a linter that rejects syntactically broken edits, and short search output. GPT-4 Turbo went from 11.0% on SWE-bench Lite with a plain shell to 18.0% with this interface; with the edit action removed it dropped to 10.3%. The figures come from secondary summaries; the paper’s table is authoritative secondary source.

      Model fixed, harness varied: the measurements

      In each study the grey bar is “before” and the colored bar is “after”. The badges show the type of source. The last tab is an unverified compilation; open it only after reading its warning.

      Why does a small change make such a big difference?

      At first glance it is surprising: how can an edit format or a verification step be worth dozens of points? The answer is that agent tasks are long chains of steps. Anthropic’s “Building effective agents” post says it plainly: in agents, errors compound. Think of a simple calculation (an illustrative one, not a measurement): an agent that gets each step right with 98% probability finishes a 50-step task without a single mistake about 36% of the time (0.9850). Raise per-step success to 99% and that rate climbs to about 60%. A one-point improvement per step makes a difference of more than twenty points at the task level.

      The harness acts on exactly that per-step probability. A vague error message wastes a step; a patch that does not apply wastes a turn on re-reading; the absence of a verifier lets a small mistake ride along for twenty steps. The reverse holds too: even if a good harness cannot prevent an error entirely, it catches it early and cheaply. A test turning red right away, a linter rejecting a broken edit, a hook stopping a write to the wrong file and saying why: each of these lets the next link in the chain start from solid ground. The linted edit command in SWE-agent and the verification step at LangChain are two implementations of the same idea.

      That is why, when you evaluate a harness, these questions matter as much as “how smart is the model”: how many steps later does it see the error, how clearly does it see it when it does, and how many turns does the fix cost?

      How should you read these numbers?

      There are compilations going around that show the same model scoring very differently with different harnesses on the Terminal-Bench leaderboards. One secondary compilation from around April 2026 says that with Claude Opus 4.6 the best harness scored about 82% and Claude Code about 58%, a 24-point spread on a single model. We could not verify this; it sits in a separate tab of the diagram, with a warning. LangChain’s post also notes separately that Opus 4.6 trailed the other harnesses by a wide margin inside Claude Code.

      When you read a gap like that, do not forget one important distinction: leaderboard harnesses are tuned for the benchmark. They run non-interactively, choose timeouts to fit the tasks and allow everything. Product harnesses optimize for other things: asking the user, permissions, sandbox, cost, reversibility. Claude Code trailing on a benchmark does not mean it will be worse in your repo; it may mean it spends its budget on things the benchmark does not measure. The reverse is also true: the permission model of a harness that shines on a benchmark may be unacceptable for your company.

      Myth“Model X is so many points better than model Y.” Model comparisons often quietly include a harness. The reported score is the score that model got with that harness and those settings. You cannot carry the number on a model card over to your own toolchain; when you do, expect a deviation as large as the harness gap.

      When debugging: model or harness?

      In day-to-day work, this evidence translates into a debugging habit. When the agent does something you did not expect, instead of blaming the model right away, look in this order: what was in the context, what did the tool return, which rule was in effect, what feedback did the environment give? The diagram below shows that checking order for common symptoms.

      Symptom → layer to inspect

      Click a symptom. You get the checking order, the likely layer and the first command to run. This is not a decision tree but a flashlight: it shows which layer to look at first.

      Pick a symptom.

      Key takeaways

      • With the model fixed, changing only the harness can make a difference of anywhere from a few points to dozens (LangChain 52.8 → 66.5, vendor-reported).
      • Even a tool decision that looks small, such as the edit format, can make a big difference.
      • Benchmark harnesses are tuned for the benchmark; product harnesses for safety, permissions and cost. Read scores accordingly.
      • Before blaming the agent, check the context, the tool output, the rules and the feedback, in that order.

      Model and harness evolve together

      Part of the explanation for the gaps in the previous lesson is simple: models are not trained in a vacuum. Labs train their models during the RL phase with specific tool names, specific edit formats and specific working environments. A model performs best in an environment that resembles the harness it was trained in.

      In the vendors’ own words

      OpenAI’s Codex prompting guide is unusually explicit about this. It “strongly” recommends using their own apply_patch implementation exactly as is, saying the model has been trained to excel at this diff format. It also states that the model was trained predominantly with a dedicated terminal tool, and trained to follow AGENTS.md instructions closely. Those three sentences are really a configuration manual for anyone putting a Codex model into their own harness.

      On the Anthropic side the same idea shows up as “Anthropic-schema client tools”. The schemas of the bash, text_editor, memory, computer and browser tools are trained into the model; the documentation says Claude has been optimized on thousands of successful trajectories that use these exact tool signatures. The practical consequence: these tools get called more reliably than tools that do the same job but are defined with names and schemas you made up.

      You already know thisIt is the difference between a library’s “official” client and a wrapper you wrote yourself. The official client knows every edge case the server expects; your wrapper works most of the time and quietly misbehaves in a rare case. Here the “server” is the model’s habits: speak the format it was trained on and you get fewer surprises.

      Why does the diff format matter so much?

      Editing a file is one of the most delicate outputs a model has to produce. The model does not rewrite the whole file; it produces a description of the change for the harness to apply. That description comes in three main forms, and each has a different weak spot:

      • Find and replace (str_replace in Claude’s text_editor tool, the Edit tool in Claude Code): the model writes the old text verbatim, the harness searches for it in the file and replaces it with the new text. The old text must occur exactly once. One whitespace difference gives a “not found” error, two matches an “ambiguous” one.
      • Contextual patch (Codex’s apply_patch): the model writes the lines to change plus the surrounding context lines in a patch format. The harness places the hunk using the context lines. Any drift in the context lines makes the patch impossible to apply.
      • Line-referenced (like hashline): when the file is read, each line is tagged with a short content hash; the model describes the edit as “this line, this hash”. It does not have to rewrite the old text. If the hash does not match (the file has changed), the harness rejects the edit.

      In each format, the thing the model can get wrong is different. With find and replace it has to remember the old text letter for letter; with a patch, copy the context correctly; with line references, pick the right line. Whatever format a model was trained on, it has learned to avoid that format’s mistakes. Give it a different format and it would have to learn that format’s mistakes all over again, and it cannot, because its weights are frozen.

      Same edit, three formats, four situations

      On line 88 of OrderMapper.cs in example_app there is a cast that blows up when status_code comes back NULL. Pick a format, then pick a situation: how does the harness handle the edit? The hashline rendering is schematic.

      Fitting too closely is a risk too

      LangChain’s harness anatomy post puts forward an interesting argument: products like Claude Code and Codex go through post-training with the model and the harness in the loop, and this can turn into a kind of overfitting. Change the tool logic and performance may drop; so the best harness for a task is not necessarily the one the model was trained in. This is an argument, not a result measured in that post. But the hashline result is consistent with it: some models did better in a format other than their “native” one.

      Taken together, the two observations say this: the training format is a strong default, not dogma. If you are building your own harness, start with the tool names and formats the model was trained on. If you want to try a different format, do it by measuring on your own tasks (evals in level 9).

      Practical consequences

      1. Changing the model means changing the harness too. When you switch models inside the same tool, part of the behavioral difference may come from the new model not being used to that tool’s formats. The reverse also holds: if you use a Codex model in a non-Codex tool that gives it some other edit format instead of apply_patch, you may not see the quality you expect.
      2. The name of the instruction file is part of the format. Codex was trained to follow AGENTS.md; Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md. If you use both tools in the same repo, keep the two files consistent or point one at the other (levels 7 and 8).
      3. Tool names are not trivial. In your own harness, choosing names close to the ones the model saw in training, rather than giving a tool an arbitrary name, can buy consistency. There are third-party experiences that support this, but we have not seen verified numbers; try it with your own eval.
      4. Retire the question “Which model is best?” Replace it with “Which model and harness pair is best, on my tasks, by my criteria?”
      In practiceIf the agent keeps hitting “no match found” or “patch failed to apply”, before blaming the model’s intelligence, check these: does the file mix tabs and spaces, are line endings mixed between CRLF and LF, did a formatter change the file after the agent read it? All of these are friction at the format level, and most are solved with a harness or repo setting.

      Key takeaways

      • Models are trained with specific tool names and formats: apply_patch and the terminal tool for Codex; bash, text_editor and the other trained-in schemas for Claude.
      • Each edit format has its own error surface: exact matching, copying context, or picking the right line.
      • The training format is a strong default; other formats may be better, but know that by measuring on your own tasks.
