      Where does a rule go?

      Your team has settled on a rule: “applied files in the migrations folder are never touched.” How do you teach that to the agent? Most people’s first answer is “I’ll put it in CLAUDE.md.” Sometimes that is the right answer. Most of the time it is not. This lesson teaches you how to decide which harness layer a rule belongs in.

      The basic distinction: guidance or enforcement?

      The distinction you saw in the earlier lessons becomes a decision criterion here. Line up the harness layers like a ladder, from soft to hard:

      1. CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md. Guidance that sits in the context on every request. The model reads it and usually follows it, but it may decide that a line does not apply in a given situation. Every line costs a little attention on every task.
      2. Skill. A procedure loaded on demand. The right place for long, rarely needed knowledge: only its name and description sit permanently in the context.
      3. Tool design. Bake the rule into the tool itself. A read-only database tool carries a no-writes rule better than any prompt, because the ability to write simply does not exist (level 4).
      4. Permission rule. allow, ask, deny. The harness stops a tool call based on a pattern. Simple, fast, deterministic; but patterns can be sidestepped.
      5. Hook. Your code, running on an event. PreToolUse can block a call and tell the model why; PostToolUse can run something after every edit; a Stop hook can run a check when the model says “done” and send it back to work (level 5). A command hook is deterministic.
      6. Sandbox. A file and network boundary at the operating system level. It stops even a command that sidesteps the harness’s patterns.
      7. Outside the harness: git hooks, CI. The last gate, applying to everyone, agent or human. Its feedback comes late, but nobody can skip it.

      The Claude Code documentation’s advice on this fits in one sentence: if you keep adding emphasis to a CLAUDE.md line and Claude still misses it, that line belongs in a hook. The documentation adds that “adding IMPORTANT probably won’t fix it”. As you saw in level 3, with newer models capitalised, shouting instructions also cause overtriggering: the rule starts being applied in unrelated situations too.

      You already know thisIt is the question of where you put a business rule in a database. An if in the application code is usually enough, but another client can bypass it. A CHECK constraint or a foreign key asks nobody. Critical integrity rules go into constraints, flexible business rules into code. Here CLAUDE.md is like the if in application code; hooks and the sandbox are like constraints.

      Four questions for the decision

      1. Does it have exceptions? If the rule has legitimate exceptions and telling them apart takes judgment, write it in the soft layer (CLAUDE.md), together with the reasoning. A deterministic check cuts off the exceptions too.
      2. What does a violation cost? If a violation means irreversible damage, a security hole or data loss, the rule must be enforced: a deny rule, a hook or the sandbox. “Usually complies” is not enough.
      3. Is the rule an action or a judgment? “Run the formatter after every edit” is an action; a hook does it every time. “Keep the code readable” is a judgment; no deterministic check can decide it.
      4. How often is it needed? A short rule needed on every task goes in CLAUDE.md; a long procedure needed once a month goes in a skill.

      Where does this rule belong?

      Click a rule card. On the ladder, the recommended layer is marked with a green border, and the alternatives one step softer and one step harder with a dashed line. Below you can read why it belongs there and what would happen with the alternatives. No scoring; the point is to see the reasoning.

      Rules

      Layers, soft to hard

      Pick a rule card.

      Same rule, two places: watch a session

      Let’s not leave the difference abstract. In the simulation below, the same rule lives in two different places in two different teams. The team on the left wrote the rule in CLAUDE.md; the team on the right wrote a PreToolUse hook. Both agents get the same task and run into the same temptation halfway through.

      CLAUDE.md or hook? Same session, two outcomes

      Step through it. The left lane is the team whose rule lives in CLAUDE.md; the right lane is the team where the same rule is enforced by a PreToolUse hook. The JSON is simplified; the real hook syntax is in level 8.

      Notice that the model in the simulation is not “malicious”. It read the rule, understood it, and then produced a plausible-looking reason why the rule did not apply in that situation. That is exactly the behavior CLAUDE.md is designed for: guidance gets interpreted. A hook does not interpret. On top of that, a good hook does not just block; it also tells the model what it should do instead. The block message becomes the model’s input on the next turn, and the agent switches to the right path.

      The hard layer has a cost too

      Putting every rule in the hardest layer is not the right answer either. A deterministic check does not recognize exceptions: it blocks legitimate work too. And a blocked agent does not stop; it looks for another way. If the hook in the simulation only watches the Edit and Write tools, on the next attempt the model may try to make the same change through bash with sed -i. That is not malice; the model is trying to finish the task and sees the obstacle in front of it as a technical problem. So a good block does two things: it keeps its scope wide enough to cover the real risk (with the sandbox if necessary), and its block message states the legitimate alternative explicitly. An agent that has an alternative does not look for shortcuts.

      Harnesses know about this tension and build in safety valves. According to the Claude Code documentation (as of November 2026), auto mode stops deciding and falls back to asking the user after 3 consecutive or 20 total blocks; and when a Stop hook blocks 8 times in a row, the harness overrides it (level 5). The message is clear: if a hard layer says “no” forever, the agent either locks up or tries to get around it. A hard layer should be firm, but it should not drive the loop into a dead end.

      As a practical rule of thumb: guidance layers (CLAUDE.md, skills) make sure the agent picks the right path; enforcing layers (permissions, hooks, sandbox) make sure the wrong path is closed. In a good setup the two work together: most of the time the agent never hits the block, because the guidance has already put it on the right path; and when it does hit it, the block tells it where to go.

      CautionDeterministic layers can be breached too. Even if a deny pattern stops the Read tool, the same file can be cat-ed through bash; a command pattern can be sidestepped with a different spelling. Do not rely on a single layer for a critical rule: use a deny rule together with the sandbox, and if possible take the secret itself out of the agent’s environment. Level 10 expands on this defense-in-depth idea.
      In practiceWhen you move a rule into an enforcing layer, do not delete it from CLAUDE.md; leave it as a short explanation. For example: “The migrations folder is protected by a hook; create a new migration for schema changes.” That way the model picks the right path without ever hitting the block, and you save a turn and the tokens.

      Key takeaways

      • CLAUDE.md is guidance; the model may decide a line does not apply. Hooks, deny rules, managed settings and the sandbox are enforced.
      • If you keep adding emphasis, the rule is in the wrong layer: move it to a hook or a permission rule.
      • The decision questions: are there exceptions, what does a violation cost, is it an action or a judgment, how often is it needed?
      • A good block also states the reason and the right path. Use more than one layer for critical rules.
      Sources
      1. Claude Code docs: Best practices (CLAUDE.md, hooks, emphasis)
      2. Claude Code docs: How Claude Code works (permissions, hook types)
      3. Claude prompting best practices (overtriggering)

      Building your own harness

      One day the out-of-the-box behavior of Claude Code or Codex will not be enough: a support agent that talks to an internal system, a maintenance agent that runs overnight, a review step that runs in CI. Then you will build part of the harness yourself. This lesson shows what you must not skip when you write one from scratch.

      First, don’t write it from scratch

      The first piece of advice may come as a surprise: if you can, do not write the harness from scratch. The Claude Agent SDK is the programmable form of the harness that runs Claude Code; tools, permissions, hooks, context management and subagents come ready-made. The OpenAI Agents SDK also provides its own loop, handoffs and max_turns guard. Writing your own loop is an instructive exercise; but in production, rewriting every layer means rediscovering every failure path each layer closes off.

      Anthropic’s Agent SDK post describes an agent’s work as a four-step loop: gather context, take action, verify the work, repeat. It lists three options for verification: rules (lint, tests), visual feedback (screenshots) and LLM-as-judge. About the last one the post is frank: it is generally not a very robust method. In other words, use a deterministic verifier wherever you can.

      Minimum harness checklist

      Recall the loop from level 5: one model call, a stop_reason check, a few lines that run the tools and append the results. To take that skeleton to production you add pieces, each of which closes off a failure path. In the diagram below, switch the pieces on one by one and watch the loop grow. The counter at the bottom right shows an important truth: whatever pieces you add, there is only one line with the model in it. Everything else is ordinary, testable software.

      From loop to harness, piece by piece

      Tick a piece; the lines added to the loop appear highlighted, and the failure path the piece closes off is listed below. The code is Python-like pseudocode.

      Common mistakes

      • No stop condition. A loop that starts with while True carries the bill into infinity too when the model gets stuck. max_turns and a token or cost budget are the first two things to add.
      • Error messages not written for the model. A tool result that just says “failed” makes the model repeat the same call. Error text that says what happened and how to fix it shortens the loop (level 4).
      • No verifier. It is done when the model says it is done. If verification is not inside the loop, “done” means “looks done” (level 5).
      • Permission checks living inside the model. The sentence “do not run dangerous commands” sits in the system prompt, but the executor has no check at all. However good the model is, that is not a security boundary.
      • Observability as an afterthought. Debugging a harness that does not record each turn’s request, response and tool results is like debugging a distributed system without logs. It is one reason Claude Code stores sessions as JSONL.
      • No context limit. Letting a tool return 200 KB of logs exhausts both quality and budget within a few turns. Truncate the output, and when you do, tell the model how to narrow it down.
      You already know thisThis list looks a lot like the checklist for an API gateway that handles requests from an untrusted client to a backend service: timeouts, rate and budget limits, authorization, input validation, response size limits, an audit log. The difference is that the “client” here is your own agent. Its untrustworthiness comes not from malice but from being probabilistic.

      Test the harness too

      The best thing about the harness is that it is ordinary software. You cannot unit-test the model, but you can unit-test the harness. Test the permission matcher with a list of commands: is git push --force rejected, does git status pass? Run the hook scripts with fixed JSON inputs and check their exit codes. Verify that the truncation function gives the model a hint to narrow down when it truncates. Keep the JSONL logs of real sessions; when you change the harness, replay the same tool calls and see what the new rules block. Measuring the model’s behavior is a job for evals (level 9); measuring the harness’s behavior is the testing you already know.

      When to build your own, when to use an off-the-shelf one?

      SituationReasonable choiceWhy
      Coding work on the developer’s own machineClaude Code, Codex CLIAll the layers are ready; shaped by settings files, CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md and hooks.
      A recurring agent step in CIThe ready-made CLI’s non-interactive mode, or the Agent SDKSame loop; permissions and output format are controlled from a script (level 9).
      A domain agent that talks to an internal systemAgent SDK + your own tools or MCP serverThe loop and context management are ready; the value is in your tool design.
      A job whose steps are known in advanceWorkflow: fixed code + a few model callsNo agent needed; cheaper and more predictable (level 5).
      CautionWhen you build your own harness, security becomes your responsibility too. Tool results are untrusted input; a web page or a database row can carry text that looks to the model like an instruction. Restricting privileges, network isolation and human approval for irreversible actions are the harness’s job. Do not ship an agent that faces the outside world before reading level 10.

      Key takeaways

      • If you can, do not write it from scratch: the Claude Agent SDK or the OpenAI Agents SDK gives you most of the layers ready-made.
      • Minimum production harness: stop condition, permission checks, output cap, deterministic verifier, context management, checkpoints, session log.
      • Whatever you add, there is only one line with the model in it; the rest of the harness is ordinary, testable software.
      • LLM-as-judge is the verifier of last resort; tests, lint and type checks come first.
      Sources
      1. Anthropic: Building agents with the Claude Agent SDK
      2. OpenAI Agents SDK: Running agents
      3. Anthropic: Building effective agents
      4. Anthropic: Effective harnesses for long-running agents

      Two questions that look like one

      When the “Claude Code or Codex, which is better?” debate starts in a team, the two sides are usually arguing about different things. One talks about the model (“Claude plans better”), the other about the tool (“Codex has the stricter sandbox”). Both can be right, because there is no single thing on the table: the model and the harness are separate layers.

      Remember the equation from the beginner level: Agent = Model + Harness. Claude Code is Anthropic’s harness; Claude models run inside it. Codex, as of November 2026, is the name of OpenAI’s agent product: a CLI, an IDE extension, a desktop app and a cloud environment. Models from the GPT family run inside it. The distinction used to be blurry, because for a while OpenAI shipped coding-specific models with a “-codex” suffix. Since GPT-5.4 there has been no separate coding model; coding ability was folded into the general model. So saying “the Codex model” today is technically wrong. Codex is a harness; the model is a GPT release such as gpt-6.1-sol or gpt-6-astra.

      Why do we have to separate them?

      Because when you want to fix a behavior, you need to know which layer to touch. If you are wondering why the agent changed a file without asking, the answer is not in the model but in the harness’s permission mode. If you are wondering why the agent called an API the wrong way, the answer is probably in the model’s training and in the context. As you saw in level 6, the same model produces noticeably different results in different harnesses: LangChain reports that, without changing the model at all and only changing the prompt, the tools and the middleware, it raised its Terminal-Bench 2.0 score from 52.8% to 66.5% (the company’s own measurement). According to an independent compilation, the same Opus 4.6 model spreads across a range of roughly 24 points on this benchmark depending on the harness; that figure comes from a secondary source and is not exact, but the direction is consistent.

      You already know thisThe same PostgreSQL database can perform very differently through EF Core and through hand-written SQL. And the same EF Core behaves differently on different database engines. When you see an “application performance” number, you know it measures the engine and the access layer together. Agents are no different: a score measures the model and the harness together.

      The layers are not fully independent either

      One detail complicates things a little. Both labs train their models together with their own harnesses. OpenAI’s Codex guide says plainly that the model was trained on the apply_patch diff format and a dedicated terminal tool, and tuned to follow AGENTS.md instructions closely. Anthropic likewise writes that tool schemas such as bash and text_editor are “baked into training”, and that the model has been optimized on thousands of successful trajectories with those exact signatures. The result: a model is usually most comfortable in its own “home” harness. But this is not a law; teams such as LangChain argue that the training harness does not have to be the best harness for a given task.

      In practice this means that when you use Claude Code with Claude models and Codex with GPT models, the two layers are tuned to each other. That is why, while comparing them in this level, we will always keep two questions apart: what can the model do? and what does the harness allow it to do, and what does it show it?

      Two ecosystems, layer by layer

      Pick a layer. Purple rows are products of training and the model, teal rows are harness architecture, green rows are common ground between the two worlds. Click a row to see why it matters. Information as of November 2026 (Claude Code v2.1.318, Codex CLI 0.166.0).

      Click a row.
      Myth“Codex is a plain work tool; Claude is an individual with an imagination.” Half observation, half exaggeration. What is true: the two labs emphasize different things in post-training, and that shows up in how long the explanations are, how many questions the model asks and when it considers a job “done”. What is exaggerated: both are networks that predict tokens; “character” is a consistent behavior pattern shaped by training. On top of that, half of that pattern comes from the harness: the system prompt, the tool set and the permission mode directly affect how chatty or how bold the model appears. Choose your tool by measuring it on your own tasks, not by “which one feels more creative”.

      The map of this level

      1. Model layer: the current line-ups, the prices and the two labs’ philosophies for “raising” a model.
      2. Reading benchmarks: seeing what a score measures, why SWE-bench Verified was dropped and how the harness moves the score.
      3. Sandbox and approval: the most visible architectural difference between the two harnesses. We will run the same action on both sides and watch who decides what.
      4. Instructions, hooks, skills: where the two worlds converge, and how to keep your investment portable.
      5. Which one, when: a no-hype decision guide that depends on your situation.

      Key takeaways

      • “Claude Code or Codex?” is two separate questions: the model or the harness?
      • As of November 2026 Codex is a product; there is no separate “Codex model”, GPT models run inside it.
      • A benchmark score measures the model and the harness together. The same model can move 10–20 points in a different harness.
      • Models are trained together with their own harnesses, so the “home” pairing usually works well, but it is not the only right answer.

      When comparing at the model layer, we look at three questions: what sizes are in the line-up, how much you pay per token, and what values the lab raises the model with. The tables below were taken from the official model pages as of November 2026. These numbers change every few months; check the official page again before putting them into a team decision document.

All of them have adaptive thinking: the model decides for itself how much to think. In Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 it is always on; in Claude Code it cannot be turned off for the 5.5 models.       Caution: the exchange rate between tokensPrices are “per million tokens”, but every lab has a different tokenizer. The same text splits into a different number of tokens on each side. Even within Anthropic, the new tokenizer that arrived with Opus 4.7 produces roughly 1.35 times as many tokens for the same English text. Putting the price tables side by side is a start, but you only learn the real cost by running the same task on both sides and looking at the bill.

      Same session, six models

      The cost of an agent session mostly accumulates on the input side, especially in the context re-sent on every turn. Pick a preset or play with the sliders. The calculation is a simplified model that ignores the cache write surcharge and counts both sides’ tokens as equal; the goal is to get a feel for the price structure.

      The cache difference can outweigh the price difference

      In level 2 you saw how prompt caching works. Here the difference between the two sides starts to matter. At Anthropic, a cache read is normally 0.1 times the input price; but on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 it is 0.05 times, and on Fable 5.1 0.025 times. The cache lives for 5 minutes by default and the timer resets on every hit; a 1-hour cache is also available if you want it. At OpenAI caching is automatic and on by default; a read is 0.05 times on GPT-6.1 Sol and 0.1 times on Astra. Because the overwhelming majority of input tokens in a long agent session are read from the cache, a model with a high-looking list price can turn out cheaper than expected in practice, or the other way round. In the calculator above, pull the cache ratio down to zero and watch the difference.

      Raising philosophy: constitution and Model Spec

      Both labs describe how their models should behave in a public document, but their styles differ.

      Anthropic: constitution

      In January 2026 (21–22 January) a new Claude constitution was published and released to the public under CC0. The approach is to explain the why instead of listing rules one by one: values, judgment and an order of priorities. The order is roughly safety, ethics, guidelines and helpfulness. The goal is for the model to develop judgment that behaves sensibly even in situations it has never seen.

      OpenAI: Model Spec

      Commentators find the Model Spec more rule-based and structured. At the center of the document is an explicit “chain of command”: OpenAI, then the developer, then the user. We could not verify the exact current version number of the document; its principled structure, however, has been widely reported.

      In chat mode this difference is felt as a difference in style, but for agents what matters is the common ground: both documents define an authority hierarchy. An operator or developer instruction, a user message and tool output do not carry the same weight. Tool output in particular, meaning a web page that was read, an issue body or a file, is data; it is not a party that gives instructions. This is the model-side half of the defense against prompt injection. The other half lives in the harness and is the subject of level 10. The model-side half is probabilistic: training lowers the chance that the model mistakes data for instructions, but does not bring it to zero.

      Go deeper: is effort a model setting or a harness setting?Both. Effort (the thinking budget) is a parameter sent to the model in the API; but the harness decides what value it is sent with. In Claude Code you can raise it for a session with /effort high or /effort xhigh; that is also what is recommended for hard bugs and schema changes. The default effort depends on the model (see the table above). Higher effort is not always better: OpenAI also writes that high effort can increase the tendency to “overthink” and run unnecessary searches. In the next topic you will see why effort is a separate axis in benchmark comparisons.

      Key takeaways

      • As of November 2026 the Claude line-up is Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, all with 1M context. On the Codex side: gpt-6-astra, gpt-6.1-sol, gpt-6.1-terra, gpt-6-luna.
      • Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol have the same list price ($2 / $10); Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra are the same too ($10 / $50).
      • In long sessions the cache read multiplier can matter more than the list price.
      • Both labs define an authority hierarchy; tool output is data, not instructions. This model-side defense is probabilistic.

      What does a score measure?

      When a new model comes out, the first thing you see is a benchmark table: “model X scores 80% on this test”. Learning to read that number is the cheapest way to protect yourself from marketing when choosing a tool. The rule is simple: a score is a single point in the product task set × version × model × harness × effort × infrastructure. If any of these axes differs, putting two scores side by side is like comparing two response times measured with different queries on two different databases.

      Why was SWE-bench Verified dropped?

      SWE-bench Verified was a subset of real issues from open-source Python projects plus their tests, verified by humans as “solvable”. Throughout 2024–2025 it was the main showcase for coding agents. On 23 February 2026 OpenAI announced that it would no longer report this benchmark. The reasoning has two parts:

      • Broken tests: An audit of the hardest 138 problems found that in at least 59.4% of them the tests also rejected correct solutions. In other words, the ceiling of the score was the quality of the tests, not the model’s ability.
      • Contamination: Models such as GPT-5.2, Opus 4.5 and Gemini 3 Flash could reproduce some fixes from memory. The benchmark itself had leaked into the training data.

      In its place OpenAI recommended SWE-bench Pro, a harder set designed against Verified’s weaknesses. But you need to be careful here too: in Scale’s standardized common setup (SEAL), as of October 2026 the top results are around 60% (e.g. Muse Spark 1.1 at 61.5%, GPT-5.4 xHigh at 59.1%). The 89.9% that Anthropic reports for Opus 5.5, on the other hand, is a vendor figure measured in a different setup and not independently verified. Both carry the same benchmark name but cannot be compared.

      Terminal-Bench and the weight of the harness

      Terminal-Bench tests the agent with terminal tasks in a container: build, configure, debug, process data. For coding agents it is a more “agentic” measure than SWE-bench. As of November 2026 the official site shows version 4.0 as current. The figures circulating for this version come from aggregator sites and have not been verified, so in the lab below we use the better-documented results of version 2.0. These results show the core lesson very clearly: at the top of Snorkel’s 2.0 table are GPT-5.5 entries run with custom harnesses (84.7%) and Opus 4.7 with a custom harness (80.2%). When the same models are measured with vals.ai’s fixed harness (Terminus 2), GPT-5.5 scores 73.2% and Opus 4.8 70.0%. The 10-point gap in between is largely the harness’s doing.

      Then there is infrastructure noise. Anthropic’s February 2026 post on “infrastructure noise in agentic coding evals” shows that infrastructure differences alone (timeouts, resource limits, network) can move scores. So a two-point difference may simply be the result the same model got on a different day.

      Leaderboard reading lab

      Real results with known sources. Pick two rows; the widget shows which axes are the same and which differ, and explains whether the two numbers can be put side by side. Source type: “independent” is a fixed evaluator, “vendor” is the company that builds the model or the harness.

      Pick two rows.

      Five questions to ask when reading a table row

      1. Which set, which version? “SWE-bench” and “SWE-bench Pro”, “Terminal-Bench 2.0” and “4.0” are different exams.
      2. Which harness? The vendor’s own agent, the benchmark’s reference harness, or a custom harness tuned for the competition? Harnesses tuned for benchmarks differ from product harnesses in things like timeouts and non-interactivity; a product harness is optimized for safety, permissions and cost.
      3. Which effort? A result measured at “xHigh” is not the result you will get with your default setting; its cost is different too.
      4. Who measured it? A vendor figure is not wrong as such, but its setup is usually not published in full.
      5. Does it resemble my work? Python library bugs and the migration of an enterprise .NET application are not the same skill.
      In practiceUse benchmarks as a “shortlist” tool, not a decision tool. For the real decision, pick 20–30 real tasks from your own repository, run each at least three times in both tools, and record whether the tests pass and what it cost. In level 9 we will look in detail at how to do this, why a single run is not enough and the difference between pass@k and pass^k.
      Myth“The model that is number one on the leaderboard will be number one in my agent too.” The table shows that model’s best result with that harness, at that effort, on that infrastructure. Your harness, your tools and your repo are a different experiment.

      Key takeaways

      • Because of broken tests and contamination, OpenAI has not reported SWE-bench Verified since February 2026 and recommends SWE-bench Pro instead.
      • Under the same benchmark name, independent (~60%) and vendor (89.9%) figures can sit side by side; their setups differ.
      • Harness and effort can move a score by more than 10 points; infrastructure noise moves it by a few points too.
      • Benchmarks are for the shortlist; the decision is made with repeated measurements on your own tasks.

      Two different security philosophies

      The most visible architectural difference between the two harnesses is how the decision to let the agent “do something” is made. Roughly speaking, Codex is designed sandbox-first and Claude Code permission-first. Each later added the other’s mechanism, so today they share largely the same building blocks; but the defaults and the way of thinking differ.

      Codex: walls first, questions second

      In Codex every command runs inside an operating-system sandbox, and that is an inseparable part of the model. sandbox_mode takes three values:

      • read-only: can read, cannot write.
      • workspace-write: can write to the working directory; network is off by default (enabled with [sandbox_workspace_write] network_access = true). .git, .agents, .codex and .aws are read-only even when they are inside the writable root.
      • danger-full-access: no walls.

      What happens to a command that hits the wall is decided by approval_policy: on-request lets the model ask for escalation and you approve it; never never asks, and the error goes back to the model. There is also a detailed (granular) table option. The old untrusted value has been retired; if it lingers in an old config file it can prevent Codex from starting. Codex’s “Auto” preset means workspace-write + on-request in folders under version control and read-only elsewhere. codex exec (non-interactive mode) is read-only by default. On the platform side, Codex uses Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap and seccomp on Linux, and the preferred “MXC” sandbox on Windows.

      approval_policy = "on-request"
sandbox_mode    = "workspace-write"

[sandbox_workspace_write]
network_access = false

[features.network_proxy]
enabled = true
domains = { "registry.npmjs.org" = "allow", "db.example.test" = "deny" }

      Claude Code: rules first, sandbox optional

      In Claude Code every tool call goes through a permission mode and permission rules. The modes: default (“Manual” in the UI: asks about most things), acceptEdits (accepts file edits without asking), plan (read-only, no edits until the plan is approved), auto (a classifier model decides), dontAsk and bypassPermissions (never asks). As of November 2026 the default starting mode in the interactive terminal and in VS Code is auto (since v2.1.283); in claude -p and the SDK it is Manual (since v2.1.302). The 2025-era knowledge that “the default asks about everything” is out of date.

      The operating-system sandbox in Claude Code is optional and off by default. When enabled, it uses Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap with socat on Linux and WSL2. There are two important limits: there is no native sandbox for Windows (you need WSL2), and the sandbox only wraps shell commands (Bash, PowerShell, Monitor); Read, Edit, WebFetch, MCP tools and hooks are outside the sandbox, under the control of the permission system. The network is restricted through a proxy with a domain allowlist (sandbox.network.allowedDomains, which starts empty). Anthropic reports that the sandbox cut permission prompts by 84%, because there is no need to ask about commands that stay inside the walls.

      {
  "permissions": {
    "defaultMode": "acceptEdits",
    "allow": ["Bash(npm run test *)"],
    "deny":  ["Read(./.env)", "Bash(curl *)"]
  },
  "sandbox": {
    "enabled": true,
    "network": { "allowedDomains": ["registry.npmjs.org"] }
  }
}

      On both sides some paths are protected. In Claude Code, writes to paths such as .git, .claude, .vscode, .idea, .husky, .devcontainer, shell startup files, .npmrc and .mcp.json are never auto-approved in any mode except bypassPermissions. The logic is the same: these files can run code on the next command or in the next session.

      Same action, two harnesses

      The settings on the left configure Claude Code, those on the right configure Codex. Each row is an action the agent wants to take; the cells show the outcome and which mechanism makes the decision. This is a simplified model built from the rules in the documentation; your own rules and hooks change the outcome.

      ActionClaude CodeCodex
      RunsAsksClassifier decidesBlocked

      There are three things I want you to notice in the lab. First, the workspace-write sandbox runs rm -rf build/ without asking: the sandbox does not block destructive operations inside the working directory, it only blocks getting out of it. Second, in Claude Code, even with the sandbox on, editing ~/.bashrc is caught by the permission system, not by the sandbox, because the Edit tool is outside the sandbox’s scope. Third, auto mode is a classifier, and it is probabilistic.

      Model-based approvers: auto mode and auto_review

      Both sides added an “approver model” to spare the human from being asked at every step. The reason is real data: according to Anthropic’s March 2026 post, users approve 93% of permission prompts. A prompt that gets “yes” that often becomes, after a while, a habit rather than a safeguard. Claude Code’s auto mode uses a two-stage transcript classifier and a server-side injection probe. The classifier only sees user messages and tool calls; the assistant’s own prose and tool results are stripped out so that injected text cannot “argue” with the classifier. The reported figures: a false-positive rate of 0.4% on 10,000 real actions; a miss rate of 17% on 52 real “overeager” actions; a miss rate of 5.7% on synthetic data-exfiltration attempts. After 3 consecutive or 20 total denials it hands back to the human. In Codex, approvals_reviewer = "auto_review" does a similar job: a reviewer agent looks at requests that already need approval and denies them when it is unsure (fail closed).

      Caution: YOLO flagsIn Claude Code --dangerously-skip-permissions and in Codex --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox (short name --yolo) remove all protection. Codex’s old --full-auto flag is no longer supported. In the Nx “s1ngularity” attack of August 2025, malicious npm packages invoked the agent CLIs installed on the machine with exactly these flags and sent them hunting for secrets. Only use these flags in a disposable container; consider disabling them by policy on team machines (in Claude Code, disableBypassPermissionsMode).

      Key takeaways

      • In Codex the sandbox (sandbox_mode) is always there; approval_policy says what happens when you hit the wall.
      • In Claude Code the permission mode and rules are the foundation; the OS sandbox is optional, starts off, is not native on Windows and only wraps shell commands.
      • A sandbox does not block a destructive operation inside the working directory; it blocks getting outside the boundary.
      • Auto mode and auto_review are probabilistic layers; they go next to deterministic rules, not in place of them.

      1. Codex: Agent approvals and security
      2. Codex: Non-interactive mode
      3. Claude Code: Permission modes, Permissions
      4. Claude Code: Sandboxing
      5. Anthropic: Claude Code sandboxing

      7. GitGuardian: Nx s1ngularity

      Different names, converging architecture

      The good news: the extension mechanisms of the two harnesses are converging fast. Instruction files, the hook contract and the skill format now have largely the same shape. That means the investment your team makes in these tools (rules, automations, procedures) is not locked into one tool. But the differences in the details are worth knowing, because they may be the answer to “why wasn’t this rule loaded?”.

      Instruction files: CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md

      Claude Code

      A managed (organization) file, the user file ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, the project file ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md, and the personal ./CLAUDE.local.md that stays out of git. At startup the ancestors from the root down to the working directory are loaded; those in subdirectories are loaded when a file in that directory is touched. Files are merged, they do not override each other; the closer one is read later. You can import with @path (up to 4 hops). .claude/rules/*.md files with a paths: header are loaded only when a matching file is touched. Target: under 200 lines per file.

      Codex

      Globally ~/.codex/AGENTS.override.md, otherwise ~/.codex/AGENTS.md (the first non-empty file). In the project, one file per directory from the root down to the working directory: AGENTS.override.md first, otherwise AGENTS.md, otherwise the fallback names you define with project_doc_fallback_filenames. All of them are merged; reading stops when the total reaches the project_doc_max_bytes limit (32 KiB by default). It is said to have no import mechanism, but only a third-party source says so.

      If your team uses both tools, the most robust setup is this: keep the shared project rules in AGENTS.md, and put only an @AGENTS.md line and a few Claude-specific notes in CLAUDE.md. How Claude Code handles an AGENTS.md file directly has changed from version to version, so do not guess what gets loaded; check it in Claude Code with /context. On the Codex side, too, checking which files were read at the start of a session is a good habit.

      Which instruction file gets loaded?

      An imaginary example_app repository. Pick the harness and the working directory, and toggle the optional events. The list shows the order in which files enter the context and their size. In Codex the part beyond the 32 KiB limit is cut off; in Claude Code imports do not reduce the context cost.

      Hooks: the same contract

      In level 8 we will go deep into Claude Code hooks; here the comparison is what matters. As of November 2026 Claude Code offers 33 hook events and five handler types (command, http, mcp_tool, prompt, agent). Codex has 14 events: SessionStart, SessionEnd, PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PostToolUse, PreModelRequest, PostModelRequest, PreCompact, PostCompact, UserPromptSubmit, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, Stop and Interrupt. What really matters is the shape of the contract, and that is almost identical:

      • The hook receives the event information as JSON on stdin.
      • Exit 2 blocks the action; text written to stderr goes back to the model as the reason.
      • For PreToolUse, hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision: "deny" in the JSON output blocks.
      • For Stop and UserPromptSubmit, a top-level {"decision": "block", "reason": "…"} is used.

      The difference is in the trust model: Codex runs hooks with hash-based trust, meaning that if the content of a hook you approved changes, it needs to be trusted again. In Claude Code a project’s hooks become active once workspace trust has been granted. Both approaches exist for the same reason: a configuration file in the repository is a file that can run code on your machine. In level 10 we will look at real CVEs for this.

      Skills: SKILL.md is now a common standard

      A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file inside that has a front-matter header. At first only its name and description enter the context; the body is loaded only when needed, and extra files only when referenced. Thanks to this “progressive disclosure”, defining dozens of skills does not fill up the context. Anthropic handed the SKILL.md format over to the Agentic AI Foundation on 22 October 2026; the format no longer belongs to a single company. Together with AGENTS.md and MCP, it forms the common language of the two worlds.

      You already know thisThis convergence resembles the Language Server Protocol in the editor world. Once, every editor needed a separate plugin for every language; with LSP, language support became an asset independent of the editor. AGENTS.md, SKILL.md, MCP and the shared hook contract likewise turn your team’s knowledge and automation into an asset independent of the harness.
      In practiceWrite hook scripts without depending on harness-specific fields: read tool_name and tool_input from stdin and give the decision with exit 2. That way the same block-db-writes script works in both tools. The only tool-specific part is the configuration file you wire the script into.

      Key takeaways

      • Claude Code merges instruction files, allows imports and loads rules by path; Codex takes one file per directory and cuts off at 32 KiB.
      • Keep shared rules in AGENTS.md and import them from CLAUDE.md; verify what was loaded with /context.
      • The hook contract is the same on both sides: stdin JSON, exit 2 to block, permissionDecision, decision: "block".
      • SKILL.md, AGENTS.md and MCP are harness-independent assets; invest in them.
      Sources
      1. Claude Code: Memory (CLAUDE.md)
      2. Codex: AGENTS.md
      3. Claude Code: Hooks, Codex: Hooks
      4. Claude Code: Skills
      5. Anthropic News: SKILL.md handed over to the Agentic AI Foundation (22 October 2026)

      A no-hype decision guide

      We will not declare a winner in this topic, for two reasons. First, both sides ship a release every few weeks; today’s advantage may be reversed three months from now. Second, the answer to “which is better?” depends on your work: which operating system, which security requirement, which kind of work, which budget. What we will do in this topic is lay out, situation by situation, the real differences that affect the decision.

      The differences that actually affect the decision

      AxisClaude CodeCodex
      OS sandboxOptional, starts off; on Windows only via WSL2Always there; MXC on Windows
      Permission granularitydeny/ask/allow rules at tool and argument level, 6 modesapproval_policy + granular table
      Hook events33 events, 5 handler types14 events, hash-based trust
      Non-interactive modeclaude -p, --bare, JSON / stream-jsoncodex exec, starts read-only, JSONL events
      CIanthropics/claude-code-action@v1openai/codex-action
      SDKAgent SDK: Python and TypeScriptCodex SDK: TypeScript; app-server API
      InterfacesTerminal, VS Code, JetBrains, desktop, web, SlackCLI, IDE extension, Codex app, ChatGPT Work, iOS
      CloudIsolated sandbox on the web; git credentials outside the sandbox, behind a scoped git proxyTwo phases: network and secrets during the setup phase; during the agent phase network off, secrets removed

      What stands out in your situation?

      Tick the situations that fit your team. The widget does not pick a winner; for each situation it lists what to watch for on each side and the note that applies to both.

      A protocol for running your own comparison

      If you need to make a real decision, a small experiment you can run over a weekend is enough. What matters is that the experiment follows the eval discipline you will see in level 9.

      1. Pick tasks: 20–30 jobs your team actually did in the last three months. Mix easy, medium and hard. The success of each must be checkable automatically: certain tests must pass, certain files must not change.
      2. Level the environment: The same commit, the same instruction file (shared AGENTS.md, imported by CLAUDE.md), the same permission level. If the sandbox is on in one and off in the other, what you are comparing is the security setting.
      3. Repeat: Run each task at least three times in each tool. A single run is chance.
      4. Record four things: did the tests pass, how many turns did it take, what did it cost, would a human accept the diff.
      5. Read the transcripts: Check whether the failures were “fair”. Was the task ambiguous, did the harness block it, or did the model get it wrong?
      In practice: using both togetherMany teams use the two tools together, and that is a legitimate choice. For example, having one tool write the code in a session and the other do an independent review can catch different mistakes than having the same model review its own work. All you need for this is to keep instruction files, skills and hook scripts portable; you saw how in the previous topic.
      Myth“One is secure, the other isn’t.” The security of both tools depends largely on your settings. If you run Codex with --yolo, there is no sandbox; if you set up Claude Code with the sandbox, deny rules and PreToolUse hooks, you get a fairly narrow box. The defaults differ; the ceilings are similar.

      Key takeaways

      • There is no winner; there are differences that stand out depending on your work, operating system, security requirements and budget.
      • For a team working natively on Windows the sandbox difference is concrete: Codex has a native Windows sandbox, Claude Code needs WSL2.
      • To decide, measure repeatedly on your own tasks in a level environment; read the transcripts.
      • If you keep your investment in instructions, skills and hooks portable, switching tools gets cheap.
