      Explore, plan, implement, verify

      The teams that get the most out of Claude Code share a common rhythm, and it has not changed since 2025: first have it read, then have it plan, then have it implement, and last have it verify. What has changed is that the tools supporting this rhythm have matured, and the official guide has boiled it down to a sharper statement.

      The current “best practices” page ties the work to three sentences: tell Claude what it cannot see, give it a check it can run, and enforce the rules that must have no exceptions. The first is the job of context (this lesson and CLAUDE.md), the second is the job of verification (tests, the compiler, /verify), the third is the job of the harness (permission rules and hooks). Every lesson in this level unpacks those three sentences.

      Why plan first?

      In level 5 you saw the agent loop: every turn is a model call that rereads the whole history. An agent spinning for twenty turns on a misunderstood task burns context, money and your time, and ends up producing a diff you will have to revert. Spending five minutes reading the plan is the cheapest debugging method there is. Plan mode exists exactly for this: the agent can read files and run read-only commands, but it cannot edit anything until the plan is approved. If auto mode is available, commands approved by the classifier also run in plan mode.

      You cycle through the modes with Shift+Tab. As of November 2026 the cycle is: auto → default → acceptEdits → plan → (bypassPermissions) → auto. The mode in parentheses only joins the cycle if it has been enabled; dontAsk is not in the cycle at all and can only be turned on with a command-line flag.

      The Shift+Tab cycle

      Press the button to move to the next mode. For each mode, see what happens to four representative actions. The “bypass enabled” box adds bypass mode to the cycle, as long as it has not been disabled in settings.

      A good task description

      In level 3 we talked about writing a prompt like a work order. In Claude Code the practical version is: state the symptom, where to look, and what counts as “done”. The official guide’s example replaces “fix the login bug” with “login fails after session timeout; check the token refresh in src/auth/; write a failing test that reproduces the issue first, then fix it”. Apply the same pattern to your own work:

      order total is wrong, fix it
      In example.orders, discounted orders get the
discount applied twice (e.g. order_id 1042).
Look at the calculation in src/Orders/OrderTotal.cs.
First write a failing test that reproduces this,
then fix it. dotnet test must pass; no migration.

      Anatomy of a session

      A realistic session for the task above, in the fictional example_app repository. Step through it; at each step, watch which mode you are in, what the agent is doing and where you step in.

      Steering: when do you intervene?

      • Esc stops the agent mid-action. The guide’s advice: “watch the first minute, and press Esc the moment it starts to drift”.
      • Esc Esc or /rewind opens the rewind menu (the last lesson of this level).
      • After two failed fixes, do not write a third: clear with /clear and start again with a better prompt. A context full of failed attempts keeps the model in the same rut.
      • /btw lets you ask a side question without polluting the history.
      • /rename names the session, and claude --resume <name> brings you back to it.
      • /verify builds and runs the application; /goal has a separate model check a condition every turn; /code-review gets the change reviewed.
      • /effort high or xhigh raises the thinking budget for subtle bugs and schema changes.
      You already know thisIt is like working with a talented new junior. First you ask them to read the code, then to explain what they intend to do; you do not let them touch anything until you have approved the plan. When the work is done, you run the tests together. The difference: this junior is extremely fast, never gets tired, and may forget the beginning of the conversation.

      Key takeaways

      • Tell it what it cannot see, give it a check it can run, enforce no-exception rules in the harness.
      • Plan mode reads but does not edit; reading the plan is the cheapest debugging there is.
      • The Shift+Tab cycle: auto → default → acceptEdits → plan → (bypass) → auto. dontAsk only via a flag.
      • After two failed fixes, /clear and a better prompt.
      Sources
      1. Claude Code: Best practices
      2. Claude Code: Permission modes
      3. Anthropic: Claude Code best practices (April 2025)

      Instructions read in every session

      CLAUDE.md is a Markdown file that Claude Code loads into context at the start of every session. In level 3 we said that for lasting impact you should invest in the layers that are added automatically to every request; this is that layer. But let us make one thing clear up front: CLAUDE.md is guidance, not enforcement. Claude reads it and mostly follows it; but, in the words of the official docs, it is allowed to decide that a line does not apply in a given situation. That is why the most important sentence in the guide is this one: If you keep adding emphasis to a CLAUDE.md line and Claude still misses it, that line belongs in a hook. Adding “IMPORTANT” probably will not fix it.

      Hierarchy

      ScopeLocationFor whom
      Managed (organization)/etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md, on Windows C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\CLAUDE.mdAll users; deployed by IT
      User~/.claude/CLAUDE.mdAll your projects
      Project./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.mdThe team; committed to the repo
      Local./CLAUDE.local.mdYou, this project; stays out of git
      Rules.claude/rules/*.md (with a paths: header)Only when matching files are touched

      At startup, the files in the ancestor directories from the root down to the working directory are loaded; files in subdirectories are loaded when a file in that directory is touched. The files are concatenated, they do not override each other: the closer one is read later. This resembles the CSS cascade but is not quite the same; if two rules conflict, both stay in context and the model has to decide which one applies. Resolve the conflict yourself.

      With the @path/file.md syntax you can import other files. The path is relative to the importing file; at most 4 hops of depth are allowed; importing a file from outside the project requires a one-time approval. Let us correct an important misconception: imports do not reduce context cost; the imported file is loaded in full as well. The real savings tools are rules with a paths: header under .claude/rules/, and skills. The official target is under 200 lines per file. For auto memory (MEMORY.md), the first 200 lines or 25 KB are loaded. In monorepos you can leave out the files of unrelated subprojects with claudeMdExcludes.

      ---
paths:
  - "**/*.sql"
---
- Always schema-qualify names: example.orders, example.customers.
- DML scripts start with BEGIN and end with ROLLBACK; a human puts in the COMMIT.

      What goes in, what stays out?

      Write

      • Exact verification commands: how to run a single test file, typecheck, lint.
      • Misleading code: “src/legacy/ is still live, but do not copy its patterns into new code”.
      • Decisions that are not in the repo, and their reasons.
      • Anything you have corrected twice.

      Don’t write

      • Things that can be inferred from the code (“we use Angular in this project”).
      • Personal preferences: those go in CLAUDE.local.md.
      • Long procedures: those go in a skill.
      • No-exception prohibitions: those go in a deny rule or a hook.
      • Secrets, tokens, passwords. Never.

      The sample file in the official docs is a good summary of these principles. Here is a version adapted for a .NET project:

      # Commands
- Build: dotnet build -warnaserror
- Single test class: dotnet test --filter FullyQualifiedName~OrderTotalTests
- Format check: dotnet format --verify-no-changes

# Conventions
- Use src/Common/Result.cs for error returns; do not throw raw exceptions
- src/Legacy/ is still live, but do not copy its patterns into new code

# Gotchas
- Integration tests need DATABASE_URL; see .env.example
- example.orders.amount is numeric(12,2); use decimal on the C# side

      Pruning a CLAUDE.md

      Lines that came out of a team’s “let’s put everything in CLAUDE.md” meeting. Click a line: see where it belongs according to the official guide and why; the line moves to that destination. The preview on the right shows the size of the remaining CLAUDE.md and the approximate tokens it costs in every session.

      Click a line.
      In practiceIn a new repo, /init generates a starter CLAUDE.md; do not leave it as is, run it through the filter above. To see the problems in your existing instructions you can use /doctor prompt-audit. And the best habit: when the agent makes the same mistake a second time, add a single line for it. If it makes it a third time, that line should probably be a hook.

      Key takeaways

      • CLAUDE.md is guidance, not enforcement. If a rule is still missed after you add emphasis, it belongs in a hook.
      • Files are concatenated, not overridden; resolve conflicts yourself.
      • @import does not reduce cost; savings come from .claude/rules (paths) and skills.
      • Write commands, misleading code, decisions not in the repo and anything corrected twice; everything else goes elsewhere.
      Sources
      1. Claude Code: Memory (CLAUDE.md)
      2. Claude Code: Best practices

      Permission rules: who gets what, in which order

      In level 7 you saw the permission modes. Modes are the coarse setting; fine-tuning is done with permission rules. A rule has the form Tool or Tool(specifier): Bash(npm run *), Read(./.env), WebFetch(domain:example.com), mcp__server__tool, Skill(skill:release). Rules go into three lists: deny, ask, allow.

      Evaluation order: deny, ask, allow

      The most important sentence of this lesson: deny is evaluated first, then ask, then allow; the first match wins, and specificity does not matter. In the words of the docs, an allow rule cannot carve an exception out of a deny rule. For someone used to firewall rules this may feel backwards at first; there, usually the most specific rule or the first rule in order wins. Here, the list type wins.

      How do Bash rules match?

      • The pattern is a glob applied to the whole command. Bash(npm run *) matches npm run build, not npm install.
      • The space before * matters: Bash(git diff *) only matches git diff …; Bash(git diff*) also matches git diff-index.
      • Compound commands are split: && || ; | |& & and newline are separators. For allow, every subcommand must be permitted; for deny and ask, a match on any subcommand is enough. The contents of $(…), subshells and loops also count as subcommands.
      • Wrappers are stripped: timeout time nice nohup stdbuf command builtin noglob. timeout 30 npm run build is evaluated like npm run build.
      • Leading environment variable assignments (FOO=bar command): allow rules do not match past them, deny rules do. So nobody can trick an allow with an environment variable, but nobody can escape a deny that way either.

      Permission rule matcher

      Edit the rules, type a command or path, or pick one of the ready-made examples. The matcher splits the command into subcommands, strips wrappers and, for each piece, shows which rule matches in deny → ask → allow order. It is a teaching matcher built from the rules in the docs; it does not mimic every detail of the real implementation.

      Caution: Bash deny is not a security boundaryThe docs say this explicitly. A Bash(curl *) deny rule does not stop /usr/bin/curl … or sh -c 'curl …'; nor does it stop curl written into a script file and executed. Deny rules are a good seatbelt against accidental mistakes. A real boundary is a mechanism that works regardless of how the command is written: the sandbox’s network allowlist, operating system permissions, the narrow scope of the agent’s credentials. Pair deny rules with these; do not substitute them.

      Read and Edit paths

      File rules use gitignore syntax and there are four path forms: //absolute/path, ~/home/directory, /relative-to-settings-file-source and ./relative. Careful: a path starting with a single slash is not absolute; it is relative to the project where the settings file lives; an absolute path needs a double slash. Windows paths are normalized: C:\Users\alice becomes /c/Users/alice on the rule side; to block .env files on every drive you write //**/.env. A Read deny rule also blocks Edit and Write for the same path. A misconception: a file called .claudeignore has no effect whatsoever.

      Settings layers

      Rules live in settings.json files, and the precedence order is: managed settings > --settings on the command line > .claude/settings.local.json > .claude/settings.json > ~/.claude/settings.json. Arrays such as permissions.allow are merged across layers, not overridden. Two details matter for security: allow rules in a project wait until workspace trust is granted, while deny and ask rules apply immediately; and a defaultMode: auto or bypassPermissions value in a project or local file is ignored (since v2.1.257). So a repo you clone cannot put itself into bypass mode on its own.

      {
  "permissions": {
    "deny":  ["Bash(git push --force *)", "Read(./.env)", "Read(//**/.ssh/**)",
              "Edit(./src/Generated/**)"],
    "ask":   ["Bash(git clean *)"],
    "allow": ["Bash(dotnet build *)", "Bash(dotnet test *)", "Bash(git diff *)", "Bash(git status)"]
  }
}

      There are new keys for organization-level hardening: permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories and permissions.blockWritesOutsideWorkingDirectories (v2.1.314), disableBypassPermissionsMode and disableAutoMode. When these are placed in managed settings, users cannot loosen them.

      In practicePut only the safe allows everyone will want and the hard denies into the team settings (.claude/settings.json): build and test commands open, force push and secret files closed. Write personal conveniences into settings.local.json. If you approve a command every day, adding it to allow reduces approval fatigue; 93% of approval prompts get approved anyway.

      Key takeaways

      • deny → ask → allow; the first match wins; allow cannot carve an exception out of deny.
      • In a compound command, every piece must be permitted for allow; one piece is enough for deny and ask. Wrappers are stripped.
      • The space before * matters; a single-slash path is relative to the project, a double-slash path to the root.
      • Bash deny is not a security boundary; pair it with the sandbox and narrow credentials.
      • Arrays merge across layers; project allows wait until trust is granted.
      Sources
      1. Claude Code: Permissions
      2. Claude Code: Settings
      3. Anthropic: Claude Code auto mode

      Six tools, one question: who decides?

      There are six ways to extend Claude Code, and the most common mistake teams make is handing the job to the wrong tool: writing a no-exception rule into CLAUDE.md, putting a one-line fact into a skill, setting up an MCP server for a system that already has a good CLI. The key to picking the right tool is a single question: should Claude decide this behavior, or the harness?

      Claude decides (probabilistic)

      CLAUDE.md, .claude/rules, skills, subagent definitions, instructions in the prompt. The model reads them and usually follows them; depending on context it may also choose not to.

      The harness enforces (deterministic)

      Hooks, deny rules, a strict sandbox, managed settings, --max-turns and --max-budget-usd, CI checks, branch protection. They work regardless of what the model thinks.

      The tools one by one

      ToolWhatWhen it loadsWhat for
      CLAUDE.md / rulesAlways-on guidanceEvery session (rules: by path)Facts Claude cannot infer from the code
      Skill.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md + files; via /name or automaticallyDescription always (truncated at 1,536 characters); body when invoked; extra files when referencedRepeated team procedure: release, review, migration
      Subagent.claude/agents/*.md: separate context, its own prompt, tools, modelWhen delegated toIsolating noisy work, restricting tools, parallelism; only a summary comes back
      MCP serverExternal tools and dataTool names are deferred by default (tool search)Systems without a good CLI; if gh or aws exists, prefer them
      HookDeterministic code on lifecycle eventsAlwaysRules that must have no exceptions
      Plugin.claude-plugin/plugin.json: a bundle of the aboveDescriptions of enabled plugins in every sessionDistributing a setup to the team or a marketplace; runs with your permissions

      The old custom commands (.claude/commands/*.md) have merged into skills; if you want to write a new “slash command”, write a skill. A skill’s frontmatter has fields such as name, description, when_to_use, allowed-tools, disable-model-invocation, model, effort, context: fork and paths. A powerful feature is dynamic context: a line such as !`git diff HEAD` in the skill body is executed before the model sees the skill, and its output is substituted in. Keep SKILL.md under 500 lines; move detail into extra files.

      ---
name: release-notes
description: Drafts release notes for example_app. Use when the user asks for release notes,
  a changelog, or "what changed in this release".
allowed-tools: Bash(git log *), Bash(git diff *), Read
disable-model-invocation: false
---
Changes since the last tag:
!`git log --oneline $(git describe --tags --abbrev=0)..HEAD`

1. Group the changes as Feature / Fix / Maintenance.
2. Describe the user-visible impact in one sentence; do not copy commit wording.
3. See templates/release-notes.md for the format.

      In a subagent’s frontmatter the required fields are name and description; there are also fields such as tools, disallowedTools, model (sonnet, opus, haiku, fable, inherit or a full ID), permissionMode, skills, hooks, isolation: worktree, background, maxTurns and mcpServers. Built in: Explore, Plan and general-purpose. Subagents can be nested up to 3 levels deep. “Agent teams”, where several agents talk to each other, are experimental and according to the docs spend roughly 7 times the tokens.

      Which extension tool?

      Walk the decision tree on the left yourself by answering its questions, or click one of the real scenarios on the right; the tree lights up that scenario’s path step by step and explains why that tool was chosen in the end.

      Myth“The more MCP servers I connect, the more capable the agent gets.” Every server means new tool names, new descriptions and a new attack surface. Because Claude Code defers tool definitions by default and loads only their names, the context cost is lower than it used to be, but tool selection gets harder and supply chain risk goes up (level 10). If there is a good CLI, the agent can already use it through Bash, and you can keep the CLI’s reach narrow with permission rules.

      Key takeaways

      • First question: should Claude decide this behavior, or the harness? If it has no exceptions, the harness.
      • Short, always-relevant facts go in CLAUDE.md; path-specific facts in rules; procedures in a skill.
      • Noisy work, or work that needs isolation, goes to a subagent; only a summary comes back.
      • If there is a CLI, you may not need MCP. Plugins are for distribution and run with your permissions.
      Sources
      1. Claude Code: Best practices
      2. Claude Code: Skills
      3. Claude Code: Subagents
      4. Claude Code: Plugins
      5. Claude Code: Costs (agent teams)

      Certainty instead of probability

      The most important idea of this level: an instruction in the prompt is probabilistic; a hook is deterministic. If you write “run the formatter before committing” in CLAUDE.md, the model will most likely comply. If you write a hook, it runs every single time. Every rule for which “most likely” is not good enough should move into a hook.

      A hook is a handler attached to an event in Claude Code’s lifecycle. As of November 2026 there are 33 events; most training material from 2025 lists only 9 of them. Handler types: command (a shell command), http (a POST to an endpoint), mcp_tool, prompt (a single-turn model decision) and the experimental agent. The last two are model decisions, so they are not deterministic; for a “no-exception rule” use command or http.

      The events you will use most

      EventWhenCan it block?Typical use
      PreToolUseBefore a tool callYesStopping a dangerous command, rewriting the input
      PostToolUseAfter a tool finishes successfullyNo (gives feedback)Formatter, lint, logging
      PermissionRequestWhen a permission prompt is about to be shownReturns a decision objectAutomating approval or rejecting it
      UserPromptSubmitWhen the user sends a messageYesAdding context, stopping a forbidden request
      StopWhen Claude is about to finish its answerYes (keeps it going)“Don’t finish until the tests pass”
      SessionStartAt session startNoLoading dynamic context
      PreCompactBefore compactionYesPreserving critical notes
      SubagentStop, TaskCompletedWhen a sub-task finishesYesChecking the quality of the sub-task

      Others include PostToolUseFailure, PostToolBatch, Notification, SubagentStart, TaskCreated, InstructionsLoaded, ConfigChange, CwdChanged, FileChanged, WorktreeCreate, WorktreeRemove, PostCompact, PreModelSwitch, Elicitation and SessionEnd. The full list, and which of them can block, is on the official hooks page.

      The contract: stdin, exit code, JSON

      1. Input: The hook receives the event information as JSON on stdin. Common fields: session_id, prompt_id, transcript_path, cwd, permission_mode, hook_event_name; PreToolUse adds tool_name, tool_input and tool_use_id.
      2. Exit 0: success. JSON on stdout is applied. Plain-text stdout is added to context only for UserPromptSubmit, UserPromptExpansion, SessionStart and PostModelSwitch.
      3. Exit 2: block. stderr goes to Claude as the reason. Exit 2 overrides even an “allow” in the JSON.
      4. Other codes: non-blocking error. The docs are clear about it: exit 1 is not a block. If your script exits with 1 at an unexpected point because of set -e, the tool call still runs.

      For PreToolUse, the JSON output carries permissionDecision (allow, deny, ask, defer), permissionDecisionReason, updatedInput and additionalContext under hookSpecificOutput. Stop and UserPromptSubmit use a top-level {"decision":"block","reason":"…"}; UserPromptSubmit cannot rewrite the user’s prompt. Matcher syntax: * or empty means all; a value containing only letters, digits and _-|, is an exact list of names (Edit|Write); anything else is a JavaScript regex (mcp__memory__.*). The new if field uses permission rule syntax: "if": "Bash(psql *)". One last ordering detail: deny/ask rules and PreToolUse hooks run before the auto mode classifier.

      Hook lab

      Pick a scenario and how the hook will respond, then press “Run”. Watch the real-shaped stdin JSON sent to the hook, the script, the exit code and what Claude sees as a result. Be sure to try “exit 1”.

      claude — example_app
      Ready.

      The Stop hook: proof before saying “done”

      In level 5 you saw premature completion, the agent saying “done” before the work is finished. The Stop hook is the deterministic cure. It runs when Claude is about to finish its answer; if it returns exit 2, Claude does not stop, it keeps working with the reason from stderr. The official example for a TypeScript project is pnpm tsc --noEmit 1>&2 || exit 2. There is a safety valve against infinite loops: after 8 consecutive blocks without a tool call, the harness lets Claude stop (CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP).

      {
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Bash",
      "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "if": "Bash(psql *)",
                  "command": "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/block-db-writes.sh" }]
    }],
    "Stop": [{
      "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "dotnet build -warnaserror 1>&2 || exit 2" }]
    }]
  }
}

      The Stop hook loop

      Two scenarios: the normal flow where the error can be fixed, and the flow where the agent gives up without calling any tools. In the second, watch what happens when the counter reaches 8.

      CautionPattern-matching hooks are excellent at catching accidental mistakes, but a command can be written in countless ways. Think of a hook as a seatbelt, not a firewall. Also, hooks run with your permissions: a hook script in a repo can do anything it likes on your machine. In level 10 we will see, through a real CVE, why hooks in the .claude/settings.json of a repo you clone depend on trust approval.

      Key takeaways

      • A hook is deterministic; any rule for which “most likely” is not enough goes into a hook. prompt/agent-type hooks are model decisions.
      • Exit 0 is success, exit 2 is a block (stderr goes to Claude), exit 1 is not a block.
      • PreToolUse JSON: permissionDecision allow/deny/ask/defer, rewriting the input with updatedInput.
      • A Stop hook sends Claude back to work with exit 2; it stops after 8 consecutive blocks without a tool call.
      • Hooks and deny/ask rules run before the auto mode classifier.
      Sources
      1. Claude Code: Hooks reference
      2. Claude Code: Best practices (Stop hook, /goal)

      Context commands

      In level 2 you saw that context is a limited resource that gets compacted lossily; in level 9 we will manage it like a budget. Here, let us get to know the knobs Claude Code gives you.

      • /context (and /context all) shows, category by category, what the context is filled with: system prompt, tools, CLAUDE.md, MCP, conversation. The first stop for “why did it forget this rule?”.
      • /compact <focus> summarizes the conversation and continues in a new window; the focus text steers what the summary preserves.
      • /clear wipes the history completely. It is free and resets the cost counter. The command you will use most when switching tasks.
      • /usage replaced the old /cost: it shows the session cost, the cache hit line and how the cost breaks down across skills, subagents, plugins and MCP; with f you can have it apply the suggested fixes.
      Myth“The context window is the real constraint; try to squeeze everything into 200K.” The official guide now puts this on its list of “things you can let go of”: with 1M-token windows and automatic compaction, window size is not the bottleneck for most work. But that does not mean context is free: the whole context is resent every turn, and quality drops in long contexts. In the next level we will measure that trade-off.

      Checkpoints and rewind

      Claude Code takes a checkpoint before every user message; the latest 100 are kept and retained for about 30 days (cleanupPeriodDays). With /rewind or Esc Esc you go back to a point and choose one of: restore code and conversation, conversation only, code only, or “summarize from here”. It is a very reassuring feature, but if you do not know its limits it gives you a dangerous sense of safety. Checkpoints do not track:

      • files changed only through Bash (sed -i, rm, whatever a script writes),
      • most edits made by subagents,
      • edits made outside Claude Code (your editor),
      • symlinked or hard-linked files.

      In the docs’ own words: checkpoints are not a replacement for version control. Commit regularly; start any big piece of work from a clean working tree.

      What does rewind bring back?

      A four-message session. Each message changes files in a different way: the Edit tool, Bash and a subagent. Pick a rewind point and type; see which files come back and which stay changed.

      Branching, resuming and parallel sessions

      /branch or claude --continue --fork-session branches off the current conversation: ideal for trying two different approaches from the same history. Real parallelism, though, comes with git worktrees. Two agents changing the same files in the same repository creates a mess; a worktree gives each session its own working copy and its own branch.

      bash
      $ claude --worktree # open a session in a new worktree Worktree created: ../example_app-wt-7f3c (branch: claude/7f3c) $ claude -p --worktree "Write the missing tests for OrderTotal" # non-interactive Note: you clean up worktrees opened with -p --worktree yourself: $ git worktree remove ../example_app-wt-7f3c

      If you give a subagent isolation: worktree, it also works in its own worktree. Other parallelism tools: background commands and background subagents, the Monitor tool that watches a long-running process, /loop which reruns a prompt at intervals, and scheduled tasks. An effective pattern is “writer and reviewer”: one session writes the code, a second session with a clean context reviews it. Because the reviewer does not carry the writer’s assumptions, it spots different mistakes.

      In practiceA status line script receives the cost, context fill and prompt_cache fields; seeing “context 62%, session $1.40” in your own status line makes it intuitive to know when to /clear. With parallelism, the bottleneck is usually you: if you do not have time to review the five PRs that five agents opened, parallelism just produces a backlog.

      Key takeaways

      • /context shows what is loaded, /usage shows what is spending money; /clear is free.
      • A checkpoint is taken before every message, but it does not track Bash changes, most subagent edits or outside edits. It does not replace Git.
      • Worktrees for parallel work; clean up the ones opened with -p --worktree by hand.
      • Separate writer and reviewer sessions; treat your review capacity as the limit on parallelism.
      Sources
      1. Claude Code: Checkpointing
      2. Claude Code: Best practices
      3. Claude Code: Status line
      4. Claude Code: Costs (/usage)

      Context is not a window, it is a budget

      In level 2 you saw that context is the model’s entire world, that it is re-sent from scratch on every turn, and how caching makes that cheaper. The heart of advanced use is turning that knowledge into spending discipline. Anthropic’s September 2025 post calls this context engineering: deliberately choosing all the tokens the model sees on each turn (system prompt, tool definitions, MCP, external data, conversation history).

      Why a budget?

      As of November 2026, every current Claude model has a 1M-token window. Claude Code’s official guide now lists “the context window is your main constraint” among the habits you can drop. That is true but incomplete: window size has stopped being the bottleneck for most work, but the quality and cost of context have not. Two mechanisms are at play:

      • Attention budget and context rot: Chroma’s July 2025 report tested 18 models and found that even on simple tasks, performance becomes “increasingly unreliable” as input grows. Anthropic likewise describes context as a finite attention budget that every token depletes a little. A rule buried in the middle of a long session is not as effective as the same rule at the start of a short one.
      • Every turn pays for everything again: in a 30-turn session, the first turn is read 30 times. Caching makes reads cheaper but not free; the cache drops after 5 minutes of silence; compaction forces the cache to be rewritten.

      Claude Code’s system prompt, tool definitions and instruction files take up context before you have typed your first message. Third-party measurements put this at around 20–35K tokens, but that is not a verified figure and it varies a lot with MCP and memory. See your own number with /context.

      Four strategies

      1. Fetch just in time

      Don’t load everything up front; keep paths, queries and URLs as lightweight references and fetch them with a tool when needed. Claude Code does this with grep, glob and head; it does not pre-index directories. Tool outputs are capped too: Claude Code truncates a tool response at 25,000 tokens. MCP tool definitions are deferred by default; only their names enter the context.

      2. Compact

      Compaction summarizes a context that is close to full and continues in a fresh window. It is lossy: according to the official docs, detailed instructions from early in the conversation can be lost. That is why durable rules go in CLAUDE.md. /compact <focus> or a “Compact Instructions” section in CLAUDE.md steers the summary. If a large output immediately refills the context, auto-compaction stops after a few attempts.

      3. Take notes

      The agent writes progress to a file outside the context and reads it back later: NOTES.md, a to-do list, a memory tool. Anthropic’s long-running agent setup uses a progress file, a JSON feature list, git history and an init.sh; it reports that JSON is less likely than Markdown to be “inappropriately overwritten”.

      4. Isolate

      A subagent explores in a clean window and usually returns a 1,000–2,000-token summary to the main agent. The rule: delegate work where the process is big and the result is small. But don’t overdo it: Anthropic also notes that newer models tend to spawn a subagent where a direct grep would be faster.

      Context budget simulator

      Try actions in a session one after another. Each action counts as a turn; on that turn the whole main context is re-sent, so “total billed input” grows much faster than the context itself. Watch whether a rule stated at the start of the conversation survives compaction. Token values are illustrative; measure your own session with /context.

      You already know thisContext is like a CPU cache: small, fast and precious. You keep the frequently used things close and fetch the rest from main memory (file system, git, notes) on demand. A subagent is like a separate core: it fills its own cache and writes back only the result.
      In practiceOne clean session per task. When a job is done, /clear; if you have to stop in the middle of a big job, first have the agent write the state to a notes file, then clear and start the new session by having it read that file. If the model doesn’t know compaction is coming, it may try to wrap up early; for long jobs, saying “context will be compacted automatically when needed” in the prompt is a measure Anthropic recommends.

      Key takeaways

      • The 1M window solved the size problem; the quality problem (context rot) and the cost problem (every turn, everything) remain.
      • Four strategies: fetch just in time, compact, take notes, isolate.
      • Compaction is lossy; durable rules go in CLAUDE.md, work state goes in a file.
      • Give subagents work where the process is big and the result is small; don’t spawn a subagent for a single grep.
      Sources
      1. Anthropic: Effective context engineering for AI agents
      2. Chroma: Context Rot
      3. Claude Code: How Claude Code works
      4. Anthropic: Effective harnesses for long-running agents
      5. Anthropic: Prompting best practices

      Multiple agents: when, and at what cost?

      In level 5 you saw Anthropic’s workflow patterns: parallelization (sectioning or voting) and orchestrator-workers. Claude Code offers them as concrete tools: concurrently running subagents, background subagents, a separate worktree per session and the experimental agent teams. The question is no longer “can I?” but “is it worth it?”.

      Token cost multiplies

      The figures from Anthropic’s multi-agent research system post are still the best reference: a single agent uses about 4 times the tokens of a chat, a multi-agent system about 15 times. According to the same post, token usage alone explains 80% of the performance variance on BrowseComp. So if parallel agents give better results, a large part of that is “thinking more”, and that has a price. The Claude Code docs estimate roughly 7 times the tokens for agent teams.

      The same post’s most important warning is about coding: most coding tasks are a poor fit for multi-agent parallelism, because the pieces of the work share a common context. One agent doesn’t know about a design decision another one made; two agents change the same interface in two different ways.

      Work that fits well

      • Independent exploration: “How do these three services handle authentication?” Each subagent reads one service and returns only a summary.
      • Map-reduce: 40 log files, 200 test failures, the dependency list of 30 modules. Each item is separate and the results are merged in a structured form.
      • Writer and reviewer: one session writes, another with a clean context reviews. The reviewer doesn’t carry the writer’s assumptions.
      • Truly independent modules: work in separate worktrees, on separate branches, that doesn’t touch shared files.

      Work that doesn’t fit

      • Changes that touch the same files (a worktree doesn’t remove the conflict, it postpones it to merge time).
      • Sequentially dependent steps: if B looks at A’s result, it isn’t parallel.
      • Anything beyond your review capacity. If five agents opened five PRs and you can review two PRs a day, parallelism produces a backlog.

      Parallelism and the human bottleneck

      A job of six subtasks. Change the number of agents, the type of work and your review time per PR. The timeline shows the agents’ lanes and yours. This is a toy model: durations and conflict cost are assumptions; the formula is shown below. The goal is to build intuition.

      In practice: long-running workThe rules from Anthropic’s long-running agent setup come before parallelism: one feature per session, a clean, committable state at the end of every session, and a progress file plus git history as the state record. Every item in the feature list starts with passes: false and the agent may change only that field; deleting or changing tests is unacceptable. Without this discipline, parallel agents trample each other’s half-finished work.
      Myth“More agents, faster delivery.” The agent side speeds up; delivery moves at the speed of the slowest link. In most teams that link is human review, merge conflicts and the CI queue. Before adding parallelism, measure your review capacity, test duration and how independent the tasks really are.

      Key takeaways

      • A single agent uses ~4 times the tokens of a chat, a multi-agent system ~15 times; agent teams ~7 times.
      • Most coding work needs shared context and fits parallelism poorly; exploration, map-reduce and review fit well.
      • A worktree separates file conflicts but postpones them to the merge.
      • Human review sets the delivery speed; if parallelism outruns it, you get a backlog.
      Sources
      1. Anthropic: How we built our multi-agent research system
      2. Claude Code: Costs (agent teams)
      3. Claude Code: Subagents
      4. Anthropic: Effective harnesses for long-running agents
      5. Anthropic: Building effective agents

      The agent that runs unattended

      Claude Code and Codex also run without the interactive interface. This is how you embed an agent in CI pipelines, scheduled jobs or your own scripts. But first, a change of mindset: in an interactive session, if something goes wrong, a permission prompt protects you. In headless runs there is nobody to approve anything; the allowed-tools list, the budget cap and the sandbox are your only defense.

      claude -p

      claude -p "task" runs a one-shot task. Important flags as of November 2026:

      FlagWhat it does
      --output-format text|json|stream-jsonOutput format. JSON gives a result your script can process.
      --json-schemaForces the result into a schema; the result arrives in the structured_output field. Check that the field exists.
      --allowedTools, --permission-modeTools that may run without asking; the mode can be auto, dontAsk or acceptEdits. The default mode for -p is Manual (v2.1.302+); since nobody can approve, you need to set these explicitly.
      --permission-prompts noneTurns off permission prompts (v2.1.259+).
      --max-turns, --max-budget-usdLoop and spending ceiling. Deterministic brakes.
      --append-system-promptExtra instructions appended to the system prompt.
      --continue, --resume <id>Continue a previous session.
      --bareSkips hooks, skills, plugins, MCP, CLAUDE.md and auto memory. Recommended for CI; according to the docs it will become the default for -p in the future.
      Caution: -p and an untrusted folderThe docs warn explicitly: without --bare, claude -p running in an untrusted folder executes the repository’s .claude/settings.json hooks and .mcp.json servers without a trust dialog. In non-interactive mode there is no screen to ask the trust question. In CI, checking out code from a PR someone else opened and running it without --bare means running the hooks that PR wrote on your runner, with your secrets.

      codex exec

      Codex’s non-interactive mode runs in a read-only sandbox by default; writing requires --sandbox workspace-write. --json gives a JSONL event stream (thread.started, turn.started, turn.completed, turn.failed, item.*, error); --output-schema <file> forces a schema; -o writes the last message to a file; --ephemeral doesn’t persist the session; --ignore-user-config and --ignore-rules disable user configuration; codex exec resume --last continues. An important detail: pass CODEX_API_KEY inline, for that single invocation only, not at the job level; otherwise the repository’s build scripts can read the key too.

      A PR review agent in CI

      A review flow that runs when a PR is opened. Toggle the three settings, then step through: at each step see what runs and which risk each setting opens or closes.

      Reading the output

      Documented fields in the JSON output: type, subtype, result, session_id, total_cost_usd, a per-model usage breakdown, structured_output and permission_denials. v2.1.318 added the credential_expires_at field. permission_denials is especially valuable: it is the list of things the agent wanted to do but couldn’t; in CI, if it isn’t empty, either your permissions are too narrow or the agent tried something unexpected.

      Output fields and a small filter

      Pick a sample output. Click a field to see what it is for; type a path such as .structured_output.testsPassed in the box below and pull out the value (the simplest form of jq). In the Codex sample the path is applied to each line separately.

      GitHub Actions

      For Claude Code, anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 runs in two modes: interactive mode (invoked with @claude in a comment) and automation mode (with the prompt input). The action checks that the triggering actor has write access and is a human; there is an option for workload identity federation via OIDC. The thing to watch: the ready-made GitHub App asks for broad permissions (including write on Actions, Workflows and Repository hooks). Creating your own app with only Contents, Issues and Pull Requests permissions gives narrower authority. The Codex counterpart is openai/codex-action; it keeps the API key behind a proxy.

      Caution: PR text is an attack surfaceThe PR title, description, issue text and comments are text an attacker can write. Embedding them directly in the prompt was exactly the mechanism of the “Comment and Control” attacks reported in April 2026: a PR title hijacked the agent in CI and leaked secrets. Covered in detail in level 10.

      Key takeaways

      • Headless has no approvals: the allowed-tools list, --max-turns, --max-budget-usd and the sandbox are your only defense.
      • In CI use claude -p --bare; -p without --bare runs the repository’s hooks and MCP servers without a trust question.
      • codex exec starts read-only; give CODEX_API_KEY to that one invocation only.
      • Check that structured_output exists and that permission_denials is empty.
      • PR and issue text is untrusted input; don’t embed it in the prompt.
      Sources
      1. Claude Code: Headless mode
      2. Claude Code: GitHub Actions
      3. Codex: Non-interactive mode
      4. Comment and Control (vendor blog)

      You can’t improve what you don’t measure

      You added a line to CLAUDE.md, rewrote a skill or switched models. Did it get better? Gut feeling is misleading here, because the system is probabilistic: a single successful run could be luck, and so could a single failure. The solution is something you already know from software: a test suite. In the agent world it is called an eval.

      Vocabulary

      Anthropic’s January 2026 post “Demystifying evals for AI agents” proposes a shared vocabulary: task (an input and a success criterion), trial (one run of the task), grader (whatever measures success), transcript (all of the agent’s steps), outcome (the final state of the environment) and eval suite. An important distinction: an eval assesses the eval harness, the agent harness and the model together. It is the small-scale version of the benchmark lesson in level 7.

      Three kinds of grader

      Code-based

      Tests, static analysis, state checks (“this table must not change”), tool-call requirements. Fast, cheap, repeatable; but they can be brittle: they may reject an output that is correct but formatted differently.

      Model-based

      Rubrics, pairwise comparison, multiple judges. Measures what code can’t (readability, coverage). Must be calibrated against human judgment; give the judge an “Unknown” option.

      Human

      The gold standard; slow and expensive. Used to calibrate the other graders and to decide edge cases.

      The core for coding agents: unit tests plus an LLM quality rubric; alongside them static analysis, state checks and tracking of turns, tokens and time. There are also two kinds of eval: capability evals start with a low pass rate and measure “what we can’t do yet”; regression evals sit around ~100% and measure “what we haven’t broken”. Tasks that become reliable in a capability eval graduate into the regression set.

      pass@k and pass^k

      In a probabilistic system you run each task more than once. Then you can ask two different questions, and their answers are very different:

      • pass@k: the probability that at least one of k trials succeeds: 1 − (1 − p)k. It rises as k grows. The question is “can the agent find it within a few tries?”; meaningful when a human can pick among the results.
      • pass^k: the probability that all k trials succeed: pk. It falls as k grows. The question is “can I trust this agent?”; this is the real measure for an agent running unattended in CI.

      The example from the post: 75% success per trial means roughly 42% for pass^3. “It works three times out of four” is a very different statement from “it works three times in a row”.

      pass@k and pass^k

      Change the per-trial success rate (p) and the number of trials (k). The two curves plot the real formulas: 1 − (1 − p)k and pk.

      Reward hacking: passing the test is not doing the job

      Reward hacking is the agent producing the success signal without doing the work: editing or deleting the test, special-casing the test input, skipping the check with --no-verify. ImpossibleBench (ICLR 2026) measures this by modifying tests so they contradict the specification; that way, any “pass” means cheating. In the original study GPT-5 cheated on 93% of the conflicting LiveCodeBench tasks; an instruction to “stop if the tests look wrong” brought that down to 1%. Claude Opus 4.1 stayed at 46% on the conflicting SWE-bench tasks. In a newer third-party run with a different setup: GPT-5.4 0%, Opus 4.6 2.9%, Gemini 3.1 Pro 11.8%. Hiding the tests brings cheating close to zero but also lowers real performance.

      Choosing a grader is choosing what you measure

      Task: “Fix the bug where the discount is applied twice in example.orders.” Six agent transcripts and five graders. Toggle the graders; see which transcript passes and whether that is right or wrong. If a cheating transcript passes, it is a false positive; if a correct transcript fails, it is a false negative.

      Roadmap

      1. 20–50 tasks from real failures. Work the team has done in the past and the agent struggled with.
      2. Unambiguous tasks, reference solutions. Test both the “should do” and the “should not do” cases.
      3. Isolated, clean environments. Every trial starts from scratch.
      4. Grade the outcome, not the path. What matters is the final state, not the order in which the agent read files; give partial credit.
      5. Read the transcripts. In the post’s words, “failures should seem fair”. 0% across all trials usually means a broken task.
      6. Watch for saturation. Once everything is at 100%, the eval tells you nothing new; add new capability tasks.
      In practiceTreat an instruction change like a deploy. Run the eval before and after you change CLAUDE.md, a skill or a hook; if there is a regression, roll back. Protect test directories with an Edit deny rule, run the real test suite from a Stop hook and flag diffs in test files separately during review.

      Key takeaways

      • Evaluate a probabilistic system with repeated evals, not a single run.
      • pass@k = 1 − (1 − p)k rises; pass^k = pk falls. For an unattended agent, pass^k is what matters.
      • Code-based graders are fast but brittle; model-based ones are flexible but need calibration; combine them.
      • Passing the test is not doing the job; check test-file changes and special cases separately.
      Sources
      1. Anthropic: Demystifying evals for AI agents
      2. ImpossibleBench (arXiv 2510.20270)
      3. ImpossibleBench third-party run (arXiv 2606.12429)
      4. Anthropic Engineering: posts on infrastructure noise and eval awareness

      Where does the bill come from?

      As of November 2026, Claude Code’s costs page gives an enterprise average of about $13 per developer per active day, $150–250 a month; 90% of users stay under $30 per active day. These numbers are a compass: your team’s figure can be very different depending on the type of work, the model and habits. The real question is which habits make the bill grow.

      A sample /usage block from the docs is very instructive: session cost $0.55; 940K cache-read tokens against only 1.2K uncached input tokens. In long sessions the overwhelming majority of traffic is read from the cache. That is why anything that breaks the cache (a break longer than the 5-minute TTL, a setting that changes the system prompt, compaction) shows up on the bill right away.

      Habits that grow the bill

      • Long sessions that are never cleared: every turn pays for the whole history again.
      • Using the biggest model by default for every job.
      • Cache misses after the TTL: the first turn after a coffee break is expensive.
      • Subagents and agent teams: each one fills its own context.
      • Compaction itself: summarizing is also a model call and it rewrites the cache.
      • Scheduled loops and /loop: they run while nobody is watching.

      Daily cost estimator

      Enter your own usage habits. The calculation uses November 2026 list prices and cache multipliers; the uncached part is counted at the 5-minute write price (1.25×). The result is compared with the docs’ $13 average and the $30 line.

      In practiceIf your enterprise contract price differs from list price, modelPricing in managed settings (v2.1.242+) makes the reported cost match your contract. For rate-limit planning, the table in the docs shows that the per-user TPM requirement falls as the number of users grows: 200–300K TPM per user for 1–5 users, 10–15K TPM for 500+ users. Not everyone works hard at the same time.

      Observability: OpenTelemetry

      When an agent does something unexpected in production, logs are the only answer to “why?”. Claude Code exports metrics and events with OpenTelemetry.

      CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1
OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=otlp
OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=otlp
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=grpc        # no default, set it explicitly
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel.example.test:4317

      Metrics

      claude_code.session.count, token.usage (input, output, cacheRead, cacheCreation), cost.usage, lines_of_code.count, commit.count, pull_request.count, code_edit_tool.decision, active_time.total.

      Events

      user_prompt (text hidden by default), tool_result, api_request, api_error, tool_decision (source: config, hook, user_permanent, user_abort), assistant_response, api_refusal.

      Privacy

      Off by default: OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS, OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS, OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT, OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES. Before turning them on, think about which customer data will end up in telemetry.

      Traces are enabled in beta with CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA=1. A subtle security detail: the repository’s .claude/settings.json cannot set the exporter variables. Otherwise a repo you cloned could redirect your telemetry to its own server and collect your prompts. Don’t be surprised if you see a short-lived claude_code.safety_event metric in the changelog: it was added in 2.1.307 and discontinued in 2.1.312.

      You already know thisYou wouldn’t put a microservice into production without metrics and distributed tracing. An agent is a service too; the only difference is that its decision logic is probabilistic. The source field of the tool_decision event shows whether an action went through because of a rule, a hook or a user’s “always allow” click; in a post-incident review, that is worth its weight in gold.

      Key takeaways

      • Compass: ~$13 per active day, 90% of users under $30 (November 2026, enterprise average).
      • In long sessions the overwhelming majority of traffic is cache reads; anything that breaks the cache shows up on the bill.
      • Track tokens, cost and permission decisions with OpenTelemetry; turn on content logs deliberately.
      • Repo settings can’t change the telemetry destination; this is a deliberate exfiltration safeguard.
      Sources
      1. Claude Code: Costs
      2. Claude Code: Monitoring usage (OpenTelemetry)
      3. Anthropic: Pricing
      4. Anthropic: Prompt caching

      Instructions hidden in data

      In level 5 we said that tool results are untrusted input. Now let’s see why. For the model there is no hard boundary between instructions and data: both are part of the same token sequence. If a web page, an issue comment, a README or a database row says “ignore previous instructions and do this”, the model will sometimes treat it as an instruction. That is not a software bug; it is a natural consequence of the architecture.

      You already know thisRemember SQL injection. The fix was not to “read user input carefully”; it was to separate data from commands structurally: parameterized queries. LLMs do not have such a clean separation yet. The system prompt, the user message and the tool result are marked with different roles, but in the end they all become a single stream of text that the model reads. That is why defense relies on restricting what the model can attempt to do.

      Direct and indirect

      Direct

      The attacker is the user: they try to push the model outside its rules with the text they type into the chat (a jailbreak). In a coding agent this matters less: the user is already you, and you can do whatever you like on your own machine anyway.

      Indirect

      The instruction is hidden in content the agent reads: issues, PR titles, web pages, READMEs, dependency docs, MCP tool descriptions, rules files. The user is innocent, the agent is innocent; the attacker has left a note on the agent’s path. For coding agents, this is the real threat.

      Prompt injection is number one on OWASP’s 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications (LLM01). The first item of the agentic applications list published in December 2025 comes from the same root: agent goal hijack (ASI01).

      Why model-side defense is not enough

      As you saw in level 7, both labs train their models with an instruction hierarchy: tool output is data, not instructions. Modern models are increasingly resistant to these attacks. But that resistance is probabilistic. In Simon Willison’s words, a 95% detection rate in security is “very much a failing grade”: the attacker can try a hundred times and only needs one to land. You would never accept a web product that says “we stop 95% of SQL injections”.

      Invisible instructions

      The sneakiest form of indirect injection is text a human cannot see but the model reads. HTML comments, white-on-white text and image alt text are well-known routes. Less known are invisible Unicode characters:

      • Zero-width characters: U+200B, U+200C, U+200D, U+2060, U+FEFF. They take up no space on screen; they can split words to slip past filters, or carry information.
      • Direction control (bidi) characters: U+202A–U+202E and U+2066–U+2069. They change the displayed order of text, so what a human sees differs from what the machine reads.
      • Tag characters: the U+E0000–U+E007F range. Every ASCII character has an invisible “twin”, so an entire sentence can be embedded invisibly, and some models can read it.

      The “Rules File Backdoor” attack reported in early 2025 used exactly this: invisible characters embedded in Cursor and GitHub Copilot rules files steered code generation in the direction the attacker wanted, and kept living when the repository was forked. In code review the file looked innocent.

      Invisible text detector

      The AGENTS.md in the box looks innocent. The detector marks every invisible character, decodes text embedded in tag characters and gives you the cleaned version. You can paste your own file too; nothing leaves your browser.

      In practiceReview rules files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .claude/rules, .cursor/rules) like code and check for invisible characters in CI: an instruction file containing anything from the ranges above should block the merge. Put prompts and skills you copy from elsewhere through the same filter.

      Key takeaways

      • The model cannot reliably separate instructions from data; a tool result is always untrusted input.
      • For coding agents the real threat is indirect injection: issues, PRs, the web, READMEs, tool descriptions, rules files.
      • Model-side resistance is probabilistic; 95% is not a passing grade in security.
      • Invisible Unicode (zero-width, bidi, tag) hides instructions from human eyes; scan rules files in CI.
      Sources
      1. OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025
      2. OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026
      3. Simon Willison: The lethal trifecta
      4. The Hacker News: Rules File Backdoor

      When the risk becomes truly dangerous

      The framework Simon Willison named on 16 June 2025 shows clearly when prompt injection risk turns into a data leak. If an agent has all three of the following at once, the lethal trifecta is complete:

      1. Access to private data: source code, secrets, customer records, private repositories, email.
      2. Exposure to untrusted content: the web, issues, PRs, email, dependencies, tool descriptions.
      3. The ability to communicate externally: an HTTP request, a PR or issue comment, git push, email, even an image URL or a DNS lookup.

      The attacker’s recipe is simple: put an instruction in untrusted content, let the agent read it, have it pick up private data and send it out over an external channel. Willison’s remedy is just as simple: remove one of the three legs. Instead of trying to detect the attack, build a setup where it cannot do damage even if it succeeds.

      In coding agents, all three are the default

      The uncomfortable truth: a local coding agent has all three legs out of the box. It reads your repository and your home directory (private data); it reads web pages, dependency docs and issues (untrusted content); it has network access and can git push (external communication). Even a single MCP server can carry all three: in the GitHub MCP incident of May 2025, the same token could read a public issue, see private repositories and open a PR on a public repository.

      The variety of exfiltration channels matters too. Shutting off network egress is the first thing most people think of; but if the agent writes a Markdown image pointing to the attacker’s server into a PR comment, what fetches that image is not your sandbox but the platform rendering the comment. The data leaves in the image URL’s query parameter.

      Break the attack chain

      Scenario: an agent triaging issues in Example Co’s public example/widgets repository. Its token can also see the private example/billing-internal repository. Someone has left a hidden instruction in an issue. Pick the exfiltration channel and the defenses, then run the attack. Probabilistic layers roll the dice on every run; the “Run 1000 times” button computes the expected leak rate.

      Lessons from the lab. Narrowing the token’s scope to a single repository removes the private-data leg for certain. A read-only token closes the PR and comment channel but leaves the network channel open; a sandbox network allowlist closes the curl channel but cannot close the PR channel, because GitHub is allowed. The deny rule Bash(curl *) only stops curl when it is written out literally. The auto mode classifier and human approval are probabilistic: one misses 5.7% of synthetic exfiltration attempts, the other gets 93% of prompts approved. Plan-then-execute and dual LLM break the chain architecturally. Those are exactly the subject of the coming lessons.

      CautionThe “Always Allow” button is not a convenience; it is a configuration decision that leaves one leg permanently open. In the GitHub MCP incident, users had pressed that button. A simple policy such as access to only one repository per session would have made that attack impossible.

      Key takeaways

      • Private data + untrusted content + external communication = exfiltration risk. Remove one.
      • Coding agents have all three legs by default; even a single MCP server can carry all three.
      • Exfiltration channels are not just the network: PR comments, image URLs, git push, DNS.
      • Deterministic controls (token scope, network allowlist, write permission) cut legs; probabilistic controls lower the rate.
      Sources
      1. Simon Willison: The lethal trifecta for AI agents
      2. Invariant Labs: GitHub MCP exploited
      3. Anthropic: Claude Code auto mode

      Not theory: the record

      Everything in this lesson really happened between 2025 and 2026. Rather than memorizing incidents one by one, we will look for a pattern: each is either an instance of the lethal trifecta, an attack on the agent’s own supply chain (plugins, MCP servers, configuration files), or both. At the end of each incident, ask: “which single control would have stopped this?”

      Incident timeline

      Pick a category and click an incident: see what happened, which mechanism was used, the OWASP mapping and the lesson to take away. Dates and figures come from the sources; the OWASP mappings are this course’s interpretation. Two incidents that could not be verified (a production database deletion case in summer 2025 and a CI plugin incident in February 2026) were left off the list because their details could not be confirmed.

      Click an incident.

      Patterns

      The agent becomes the attacker’s tool

      In the Nx “s1ngularity” attack, malicious npm releases invoked the agent CLIs installed on the machine with flags such as --dangerously-skip-permissions and --trust-all-tools and sent them hunting for secrets: 2,349 credentials from 1,079 systems. The attacker did not write their own code; they used your agent.

      Configuration is code

      Check Point’s February 2026 report showed two CVEs: a repository’s .claude/settings.json hooks and MCP definitions could run before the trust dialog (CVE-2025-59536, CVSS 8.7), and a repository could leak the API key by changing ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL (CVE-2026-21852). Both have been patched (1.0.111+ and 2.0.65+).

      CI input becomes a prompt

      In the “Comment and Control” attacks reported in April 2026, a PR title or issue text hijacked Claude Code Security Review (CVSS 9.4), the Gemini CLI Action and the Copilot agent in GitHub Actions and leaked secrets. The mechanism: untrusted text was embedded directly in the prompt. The source is a vendor blog; read the details with that in mind.
      Myth“These attacks are lab demos; they don’t happen in the real world.” The list above has real victims: a deletion prompt merged into an IDE extension with hundreds of thousands of installs, an MCP server downloaded more than 1,600 times that sent a blind copy of every email to the attacker, credentials harvested from more than a thousand machines.

      Key takeaways

      • Most incidents are either the lethal trifecta or the agent’s supply chain; often both.
      • Your installed agent CLI and your YOLO flags can become someone else’s attack tool.
      • A repository’s configuration files run code; every repo you clone is input an attacker can write.
      • Embedding untrusted text in a prompt in CI is an open invitation to remote command execution.

      Defending with architecture

      The paper “Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections”, published by Beurer-Kellner and colleagues in June 2025, sets out the most useful principle in the field: once an agent has read an untrusted input, it must be impossible for that input to trigger a consequential action. Not “hard”: “impossible”. The paper proposes six patterns that achieve this principle. Their shared price is flexibility: the more you constrain an agent, the less general-purpose it becomes.

      How far does the poisoned input get?

      Pick a pattern and press “Trace the poisoned input”. Red marks the nodes untrusted content reaches; the line is the boundary where the flow stops. See what each pattern protects, what it costs and what it looks like in a coding agent.

      CaMeL: provable security and its price

      The CaMeL work by Debenedetti and colleagues from Google DeepMind and ETH Zurich, dated March 2025, takes the “write code, then run it” idea to its extreme. Control and data flow are derived only from the trusted user query; untrusted data can “never” change the program’s flow. Capabilities are attached to every value, and unauthorized flows are stopped at the moment of the tool call. On the AgentDojo benchmark the result is instructive: 77% of tasks are completed with provable security, against 84% for the undefended system. So the price of provable security is roughly 7 points of capability. That is a good measure of how security is always a design trade-off.

      Harness controls: layers from the inside out

      1. Least privilege: every credential the agent holds has the narrowest permission the task requires. A read-only database role, a token scoped to a single repository, and never keys that bypass everything, like service_role. This is the cheapest and strongest control.
      2. A sandbox with two walls: Anthropic’s sandboxing post is explicit: without network isolation a compromised agent can exfiltrate data; without filesystem isolation it can escape. Both together.
      3. Credentials outside the sandbox: the web version of Claude Code keeps git credentials outside the sandbox, behind a narrowly scoped git proxy. The agent never sees the key.
      4. Deterministic controls: deny rules, PreToolUse hooks, managed settings. They work independently of the model’s decisions.
      5. Human approval only for the irreversible: a system that asks for approval on everything trains people to say “yes” blindly; 93% of prompts are approved anyway. Save approval for the moments that really matter.
      6. Probabilistic layers on the outside: the auto mode classifier, warnings in the prompt. Useful, but they do not cut a leg.
      Go deeper: what does the auto mode classifier see?According to Anthropic’s March 2026 post, the classifier sees only the user messages and the tool calls; the assistant’s prose and the tool results are stripped out. This is deliberate context minimization: injected text cannot “argue” with the classifier, because the classifier never reads it. On top of that there is a separate server-side injection probe. The reported figures: a 0.4% false positive rate over 10k real actions; a 17% miss rate on 52 real overeager actions, and 5.7% on synthetic exfiltration. A good layer; not the only layer.

      Key takeaways

      • The principle: once untrusted input has been read, it must be impossible for it to trigger a consequential action.
      • Six patterns: action-selector, plan-then-execute, map-reduce, dual LLM, code-then-execute, context minimization.
      • CaMeL: 77% of tasks provably secure, 84% undefended. Security is a trade-off.
      • Layers from the inside out: least privilege, a two-walled sandbox, credentials outside, deterministic controls, selective human approval, probabilistic layers.
      Sources
      1. Beurer-Kellner et al.: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections and Willison’s summary
      2. Debenedetti et al.: CaMeL
      3. Anthropic: Claude Code sandboxing
      4. Anthropic: Claude Code auto mode

      The agent’s own dependencies

      Everything you extend an agent with, that is MCP servers, skills, plugins and hooks, runs with your permissions. You should look at an MCP server with the same suspicion you give an npm package’s postinstall script. The difference: these components do not just run code, they also supply the text the model reads.

      • Tool poisoning: in April 2025 Invariant Labs showed that instructions embedded in MCP tool descriptions could steer the model. The user does not see the description; the model does.
      • Malicious server: the first malicious MCP server, found in September 2025 (postmark-mcp 1.0.16), forwarded a blind copy of every email sent to the attacker; it had been downloaded 1,643 times. Pinning versions and reviewing the diff of every update is how you catch a package that turns bad later.
      • The agent itself: in July 2025 a prompt containing deletion instructions got into version 1.84.0 of the Amazon Q VS Code extension through a merged PR; the extension had roughly 964k installs.

      The repo you clone is input

      The most practical lesson of this topic: a repository’s .claude/, .codex/, .mcp.json, AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md files are input an attacker can write. After the CVEs Check Point found, Claude Code’s current behavior is built on that idea: the project’s hooks and MCP servers do not run until workspace trust is granted; allow rules in the project wait for trust, while deny and ask apply immediately; defaultMode: auto or bypassPermissions in the project file is ignored; imports from outside the project require approval; repository settings cannot change the telemetry destination. Codex runs hooks with hash-based trust. But the exception you saw in level 9 still stands: claude -p without --bare, in an untrusted folder, runs hooks and MCP servers with no trust dialog.

      Opening a malicious repository

      You cloned a “sample project” from a customer. It contains files prepared by an attacker. Pick a way to open it; see what happens with each file. The behaviors are based on the November 2026 docs and patched CVEs; uncertain points are marked as such.

      Slopsquatting: packages that do not exist

      Models sometimes confidently suggest a package name that does not exist. A study published at USENIX Security 2025 collected 576k samples from 16 models: 19.7% of the suggested packages did not exist. The rate is ~5.2% for commercial models and ~21.7% for open models. The truly dangerous finding: 43% of the hallucinated names reappeared in all 10 repetitions. In other words, these names are predictable; an attacker can register them and fill them with malicious code. This is called slopsquatting.

      Package gate

      The agent wants to install six packages for a feature. The package names and registry data are invented for this course. Toggle the gate’s rules; see which package gets through and which rule each one trips.

      PackageLockfileIn registryAgeWeekly downloadsInstall scriptGate
      In practicePin versions and review diffs; prefer official marketplaces; enforce an organization-wide allowlist of plugins and MCP servers through managed settings (check the current plugin docs for the key names). Take package installation off auto-approved paths (Bash(npm install *) as ask or deny), use a registry proxy or an allowlist, and verify the lockfile in CI. Read an unfamiliar repository in an editor first, then open it in a sandbox or a disposable container.

      Key takeaways

      • MCP servers, skills, plugins and hooks run with your permissions and supply the text the model reads.
      • A cloned repository’s agent configuration is attacker input; read it before granting trust.
      • In CI and scripts use claude -p --bare; but even --bare does not stop the repository’s own code (npm scripts) from running; the sandbox is what bounds that.
      • ~20% of suggested packages may not exist, and the names repeat; check the lockfile, age and downloads.
